distractor_mistakes.A: reads the row one step below the conductor size
distractor_mistakes.C: applies an electrode conductor limit to a bonding jumper
distractor_mistakes.D: reads the row one step above the conductor size

explanation: The correct answer is B (2 AWG copper, from the row for ungrounded conductors over 3/0 through 350 kcmil): The main bonding jumper is sized from the table using the size of the ungrounded service conductors. A 4/0 AWG copper conductor sits in the row over 3/0 through 350 kcmil, which calls for 2 AWG copper. The 4 AWG answer reads the row for smaller conductors, and the 1/0 AWG answer reads the next row up. The 6 AWG figure is an electrode conductor limit and has no role in bonding jumper sizing.

question: A single building holds several tenant suites under one roof. The design provides each tenant with its own service disconnecting means, grouped at one location. A tenant asks who must be able to reach each disconnect. Which statement matches the NEC for multiple-occupancy buildings?

options.A: Every occupant must reach every disconnect in the group, so all tenants share one access key
options.B: Management alone must reach each tenant disconnect, because the grouped location is common space
options.C: Each occupant must reach their own disconnect, unless management supervision applies
options.D: Each occupant must reach their own disconnect, which must be located inside the occupant's own suite

distractor_mistakes.A: gives every tenant access to every disconnect
distractor_mistakes.B: treats the management exception as the general rule
distractor_mistakes.D: requires the disconnect to be inside each suite

explanation: The correct answer is C (Each occupant must reach their own disconnect, unless management supervision applies): In a multiple-occupancy building each occupant must have access to the occupant's own service disconnecting means. The exception allows management-only access where building management supplies power and maintenance under continuous supervision. That exception is not the general rule. The disconnects may be grouped at one location, so the code does not require them to sit inside each suite, and it does not give each tenant access to every disconnect.

question: In a mechanical room, a panelboard has equipment doors that can swing open to 120 degrees. The installer is checking whether the open doors block the required egress path from the working space. Under the 2026 NEC, how is the 24 inch wide, 6.5 foot high egress path measured?

options.A: With equipment doors open to 90 degrees, even if they can swing farther
options.B: With the doors fully open at their maximum swing of 120 degrees from the wall
options.C: With the doors closed, since open doors are only a temporary condition
options.D: With the doors open to 45 degrees, the typical position for servicing

distractor_mistakes.B: measures at the maximum swing instead of the 90 degree reference
distractor_mistakes.C: measures with doors closed, ignoring the open-door condition
distractor_mistakes.D: uses an invented 45 degree servicing position

explanation: The correct answer is A (With equipment doors open to 90 degrees, even if they can swing farther): The 2026 NEC says equipment doors must not impede the required egress path, 24 inches wide and 6.5 feet high, when opened to 90 degrees. The measurement is made at 90 degrees even if the doors can open farther. Checking with the doors closed ignores the working condition the rule is aimed at. Using a larger swing or a smaller one does not match the 90 degree reference point.

question: A hospital campus building has one normal service. The owner adds a fire pump and wants it fed from a separate service, with its own service disconnecting means, instead of from the main. The utility agrees to supply it. Which NEC provision allows this second service to the same building?

options.A: None, because the code limits a building to one service even when the utility agrees
options.B: The capacity rule, which permits extra services only above 2,000 amperes of load
options.C: The special-conditions rule for additional services, which names fire pumps and emergency systems
options.D: The different-characteristics rule, which permits extra services only for another voltage or phase

distractor_mistakes.A: claims one service is the limit in every case
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the capacity rule instead of the special-conditions rule
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the different-characteristics rule when characteristics match

explanation: The correct answer is C (The special-conditions rule for additional services, which names fire pumps and emergency systems): Article 230 allows additional services for special conditions, and the list includes fire pumps, emergency systems and standby systems. A fire pump therefore qualifies for its own service without any load threshold. The 2,000 ampere capacity rule is a separate basis for extra services and does not apply here. The different-characteristics rule needs another voltage, frequency or phase, which the stem does not describe.

question: Six normal service disconnects are grouped in the main electrical room of a shopping center. The design adds a seventh disconnect that supplies only a fire pump, mounted in a separate room at the far end of the building. How does the NEC treat this seventh disconnect?

options.A: Not acceptable, because six is the limit for service disconnects of any type or purpose
options.B: Acceptable, since it is installed remote from the normal service disconnects
options.C: Acceptable only if it is mounted in the same group beside the six
options.D: Acceptable only if the fire pump disconnect is rated 100 amperes or less

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the six disconnect limit to fire pump disconnects
distractor_mistakes.C: requires grouping when the rule requires remoteness
distractor_mistakes.D: invents a rating limit for the fire pump disconnect

explanation: The correct answer is B (Acceptable, since it is installed remote from the normal service disconnects): Additional service disconnects for fire pumps and emergency systems are not counted among the one to six normal disconnects. They must be installed sufficiently remote from the normal service disconnects to limit the chance of both being interrupted at once. Placing it beside the six would defeat that purpose. The six-disconnect limit applies to normal service, and the rating of the pump disconnect does not decide the matter.

question: Plans for a new 120/240 volt, single-phase dwelling call for a 400 ampere service. The designer asks whether the service-entrance conductors must have ampacity equal to the full 400 ampere rating or may use the dwelling allowance. Which statement gives the minimum ampacity for dwelling service conductors in this range?

options.A: At least 100 percent of the 400 ampere rating, since no reduced allowance exists for dwellings
options.B: At least 125 percent of the 400 ampere rating, to cover continuous use of the service
options.C: At least 83 percent of the service rating, for dwelling services rated 100 through 400 amperes
options.D: At least 80 percent of the service rating, the same factor that limits branch circuit loading

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the general rule when the specific dwelling rule governs
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the continuous-load factor to the service rating
distractor_mistakes.D: borrows the 80 percent branch-circuit loading figure

explanation: The correct answer is C (At least 83 percent of the service rating, for dwelling services rated 100 through 400 amperes): The specific dwelling-unit rule permits service-entrance conductors for 120/240 volt single-phase dwelling services rated 100 through 400 amperes to have ampacity of at least 83 percent of the service rating. For 400 amperes that is 332 amperes. The general rule of full rating applies when the specific allowance does not, and the specific rule governs here. The 125 percent factor applies to continuous loads, and 80 percent is a branch-circuit loading limit, not a service conductor factor.

question: Three parallel sets of 350 kcmil copper conductors per phase make up a 1,200 ampere service. The electrician sizes the copper grounding electrode conductor to a metal underground water pipe, using the grounding electrode conductor table. Using the combined area of the paralleled conductors, what minimum copper size is required?

options.A: 2/0 AWG copper, from the row for over 600 through 1100 kcmil
options.B: 2 AWG copper, from the row for a single 350 kcmil conductor
options.C: 3/0 AWG copper, from the row for over 1100 kcmil of total conductor area
options.D: 1/0 AWG copper, from the row for a total area over 350 through 600 kcmil

distractor_mistakes.B: sizes from one conductor instead of the combined area
distractor_mistakes.C: reads the row for over 1100 kcmil total area
distractor_mistakes.D: reads a row below the combined area

explanation: The correct answer is A (2/0 AWG copper, from the row for over 600 through 1100 kcmil): When ungrounded conductors are paralleled, the grounding electrode conductor is sized from the total circular mil area of one phase. Three sets of 350 kcmil add up to 1,050 kcmil. That falls in the table row over 600 through 1100 kcmil, which requires 2/0 AWG copper. Using a single 350 kcmil conductor undersizes the result, and 3/0 AWG applies only above 1100 kcmil.

question: Open service conductors pass a second-floor window designed to be opened. The conductors run horizontally 30 inches from the window edge. Without changing the conductor type, how much farther must the run be moved to meet the minimum clearance from windows that open?

options.A: 6 inches, to reach the 3 foot minimum
options.B: 18 inches, to reach the 4 foot figure used for ladders
options.C: None, because 30 inches already meets the minimum for operable windows
options.D: 30 inches, to reach a 5 foot distance from the window edge

distractor_mistakes.B: uses an invented 4 foot figure for window clearance
distractor_mistakes.C: believes 30 inches is the minimum
distractor_mistakes.D: uses an invented 5 foot window clearance

explanation: The correct answer is A (6 inches, to reach the 3 foot minimum): Service conductors installed as open conductors must keep at least 3 feet from windows designed to be opened, as well as doors, porches, balconies and similar locations. The run is at 30 inches, so it falls 6 inches short of 36 inches. No other distance in the options is the governing minimum for this situation. The conductors would have to go above the top level of the window only if the clearance were met another way.

question: On a service with 500 kcmil copper ungrounded conductors, grounding is to a ground ring made of bare 2 AWG copper encircling the building. The grounding electrode conductor connects only to the ring. What is the minimum copper size of the grounding electrode conductor?

options.A: 1/0 AWG copper, from the row for 500 kcmil service conductors
options.B: 6 AWG copper, the limit for a sole connection to a rod
options.C: 2 AWG copper, which need not exceed the size of the ring conductor
options.D: 4 AWG copper, the limit for a sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode

distractor_mistakes.A: reads the table and skips the ring conductor limit
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the rod-only limit to a ground ring
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the concrete-encased limit to a ground ring

explanation: The correct answer is C (2 AWG copper, which need not exceed the size of the ring conductor): The table gives 1/0 AWG copper for 500 kcmil service conductors, but a grounding electrode conductor to a ground ring is not required to be larger than the ring conductor. The ring is 2 AWG copper, so 2 AWG is the minimum. The 6 AWG and 4 AWG limits apply to rods and concrete-encased electrodes only. Reading the table without the ring limit would oversize the conductor.

question: A homeowner upgrades the service disconnect from 100 to 200 amperes and wants to reuse the existing meter socket marked 100 amperes to save cost. The utility has not objected. What must the electrician confirm about the existing meter socket?

options.A: That the socket rating matches the original 100 ampere disconnect, because the utility owns it
options.B: That only the socket jaws, not the enclosure, are rated for 200 amperes
options.C: That the socket is listed and marked for at least the 200 ampere service rating
options.D: That the socket rating is no higher than the feeder serving the panel

distractor_mistakes.A: treats utility ownership as a reason to ignore the rating
distractor_mistakes.B: splits the rating between jaws and enclosure
distractor_mistakes.D: limits the socket rating to the feeder, which reverses the requirement

explanation: The correct answer is C (That the socket is listed and marked for at least the 200 ampere service rating): Service equipment, including a meter socket, must be listed and used within its marked rating. A socket marked 100 amperes cannot carry a 200 ampere service. The socket must be rated at least equal to the new service. Utility ownership does not change the rating limit, and a socket rating limited to the feeder size works backward.

question: On the panel schedule, six individually mounted disconnects, each serving a different tenant, together form the service disconnecting means of a building. The inspector asks how the NEC requires these disconnects to be arranged and identified. What does the code require?

options.A: They must be grouped together, and each must be marked with its ampere rating and voltage
options.B: They must be grouped inside one enclosure, with each disconnect marked for the load it serves
options.C: They must be grouped, and each must be marked with the tenant name and unit address
options.D: They must be grouped together, and each must be marked with the load it serves

distractor_mistakes.A: marks each disconnect with a rating instead of the load served
distractor_mistakes.B: requires one enclosure when separate enclosures are allowed
distractor_mistakes.C: identifies the tenant instead of the load served

explanation: The correct answer is D (They must be grouped together, and each must be marked with the load it serves): Section 230.71 allows the disconnecting means to be up to six switches or breakers, and Section 230.72 requires them to be grouped. Each one must be marked to indicate the load it serves. A rating or voltage marking does not tell a worker what the disconnect controls, and a tenant name does not identify the load. A group of separate enclosures is allowed, so a single enclosure is not required.

question: For a one-family dwelling, a journeyman totals the service load at 42,000 VA on a 240 volt, single-phase supply. None of the load is continuous. She needs the smallest standard overcurrent device rating that carries the calculated load. Which rating from the standard list should she choose?

options.A: 150 amperes, rounding the 175 ampere calculated result down to a standard size
options.B: 225 amperes, applying 125 percent to the 175 ampere result before choosing the size above
options.C: 175 amperes, from 42,000 VA divided by 240 volts, already a standard size
options.D: 350 amperes, from dividing 42,000 VA by 120 volts

distractor_mistakes.A: rounds down below the calculated load
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the continuous-load factor to a noncontinuous load
distractor_mistakes.D: divides by 120 volts instead of 240 volts

explanation: The correct answer is C (175 amperes, from 42,000 VA divided by 240 volts, already a standard size): Single-phase current equals volt-amperes divided by voltage, so 42,000 divided by 240 equals 175 amperes. No part of the load is continuous, so no 125 percent factor applies. 175 amperes is itself a standard size, so it is the smallest rating that carries the load. Rounding down to 150 amperes overloads the device, and 350 amperes comes from using 120 volts.

question: Service at 480Y/277 volts, 3-phase, 4-wire, solidly grounded, has a 2,000 ampere main overcurrent device in a new warehouse electrical room. The engineer must set the required equipment ground-fault protection. What is the maximum ground-fault pickup setting the NEC permits for this service?

options.A: 2,000 amperes, equal to the main device rating
options.B: 1,000 amperes, the rating at which protection first becomes required
options.C: 600 amperes, set at 30 percent of the main device rating
options.D: 1,200 amperes, the maximum pickup permitted for ground-fault protection of equipment

distractor_mistakes.A: sets pickup equal to the main device rating
distractor_mistakes.B: confuses the requirement threshold with the setting limit
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a percentage of the main device that the rule does not contain

explanation: The correct answer is D (1,200 amperes, the maximum pickup permitted for ground-fault protection of equipment): Ground-fault protection of equipment is required on solidly grounded wye services of more than 150 volts to ground, up to 1000 volts phase to phase, rated 1000 amperes or more. The maximum pickup setting is 1,200 amperes, regardless of the main device rating. A 2,000 ampere setting would exceed that cap. The 1,000 ampere figure is the threshold that triggers the requirement, not a setting limit.

question: To reach a storage building, a service lateral will run in Schedule 40 PVC conduit beneath an open lawn, with no driveway, building or slab above it. The trench is being excavated. What minimum cover does the burial table require for this wiring method and location?

options.A: 24 inches, the cover for direct-buried cables under open ground
options.B: 6 inches, the cover for rigid metal conduit under open ground
options.C: 18 inches, the cover for nonmetallic raceways listed for direct burial under open ground
options.D: 12 inches, the cover for residential 120 volt GFCI-protected branch circuits

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the direct-buried cable depth for a raceway
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the rigid metal conduit depth for PVC
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a residential branch-circuit depth for a service lateral

explanation: The correct answer is C (18 inches, the cover for nonmetallic raceways listed for direct burial under open ground): The burial table gives 18 inches of cover for rigid nonmetallic conduit listed for direct burial, such as Schedule 40 PVC, under open ground. Direct-buried cables need 24 inches, and rigid metal conduit needs only 6 inches. The 12 inch figure belongs to certain residential 120 volt branch circuits with GFCI protection, not to a service lateral. The wiring method and location together decide the column and the depth.

question: Outside a new one-family dwelling, an emergency disconnect hangs on the exterior wall. The electrician labeled it with a handwritten tag in permanent ink reading MAIN, and the inspector asks for a correction. Under the 2026 NEC marking rules, how must this disconnect be marked?

options.A: SERVICE DISCONNECT on a permanent plate, as for all dwelling disconnects
options.B: MAIN in permanent handwriting, since weather-resistant ink is acceptable
options.C: EMERGENCY DISCONNECT in white on a red background, at least 1/2 inch high
options.D: EMERGENCY DISCONNECT in black letters on a yellow background, at least 1 inch high

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the marking for other occupancies
distractor_mistakes.B: relies on handwriting, which is not permitted
distractor_mistakes.D: uses wrong colors and an invented letter height

explanation: The correct answer is C (EMERGENCY DISCONNECT in white on a red background, at least 1/2 inch high): For a one- or two-family dwelling, the 2026 NEC requires the outdoor disconnect enclosure to be marked EMERGENCY DISCONNECT. The marking is white text on a red background, at least 1/2 inch high, on the outside front. Handwritten markings are not permitted for these required markings. The SERVICE DISCONNECT wording is for other than one- and two-family dwellings.

question: Service-entrance conductors cross a flat commercial roof that workers reach regularly on foot, and the roof has no parapet. Open conductors rated 240 volts currently sit 66 inches above the roof surface. How much higher must they be raised to meet the basic roof clearance?

options.A: 30 inches, to reach 8 feet above the roof surface
options.B: None, since 66 inches exceeds the 3 foot reduced clearance
options.C: 78 inches, to reach 12 feet as over residential property
options.D: 150 inches, to reach 18 feet as over truck-traffic streets

distractor_mistakes.B: applies the sloped-roof reduction to a flat roof
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a ground-level clearance for residential property
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the over-street clearance for a roof

explanation: The correct answer is A (30 inches, to reach 8 feet above the roof surface): Service conductors must have at least 8 feet of vertical clearance above the highest point of a roof. The reduced 3 foot value applies to roofs with a slope of 4 in 12 or more, and this roof is flat and accessible. The conductors are at 66 inches, or 5 feet 6 inches, so they must be raised 30 inches. The 12 and 18 foot values apply to areas over ground, not roofs.

question: An inspector finds a load center used as service equipment in a small office. The enclosure is a general-purpose panelboard with no marking showing it is suitable for service use, although it contains a main breaker. What does the NEC require of service equipment in this regard?

options.A: It must be listed and marked suitable for use as service equipment, whichever breaker it contains
options.B: It must be marked with its short-circuit current rating, which then qualifies it for service use
options.C: It must contain a main overcurrent device, and that device qualifies the enclosure for service use
options.D: It must be listed as a panelboard under Article 408, which qualifies it for service use

distractor_mistakes.B: treats a short-circuit rating marking as service suitability
distractor_mistakes.C: assumes a main breaker makes a panelboard service equipment
distractor_mistakes.D: treats panelboard listing as service equipment listing

explanation: The correct answer is A (It must be listed and marked suitable for use as service equipment, whichever breaker it contains): Service equipment must be listed and marked as suitable for use as service equipment. A general-purpose panelboard with a main breaker has not been evaluated for service use, so the breaker does not change its status. A short-circuit current rating is a separate marking that says nothing about service suitability. Panelboard listing under Article 408 covers the panelboard, not its use as service equipment.

question: Over a house, a 120/240 volt service drop passes 9 feet above a rear porch deck that people can step onto from the yard. Only pedestrians use the area, and no vehicles can reach it. The inspector asks what minimum clearance the NEC requires above that deck for these conductors. What is it?

options.A: 10 feet, above platforms where conductors could be reached by pedestrians
options.B: 12 feet, the clearance over residential property and driveways for lower voltages
options.C: 15 feet, the clearance over areas with voltage above 300 volts to ground
options.D: 18 feet, the clearance over public streets and truck-traffic areas

distractor_mistakes.B: uses the residential driveway clearance
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the clearance for conductors above 300 volts to ground
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the public street clearance

explanation: The correct answer is A (10 feet, above platforms where conductors could be reached by pedestrians): For service drop conductors not over 150 volts to ground, the minimum clearance is 10 feet at the point of attachment and above finished grade, sidewalks, and platforms or projections from which they might be reached. The 9 foot height over the porch deck falls short. The 12 foot figure applies over residential driveways, 15 feet applies to higher voltages, and 18 feet applies over public streets.

question: During plan review for a strip mall, the engineer asks which equipment the NEC allows to connect to the supply side of the service disconnecting means. The drawings show several candidates ahead of the main. Which of these may be connected on the supply side of the service disconnect?

options.A: A lighting contactor that controls the parking lot luminaires through a branch circuit
options.B: A dry-type transformer supplying the tenant lighting panelboards through a feeder disconnect
options.C: A packaged electric vehicle charger fed through its own dedicated breaker in the equipment room
options.D: A meter socket enclosure containing only metering equipment

distractor_mistakes.A: connects a branch-circuit load contactor ahead of the main
distractor_mistakes.B: places a transformer ahead of the service disconnect
distractor_mistakes.C: connects an end-use load ahead of the service disconnect

explanation: The correct answer is D (A meter socket enclosure containing only metering equipment): Section 230.82 lists the few items that may connect on the supply side of the service disconnecting means, and a meter socket enclosure containing only metering equipment is one of them. A contactor, a transformer and a charger are all equipment that serves loads, so each belongs on the load side where the main can switch it off. The list is short because supply-side equipment has no overcurrent protection ahead of it.

question: During rough-in of a new retail tenant space, the foreman marks the location for the service disconnecting means. The space is not a dwelling and has no bathrooms near the entrance. Which location rule governs where this disconnecting means must be placed?

options.A: A readily accessible spot, outside or inside, nearest where the service conductors enter the building
options.B: A readily accessible spot, outside or inside, nearest the largest connected load within the tenant space
options.C: A readily accessible spot, outside or inside, nearest the main panelboard serving the tenant space
options.D: A readily accessible spot outdoors, on or within sight of the building, as dwellings require

distractor_mistakes.B: places the disconnect by the largest load
distractor_mistakes.C: places the disconnect by the main panelboard
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the dwelling outdoor-location rule to a non-dwelling

explanation: The correct answer is A (A readily accessible spot, outside or inside, nearest where the service conductors enter the building): Section 230.70(A) requires the service disconnecting means at a readily accessible location, either outside or inside, nearest the point where the service conductors enter the building. The location is set by the entrance point, not by the largest load or the main panelboard. The outdoor-only location rule belongs to one- and two-family dwellings, and this tenant space is not a dwelling.

question: A warehouse has a new 200 ampere panelboard that is service equipment, in a space that is not a dwelling unit. A contractor assumes arc flash marking is not needed because the equipment is small. Under the 2026 NEC, what marking requirement applies to this equipment?

options.A: No marking, because the rule applies only to equipment rated 1,000 amperes or more
options.B: Marking with nominal voltage, arc flash boundary, incident energy or PPE level, and assessment date
options.C: Marking with nominal voltage and the date the label was applied, nothing else
options.D: Marking required on feeder equipment only, not on service equipment of this size

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the 2023 amperage threshold
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the 2023 label application date and leaves out required content
distractor_mistakes.D: excludes service equipment, which the rule includes

explanation: The correct answer is B (Marking with nominal voltage, arc flash boundary, incident energy or PPE level, and assessment date): The 2026 NEC removes the 1,000 ampere threshold, so all service and feeder equipment in other than dwelling units needs the arc flash marking. The marking carries the nominal system voltage, the arc flash boundary, the available incident energy or minimum PPE level, and the date the assessment was completed. The 1,000 ampere threshold is the 2023 rule. The date the label was applied was the 2023 content, and the rule covers service as well as feeder equipment.

question: On a house job, an installer wants to use standard nonmetallic-sheathed cable, Type NM, run through the basement joists, as the sole wiring method for the service-entrance conductors between the meter and the main panel of a house. The installer asks the inspector whether this is acceptable. How does the NEC treat this?

options.A: Permitted in a dwelling, because Article 334 allows Type NM for one- and two-family dwellings
options.B: Permitted when the cable is run inside a raceway from the meter to the main panel
options.C: Permitted when the cable is encased in 2 inches of concrete along the whole run
options.D: Not permitted, since Type NM is not a listed service-entrance wiring method

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the branch-circuit and feeder rule of Article 334 to a service
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes a raceway makes Type NM a service-entrance method
distractor_mistakes.C: treats concrete encasement as making an unlisted cable acceptable

explanation: The correct answer is D (Not permitted, since Type NM is not a listed service-entrance wiring method): The wiring methods allowed for service-entrance conductors are listed in Article 230, and Type NM cable is not on that list. Article 334 allows NM for branch circuits and feeders in dwellings, but service-entrance conductors are a different category. A raceway or concrete encasement does not turn NM into a listed service-entrance method. Type SE cable, Type USE cable or a listed raceway with suitable conductors would be used instead.

question: Outside a commercial building, a contractor lists wiring methods for service-entrance conductors. The installation will be on the wall surface. Which listed wiring method is recognized for service-entrance conductors where exposed to weather, provided raintight fittings are used and the installation meets its own article?

options.A: Type UF cable in the open, clipped to the wall
options.B: Type TC power cable, secured at intervals on the wall surface
options.C: Type SO flexible cord with strain relief at each end
options.D: Electrical metallic tubing with raintight connectors and couplings

distractor_mistakes.A: picks an underground feeder cable not listed for services
distractor_mistakes.B: picks a tray cable not listed for service entrances
distractor_mistakes.C: picks a flexible cord, which is not a service wiring method

explanation: The correct answer is D (Electrical metallic tubing with raintight connectors and couplings): Electrical metallic tubing is one of the wiring methods listed for service-entrance conductors. Raintight connectors and couplings suit it to outdoor use. Type UF, Type TC and flexible cord are not on the service-entrance list, even though they appear in other parts of the code. Flexible cords in particular are not allowed as a substitute for fixed wiring.

question: On a new commercial service, the noncontinuous load is 120 amperes and the continuous load is 200 amperes. The service overcurrent device is not listed for continuous operation at 100 percent of its rating. Using the standard size list, what is the minimum service overcurrent device rating?

options.A: 350 amperes, adding 320 amperes at 100 percent and rounding to a standard size
options.B: 400 amperes, from 125 percent of 200 plus 120, then the next standard size
options.C: 450 amperes, from applying 125 percent to the continuous load twice
options.D: 300 amperes, from 80 percent of the 370 ampere total

distractor_mistakes.A: adds loads at 100 percent without the continuous factor
distractor_mistakes.C: applies the 125 percent factor twice to the continuous load
distractor_mistakes.D: multiplies by 80 percent instead of applying 125 percent to the continuous load

explanation: The correct answer is B (400 amperes, from 125 percent of 200 plus 120, then the next standard size): The continuous load is multiplied by 125 percent, giving 250 amperes. Adding the 120 ampere noncontinuous load gives 370 amperes. The next standard size at or above 370 amperes is 400 amperes. The 350 ampere answer skips the continuous factor, the 450 ampere answer applies it twice, and the 300 ampere answer uses 80 percent in the wrong direction.

question: Service size for a 2,000 square foot one-family dwelling is being calculated under the 2026 NEC standard method. The designer needs the general lighting load for the service calculation, using the minimum unit load for dwelling services. Receptacle and small-appliance loads are added separately. What is the general lighting load?

options.A: 6,000 VA, using 3 VA per square foot from the 2023 service calculation
options.B: 7,000 VA, adding the 3,000 VA small-appliance and laundry loads to the lighting
options.C: 3,200 VA, using 80 percent of the 2023 square-foot unit load
options.D: 4,000 VA, from 2 VA per square foot of floor area times the 2,000 square feet

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the 3 VA value now kept only for branch-circuit counting
distractor_mistakes.B: merges separate load items into general lighting
distractor_mistakes.C: applies an unsupported 80 percent factor

explanation: The correct answer is D (4,000 VA, from 2 VA per square foot of floor area times the 2,000 square feet): The 2026 NEC uses 2 VA per square foot as the minimum unit load for dwelling feeders and services. Multiplying 2,000 square feet by 2 VA gives 4,000 VA. The 3 VA per square foot figure remains only for counting minimum branch circuits. Adding the small-appliance and laundry loads mixes separate calculation items into the lighting load.

question: In a mechanical room, a 480Y/277 volt service panel is installed. On one side of the working space are exposed live parts, and on the opposite side is a grounded concrete wall. The room offers 40 inches of clear depth in front of the panel. How much additional depth is needed?

options.A: 2 inches, to reach 3.5 feet for live parts opposite a grounded wall
options.B: None, because 36 inches governs for every voltage up to 600 volts
options.C: 8 inches, to reach 4 feet as for exposed live parts on both sides
options.D: 20 inches, to reach 5 feet as the largest value in the table

distractor_mistakes.B: uses the first condition for all voltages
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the third condition, live parts on both sides
distractor_mistakes.D: invents a 5 foot depth

explanation: The correct answer is A (2 inches, to reach 3.5 feet for live parts opposite a grounded wall): At 277 volts to ground the 151 to 600 volt rows of the working space table apply. Exposed live parts on one side and grounded parts on the other is the second condition, which requires 3.5 feet, or 42 inches. The room provides 40 inches, so 2 inches more is needed. The 3 foot figure is the first condition, and 4 feet applies only when live parts are exposed on both sides.

question: In an indoor electrical room, a new switchboard lineup serves as service equipment. The working space has the required width, depth and height, and the room has no light fixtures and no windows. The foreman asks about lighting for the working space. What does the code require?

options.A: Illumination is required, and an automatic occupancy sensor may be the sole control for it
options.B: Illumination is required where the equipment is rated 1200 amperes or more, such as large switchboards
options.C: Illumination for all indoor working spaces, which may come from an adjacent light source
options.D: Illumination is required, with fixtures mounted inside the working space itself and no adjacent source accepted

distractor_mistakes.A: accepts automatic control as the sole means of switching the lighting
distractor_mistakes.B: adds an ampere threshold the rule does not contain
distractor_mistakes.D: rejects an adjacent light source that the rule accepts

explanation: The correct answer is C (Illumination for all indoor working spaces, which may come from an adjacent light source): Section 110.26(D) requires illumination for working spaces about service equipment, switchboards, panelboards and motor control centers installed indoors. Additional fixtures are not needed where an adjacent light source lights the space. The rule has no ampere threshold, and the lighting outlets may not be controlled by automatic means alone. Indicating lamps on the equipment are not work lighting.

question: An electrician installs a service mast through the roof of a house to carry the utility's service-drop conductors. The mast is 1 1/4 inch rigid conduit rising 4 feet above the roofline. The inspector asks what the mast must be able to do. What does the code require of a mast that supports the drop?

options.A: Be rigid metal conduit, at least 2 inch trade size, to support the service drop conductors
options.B: Attach the drop to a listed coupling mounted above the last roof securement of the mast
options.C: Use raintight raceway fittings identified for service masts, with the strength left to the utility
options.D: Have adequate strength or be supported by braces or guys to withstand the drop strain

distractor_mistakes.A: invents a minimum trade size for the mast
distractor_mistakes.B: places the drop attachment at a coupling above the last securement
distractor_mistakes.C: treats mast fittings as supplying the needed strength

explanation: The correct answer is D (Have adequate strength or be supported by braces or guys to withstand the drop strain): A service mast that supports service-drop conductors must have adequate strength or be supported by braces or guys, because the drop pulls on it. Section 230.28 sets that strength requirement and does not set a trade size. Raintight fittings identified for service masts are also required, but they keep water out and do not carry the drop strain. Attaching the drop at a coupling above the last securement is poor practice and does not satisfy the strength rule.

question: A journeyman measures 11 feet of clearance where a proposed service drop crosses a public street that delivery trucks use daily. The drop operates at 120/240 volts. How much higher must the conductors be raised to meet the minimum clearance over a public street?

options.A: 1 foot, to reach 12 feet as over a residential driveway
options.B: 4 feet, to reach 15 feet as for higher voltage
options.C: 7 feet, to reach the 18 foot clearance over public streets
options.D: 9 feet, to reach 20 feet as over railroad tracks

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the residential driveway clearance
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the higher voltage clearance over non-street areas
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a rail crossing value that does not govern a street

explanation: The correct answer is C (7 feet, to reach the 18 foot clearance over public streets): Conductors crossing public streets, alleys, roads and parking areas subject to truck traffic must have 18 feet of clearance. The drop is at 11 feet, so it must go up 7 feet. The 12 foot clearance applies to residential property and driveways, and 15 feet applies at higher voltage over such areas. The 20 foot figure is not the governing value for a street crossing.

question: During a service upgrade at a two-story farmhouse, an electrician mounts the drop attachment on a wall where an upstairs window swings open outward. The homeowner asks how much clear space the open-run service conductors must keep from that window. Under the general rule of Section 230.9, what minimum clearance applies from windows designed to be opened?

options.A: 1 foot from the window frame, measured to the nearest service conductor
options.B: 6 feet from the openable window, measured to the nearest service conductor
options.C: 3 feet from the openable window, measured to the nearest service conductor
options.D: 10 feet from the window, matching the height rule at the point of attachment

distractor_mistakes.A: uses a 1 foot spacing that is not the rule for openable windows
distractor_mistakes.B: doubles the required window clearance to 6 feet
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses the window clearance with the 10 foot attachment height above grade

explanation: The correct answer is C (3 feet from the openable window, measured to the nearest service conductor): Section 230.9 requires service conductors installed as open conductors, or multiconductor cable without an overall jacket, to keep not less than 3 feet from windows designed to be opened, doors, porches, balconies, ladders, stairs and similar locations. The 10 foot figure is the minimum height of the drop at its attachment above finished grade, a different requirement. A 1 foot or 6 foot spacing matches nothing in Section 230.9.

question: Walking through a new warehouse office, an inspector finds a lighting and appliance panelboard with a 200 ampere main breaker installed right after the utility meter as the only disconnect. The panelboard is listed, but its label says nothing about service use. What must be done to comply with Section 230.66?

options.A: Replace it with equipment listed and marked as suitable for use as service equipment
options.B: Keep it and add a permanent SERVICE DISCONNECT marking, which satisfies the listing requirement
options.C: Keep it if the enclosure carries a short-circuit current rating above the available fault current
options.D: Keep it if the listed main breaker interrupting rating exceeds the available fault current

distractor_mistakes.B: treats a service marking as a substitute for listing
distractor_mistakes.C: treats a short-circuit rating as service suitability
distractor_mistakes.D: treats a breaker interrupting rating as service suitability

explanation: The correct answer is A (Replace it with equipment listed and marked as suitable for use as service equipment): Section 230.66 requires service equipment to be listed or field evaluated and marked as suitable for use as service equipment. This panelboard is listed as a panelboard, but its label says nothing about service use, so it has not been evaluated for that duty. A service marking added in the field does not replace the evaluation behind a listing. Short-circuit and interrupting ratings are separate requirements and do not make a panelboard service equipment.

question: Serving a one-family dwelling at 120/240 volts, single-phase, from a utility transformer 90 feet away, an electrician records a calculated load of 85 amperes. The owner asks for the smallest service disconnect Section 230.79 permits that also carries the load. What rating applies?

options.A: 100 amperes, the minimum rating Section 230.79 sets for a one-family dwelling
options.B: 90 amperes, the next standard size above the 85 ampere calculated load
options.C: 110 amperes, 125 percent of the calculated load rounded to a standard size
options.D: 60 amperes, the minimum that applies to installations other than one-family dwellings

distractor_mistakes.B: picks the next standard size over the load and ignores the dwelling minimum
distractor_mistakes.C: applies the 125 percent continuous factor to a dwelling load
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the 60 ampere minimum for all other installations

explanation: The correct answer is A (100 amperes, the minimum rating Section 230.79 sets for a one-family dwelling): Section 230.79(C) requires a one-family dwelling service disconnecting means to be rated not less than 100 amperes, 3-wire. The 85 ampere load is below that, so the minimum governs and 100 amperes is the answer. The 60 ampere minimum is for installations other than one-family dwellings, and 125 percent applies only to continuous loads, which the stem does not describe.

question: Before the sizes of the service-entrance conductors are checked on a new commercial job, an inspector wants the contractor to identify the service point, because that point marks where responsibility changes. According to the Article 100 definition, what does the service point mark?

options.A: The location of the main disconnect where the conductors terminate inside the building
options.B: The point where the service drop attaches to the building or other structure
options.C: The first panelboard that supplies the branch circuits and feeders for the building
options.D: The connection between the utility's facilities and the premises wiring, not the drop

distractor_mistakes.A: places the service point at the main disconnect
distractor_mistakes.B: equates the service point with the drop attachment
distractor_mistakes.C: identifies it as the first panelboard rather than the utility connection

explanation: The correct answer is D (The connection between the utility's facilities and the premises wiring, not the drop): Article 100 defines the service point as the point of connection between the facilities of the serving utility and the premises wiring. It is a boundary of ownership and responsibility, not the main disconnect or the first panelboard. The drop attachment can be physically near it, but the definition is about the utility connection, so attachment alone does not decide it.

question: Paralleling service-entrance conductors on each phase, a contractor proposes one copper conductor and one aluminum conductor of equal circular mil area in every set. The inspector rejects the proposal under the Article 310 rules for conductors in parallel. What rule is the inspector applying?

options.A: Parallel conductors must match in length, material, size, insulation type, and termination method
options.B: Parallel conductors may differ in material when the ampacity of each is calculated separately
options.C: Parallel conductors must match in material but may vary in length when each carries equal current
options.D: Parallel conductors must run in separate raceways so heating from each set stays independent

distractor_mistakes.B: allows mixed materials with separate ampacity calculations
distractor_mistakes.C: thinks only length may differ if currents are equal
distractor_mistakes.D: invents a separate-raceway requirement for parallel sets

explanation: The correct answer is A (Parallel conductors must match in length, material, size, insulation type, and termination method): Article 310 requires conductors in parallel to be the same length, the same conductor material, the same size in circular mil area, the same insulation type, and terminated the same way. Mixing copper and aluminum breaks the material match, so separate ampacity calculations do not rescue it. Running each set in its own raceway is not the test, since parallel sets are normally run in matching raceways per phase.

question: Ungrounded conductors of 4/0 AWG copper feed a commercial service. The metal water pipe includes a plastic section and a water meter, and the plumber adds a bonding jumper around the meter. Using the table for grounding electrode conductors, what minimum copper size is needed for that jumper?

options.A: 4 AWG copper, the most that a concrete-encased electrode connection requires
options.B: 6 AWG copper, the most that a driven rod connection requires
options.C: 4/0 AWG copper, matching the size of the service-entrance conductors
options.D: 2 AWG copper, the table value for conductors over 3/0 through 350 kcmil

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the 4 AWG cap for concrete-encased electrodes to a pipe jumper
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the 6 AWG cap for rods to a pipe jumper
distractor_mistakes.C: sizes the jumper equal to the ungrounded conductors

explanation: The correct answer is D (2 AWG copper, the table value for conductors over 3/0 through 350 kcmil): The jumper around the meter is sized from the table for grounding electrode conductors using the largest ungrounded service conductor. A 4/0 AWG copper conductor is 211.6 kcmil, which falls in the row for over 3/0 through 350 kcmil, giving 2 AWG copper. The 4 AWG and 6 AWG limits apply only to connections made to concrete-encased electrodes and driven rods, and the jumper is not required to match the service conductors.

question: Clamped to the rigid conduit mast that supports the power service drop on a two-story house, a communications drop draws a citation. The inspector cites Section 230.28 and asks the installer to read the general rule aloud. What does that rule say about conductors attached to a service mast?

options.A: Communications drops may attach when the mast is braced or guyed for the added tension
options.B: Power and communications drops may share the mast when both are bonded with listed clamps
options.C: Only power service-drop conductors may be attached to the service mast
options.D: Any service-drop conductors, power or communications, may attach where the mast is rigid metal conduit

distractor_mistakes.A: assumes bracing allows a communications drop on the mast
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes bonding clamps allow a shared mast
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes rigid conduit allows any drop on the mast

explanation: The correct answer is C (Only power service-drop conductors may be attached to the service mast): Section 230.28 limits what may be attached to a service mast to the power service-drop conductors. Bracing, bonding clamps and a rigid conduit mast are all about strength or grounding, and none of them changes what may be attached. A communications drop needs its own support. The rule restricts the type of conductor on the mast, not how well the mast is built.

question: Two driven 8 foot ground rods only 4 feet apart serve as the grounding electrode system on a rural property, and the inspector finds this spacing too short. The first rod measured above 25 ohms, so a second rod is permitted. How many feet farther apart must the rods be moved to meet the minimum spacing?

options.A: 2 feet farther apart, reaching the 6 foot minimum spacing between rods
options.B: 4 feet farther apart, reaching 8 feet to equal the rod length
options.C: 6 feet farther apart, adding the full minimum spacing to the existing distance
options.D: 8 feet farther apart, reaching 12 feet by doubling the minimum spacing

distractor_mistakes.B: adds the difference needed to match the rod length
distractor_mistakes.C: adds the whole 6 foot minimum to the existing spacing
distractor_mistakes.D: doubles the minimum spacing instead of finding the shortfall

explanation: The correct answer is A (2 feet farther apart, reaching the 6 foot minimum spacing between rods): Where more than one rod is used, Section 250.53 requires the rods to be not less than 6 feet apart. The rods are 4 feet apart now, so the shortfall is 6 minus 4, which is 2 feet. Spacing equal to the rod length performs better, but it is not the code minimum. Adding the whole minimum or doubling it counts spacing that the rule does not require.

question: Over a new 400 ampere switchboard standing 6 feet tall, a designer routes a suspended ceiling grid 8 feet above the floor, with no structural ceiling nearby. The inspector objects under Section 110.26. How high does the dedicated electrical space above that switchboard extend?

options.A: Up to the suspended ceiling grid, which counts as the structural ceiling
options.B: 3 feet above the equipment, matching the depth of the working space
options.C: 6.5 feet above the floor, matching the minimum headroom of the working space
options.D: 6 feet above the equipment, since a suspended ceiling is not structural

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the suspended grid as a structural ceiling
distractor_mistakes.B: confuses dedicated space height with working space depth
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses dedicated space with working space headroom

explanation: The correct answer is D (6 feet above the equipment, since a suspended ceiling is not structural): The dedicated space above switchboards runs from the floor to 6 feet above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. A dropped or suspended ceiling that adds no strength to the building is not a structural ceiling, so the space reaches 12 feet above the floor here and the grid at 8 feet intrudes. Headroom and working space depth are separate dimensions and do not set this height.

question: Crossing a retail store's customer parking lot, an underground service lateral will run in Schedule 40 PVC conduit with a 3.5 inch outside diameter. Table 300.5 requires 24 inches of cover there. What minimum trench depth, in inches, gives the top of the conduit the required cover?

options.A: 21.5 inches, adding the diameter to the 18 inch cover used for other locations
options.B: 27.5 inches, adding the 3.5 inch conduit diameter to 24 inches of cover
options.C: 24 inches, stopping at the cover without allowing for the conduit itself
options.D: 31.0 inches, adding the conduit diameter twice to the 24 inch cover

distractor_mistakes.A: reads the 18 inch all-locations row instead of the parking lot row
distractor_mistakes.C: forgets that cover is measured to the top of the conduit
distractor_mistakes.D: counts the conduit diameter twice

explanation: The correct answer is B (27.5 inches, adding the 3.5 inch conduit diameter to 24 inches of cover): Table 300.5 gives 24 inches of cover for nonmetallic raceways under parking lots, and cover is measured from the top of the raceway to finished grade. The trench must also hold the conduit, so 24 plus 3.5 equals 27.5 inches. The 18 inch figure is for locations not specified elsewhere, and 24 inches alone would leave the top of the conduit too shallow.

question: Service-entrance conductors of 1/0 AWG copper land on 75 degree rated terminals at a 480/277 volt commercial building. An inspector wants the largest standard service overcurrent device that does not exceed the conductor ampacity under Section 230.90, with no rounding up. Use Table 310.16. What rating applies?

options.A: 125 amperes, reading the 60 degree column for 1/0 AWG copper
options.B: 150 amperes, the 75 degree column ampacity of 1/0 AWG copper
options.C: 175 amperes, rounding up from the 90 degree column value of 170 amperes
options.D: 170 amperes, using the 90 degree column ampacity directly as the device rating

distractor_mistakes.A: reads the 60 degree column instead of the 75 degree terminal rating
distractor_mistakes.C: rounds up from the 90 degree column value
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the 90 degree column value as the device rating

explanation: The correct answer is B (150 amperes, the 75 degree column ampacity of 1/0 AWG copper): Termination temperature limits control, so the 75 degree column applies: 1/0 AWG copper is 150 amperes, which is itself a standard size, so the device is 150 amperes. The 60 degree column gives 125 amperes, which is too low for the stated terminals. The 90 degree value of 170 amperes is usable only for derating, and neither 170 nor 175 is permitted when the device may not exceed the conductor ampacity.

question: Specifying a service panel with a 10,000 ampere interrupting rating for a plant, a designer ignores the utility's report of 18,000 amperes of available fault current at the service and says the load calculation already sized the equipment. Which requirement governs and shows the design is deficient?

options.A: Equipment interrupting rating must equal or exceed the fault current available at its load terminals
options.B: Equipment interrupting rating must equal or exceed the service ampere rating shown in the load calculation
options.C: Equipment interrupting rating must equal or exceed the utility transformer's rated full-load secondary current
options.D: Equipment interrupting rating must equal or exceed the fault current available at its line terminals

distractor_mistakes.A: measures fault current at the load terminals instead of the line terminals
distractor_mistakes.B: compares the rating to the calculated load current
distractor_mistakes.C: compares the rating to transformer full-load current

explanation: The correct answer is D (Equipment interrupting rating must equal or exceed the fault current available at its line terminals): Section 110.9 requires equipment intended to interrupt fault current to have an interrupting rating at least equal to the current available at its line terminals. The panel is rated 10,000 amperes where 18,000 amperes is available, so it fails whatever the load calculation shows. Load current and transformer full-load current describe normal operation, not fault duty. Fault current is measured at the line side because that is where the equipment must open the fault.

question: Six tenant spaces in a small strip mall share one service, and their calculated loads are 60, 45, 50, 55, 40 and 36 amperes, none of them continuous. Using the 75 degree column of Table 310.16 for copper, what is the smallest service-entrance conductor size that carries the total calculated load?

options.A: 250 kcmil copper, adding only the five largest tenant loads totaling 250 amperes
options.B: 300 kcmil copper, rounding the 286 ampere total down to the 285 ampere value
options.C: 500 kcmil copper, applying 125 percent to loads that are not continuous
options.D: 350 kcmil copper, since 300 kcmil at 285 amperes falls 1 ampere short

distractor_mistakes.A: leaves out the smallest tenant load
distractor_mistakes.B: rounds the total down to match a table value
distractor_mistakes.C: applies the 125 percent continuous load factor to noncontinuous loads

explanation: The correct answer is D (350 kcmil copper, since 300 kcmil at 285 amperes falls 1 ampere short): The loads add to 60 plus 45 plus 50 plus 55 plus 40 plus 36, which is 286 amperes. In the 75 degree column, 300 kcmil copper is 285 amperes, one ampere below the load, so the next size, 350 kcmil at 310 amperes, is required. Applying 125 percent would give 357.5 amperes, which is wrong because none of the loads is continuous.

question: At the raintight service head on a new raceway mast, an electrician has to decide how the ungrounded conductors and the grounded conductor leave the head. The inspector asks what Section 230.54 requires for the openings in the service head. What is the requirement?

options.A: All conductors leave through one bushed opening when the service head is listed for that arrangement
options.B: Conductors of different potential leave through separately bushed openings in the head
options.C: Different potential conductors leave through separate openings, bushed on ungrounded conductors but not the grounded one
options.D: Conductors of different potential leave through one bushed opening, with insulating separators between the potentials

distractor_mistakes.A: assumes a listed head permits a shared opening
distractor_mistakes.C: omits the bushing on the grounded conductor opening
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes separators replace separately bushed openings

explanation: The correct answer is B (Conductors of different potential leave through separately bushed openings in the head): Section 230.54 requires service heads to have conductors of different potential brought out through separately bushed openings. The grounded conductor is at a different potential from each ungrounded conductor, so it also gets its own bushed opening. Separators inside a shared opening do not meet the wording of the rule. Drip loops address water entry and do not replace bushings.

question: On a 400 ampere service, an electrician proposes connecting four items ahead of the service disconnecting means: a meter socket, a surge arrester, cable limiters on the conductors, and a tap feeding an exterior lighting panel. How many of these items may be connected to the supply side under Section 230.82?

options.A: Four: all items, since each is wired from the service conductors
options.B: Two: the meter socket and the surge arrester, without the limiters
options.C: One: the meter socket only, since it belongs to the utility
options.D: Three: the meter socket, surge arrester, and cable limiters

distractor_mistakes.A: assumes any tap from the service conductors is allowed on the line side
distractor_mistakes.B: drops the cable limiters from the permitted list
distractor_mistakes.C: limits line-side equipment to the meter socket

explanation: The correct answer is D (Three: the meter socket, surge arrester, and cable limiters): Section 230.82 lists the only equipment allowed on the supply side of the service disconnecting means, and it includes meter sockets, surge arresters, and cable limiters or other current limiting devices. A tap feeding a lighting panel is a branch-circuit supply and must be connected on the load side of the disconnect. So three of the four items are permitted.

question: Footing inspection shows 15 feet of bare 4 AWG copper conductor laid horizontally near the bottom of the concrete foundation and tied in as the concrete-encased electrode. The builder says the copper size is right. What does the inspector conclude under Section 250.52?

options.A: It qualifies, since bare 4 AWG copper at 15 feet meets the minimum length
options.B: It qualifies if a ground rod of at least 8 feet is also driven
options.C: It does not qualify, because the minimum copper size is 2 AWG
options.D: It does not qualify, since it needs at least 20 feet of rebar or bare copper

distractor_mistakes.A: thinks 15 feet is enough length
distractor_mistakes.B: thinks adding a rod rescues a short encased conductor
distractor_mistakes.C: misstates the minimum size for the encased conductor

explanation: The correct answer is D (It does not qualify, since it needs at least 20 feet of rebar or bare copper): A concrete-encased electrode under Section 250.52 needs at least 20 feet of either rebar of 1/2 inch diameter or larger or bare copper not smaller than 4 AWG, encased in at least 2 inches of concrete. The size is correct here but 15 feet is short, so the conductor does not qualify as that electrode. Driving a rod would add another electrode but would not make the short conductor qualify.

question: Grounding a new service with 400 kcmil copper ungrounded conductors, an installer uses only a concrete-encased electrode made of 20 feet of 1/2 inch rebar. What minimum copper grounding electrode conductor size is required for the connection to that electrode?

options.A: 1/0 AWG copper, the table value for 400 kcmil service conductors
options.B: 2 AWG copper, the table value for conductors up to 350 kcmil
options.C: 4 AWG copper, the most a sole concrete-encased electrode connection needs
options.D: 8 AWG copper, the smallest size permitted for any grounding electrode conductor

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the full table value and skips the concrete-encased limit
distractor_mistakes.B: reads the wrong table row for 400 kcmil
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the smallest general size instead of the table or limit

explanation: The correct answer is C (4 AWG copper, the most a sole concrete-encased electrode connection needs): Table 250.66 would give 1/0 AWG copper for 400 kcmil conductors, but Section 250.66 limits the portion of the conductor that is the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode to 4 AWG copper. The rebar electrode is the only one, so 4 AWG is the minimum required. The 2 AWG row applies only to conductors up to 350 kcmil, and 8 AWG is too small for the table.

question: Eight disconnecting means are grouped at the first of two permitted services on a building, and three at the second, an inspector finds. Section 230.71 limits each service to a set maximum of switches or breakers. How many disconnects must be removed or consolidated at the first service?

options.A: Zero, because eleven total disconnects stays within a combined limit of twelve for two services
options.B: Two, bringing the first service down to the six-switch maximum that 230.71 allows for each service
options.C: Five, because the two services combined may have six disconnects in total
options.D: Three, since the limit counts five disconnects per service, leaving the first service over by three

distractor_mistakes.A: pools the disconnects across both services
distractor_mistakes.C: pools the six disconnect limit across both services
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a five disconnect limit instead of six

explanation: The correct answer is B (Two, bringing the first service down to the six-switch maximum that 230.71 allows for each service): Section 230.71 permits not more than six switches or six circuit breakers in the disconnecting means for each service. The limit is counted service by service, so the second service with three is within it. The first service has eight, which exceeds the maximum by 8 minus 6, or 2. Pooling the disconnects of both services, or using a five disconnect limit, does not match how the section counts.

question: Running a 120/240 volt service drop over the roof of a house with a pitch of 3 in 12, a crew works above a roof that people can reach. The inspector asks for the vertical clearance that the general rule of Section 230.24(A) requires above the roof surface. What clearance applies?

options.A: 8 feet above the highest point of the roof surface the conductors cross
options.B: 3 feet above the roof, which fits only roofs of 4 in 12 pitch or steeper
options.C: 10 feet above the roof, the pedestrian clearance at the service entrance
options.D: 12 feet above the roof, the value for residential driveways

distractor_mistakes.B: applies the reduced clearance for steeper roofs
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the 10 foot pedestrian value
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the driveway clearance

explanation: The correct answer is A (8 feet above the highest point of the roof surface the conductors cross): Section 230.24(A) requires service drop conductors to have a vertical clearance of not less than 8 feet above the roof surface they pass over. The 3 foot reduction is reserved for roofs with a slope of at least 4 in 12, and this roof is only 3 in 12. The 10 foot and 12 foot values belong to the clearance rules for grade and driveways, not for roofs.

question: Ungrounded conductors of 350 kcmil copper run in one raceway to a service disconnect, and the calculated maximum unbalanced load on the grounded conductor is 40 amperes. Using Table 250.102(C)(1) for the grounded conductor under Section 250.24, what minimum copper size is required?

options.A: 2 AWG copper, the table value for ungrounded conductors up to 350 kcmil
options.B: 8 AWG copper, sized for the 40 ampere unbalanced load alone
options.C: 1/0 AWG copper, the table value for ungrounded conductors over 350 kcmil
options.D: 350 kcmil copper, matching the size of the ungrounded conductors

distractor_mistakes.B: sizes the grounded conductor from the unbalanced load only
distractor_mistakes.C: reads the next table row up
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes the grounded conductor must equal the phase conductors

explanation: The correct answer is A (2 AWG copper, the table value for ungrounded conductors up to 350 kcmil): The grounded service conductor must be at least the size in Table 250.102(C)(1) for the largest ungrounded service conductor, besides carrying the unbalanced load. A 350 kcmil copper conductor falls in the over 3/0 through 350 kcmil row, giving 2 AWG copper, which also carries 40 amperes easily. An 8 AWG conductor would meet the load but not the table, and matching the phase size is not required.

question: Calculating for a bakery on a 208 volt service, an engineer finds 90 amperes of continuous load and 60 amperes of noncontinuous load. The terminals are rated 75 degrees. Using Section 230.42 and the 75 degree column of Table 310.16, what is the smallest copper service-entrance conductor?

options.A: 1/0 AWG copper, sized for the plain 150 ampere sum of the two loads
options.B: 2/0 AWG copper, because 175 amperes covers the 172.5 ampere minimum
options.C: 3/0 AWG copper, applying 125 percent to both the continuous and noncontinuous loads
options.D: 250 kcmil copper, applying 125 percent twice to the combined load

distractor_mistakes.A: skips the 125 percent continuous load factor
distractor_mistakes.C: applies 125 percent to the noncontinuous load too
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the 125 percent factor twice

explanation: The correct answer is B (2/0 AWG copper, because 175 amperes covers the 172.5 ampere minimum): Section 230.42 requires ampacity of at least the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load: 60 plus 1.25 times 90, which is 60 plus 112.5, or 172.5 amperes. In the 75 degree column, 2/0 AWG copper is 175 amperes, the smallest size that covers it. The 150 ampere sum ignores the continuous factor, and the other sizes come from applying 125 percent too broadly.

question: Carrying 94 amperes on one ungrounded conductor and 71 amperes on the other, a 120/240 volt single-phase commercial service supplies only 120 volt equipment on the two lines. What current flows in the grounded service conductor under those conditions, ignoring any harmonic current?

options.A: 165 amperes, the sum of the two ungrounded conductor currents
options.B: 23 amperes, the difference between the two line currents
options.C: 94 amperes, the higher of the two ungrounded currents
options.D: 71 amperes, the lower of the two ungrounded conductor currents

distractor_mistakes.A: adds the two line currents
distractor_mistakes.C: takes the higher line current
distractor_mistakes.D: takes the lower line current

explanation: The correct answer is B (23 amperes, the difference between the two line currents): On a single-phase, 3-wire system the grounded conductor carries only the unbalanced current, which is the difference between the two ungrounded conductor currents: 94 minus 71 equals 23 amperes. The currents from the two lines flow toward each other at the neutral point and offset, so the sum or either single value is wrong.

question: Two parallel 250 kcmil copper conductors per phase land on 75 degree rated terminals at a service. Using Section 230.90 and Table 310.16, what is the largest standard service overcurrent device rating that does not exceed the combined conductor ampacity of each phase?

options.A: 250 amperes, the standard size under one conductor's 255 ampere ampacity
options.B: 500 amperes, the largest standard size within the combined 510 ampere ampacity
options.C: 600 amperes, rounding the 510 ampere ampacity up to the next standard size
options.D: 400 amperes, using the 60 degree value of 215 amperes per conductor

distractor_mistakes.A: counts only one conductor of the parallel set
distractor_mistakes.C: rounds up past the combined ampacity
distractor_mistakes.D: reads the 60 degree column instead of the 75 degree column

explanation: The correct answer is B (500 amperes, the largest standard size within the combined 510 ampere ampacity): At 75 degrees, 250 kcmil copper is 255 amperes, so two in parallel carry 510 amperes. The largest standard size from Section 240.6 that does not exceed 510 is 500 amperes. Counting only one conductor gives 250 amperes, rounding up to 600 exceeds the ampacity as the stem prohibits, and the 60 degree column would give 430 amperes and a 400 ampere device.

question: Rising from the trench along the exterior wall of a warehouse, a direct-buried underground service lateral cable heads to the meter socket. Under Section 300.5, how far above finished grade must the cable be protected by a raceway or enclosure where it emerges from the ground?

options.A: To a point at least 10 feet above finished grade, matching the drop clearance over walkways
options.B: To a point at least 6 1/2 feet above finished grade, matching the working space height
options.C: To a point at least 8 feet above finished grade
options.D: To a point at least 18 inches above finished grade, matching the cover depth below grade

distractor_mistakes.A: borrows the overhead drop clearance height
distractor_mistakes.B: borrows the working space headroom height
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the cover depth as the protection height

explanation: The correct answer is C (To a point at least 8 feet above finished grade): Section 300.5(D) requires direct-buried conductors emerging from grade to be protected by an enclosure or raceway. The protection must run from the cover depth below grade to a point at least 8 feet above finished grade. Overhead clearance of 10 feet and working space height of 6 1/2 feet govern different situations. A short sleeve at grade would leave the cable exposed to vehicles and equipment.

question: Four circuit breakers in one enclosure, rated 60, 50, 40 and 30 amperes, form the service disconnecting means of a small commercial building with a calculated load of 200 amperes. By how many amperes is their combined rating short of what Section 230.80 requires?

options.A: None, because the 180 ampere combined rating meets the 60 ampere minimum for other installations
options.B: 50 amperes short, leaving the 30 ampere breaker out of the sum
options.C: 140 amperes short, counting only the largest single 60 ampere breaker
options.D: 20 amperes short, since the 180 ampere combined rating is below the 200 ampere load

distractor_mistakes.A: compares the sum with the 60 ampere minimum instead of the load
distractor_mistakes.B: leaves one breaker out of the total
distractor_mistakes.C: counts only the largest breaker

explanation: The correct answer is D (20 amperes short, since the 180 ampere combined rating is below the 200 ampere load): Section 230.80 requires the combined ratings of the switches or breakers forming the disconnecting means to be not less than the rating required by Section 230.79, which includes the calculated load. The breakers add to 60 plus 50 plus 40 plus 30, or 180 amperes, against a 200 ampere load, so the rating is short by 20 amperes. The 60 ampere minimum is a floor, not the measure against the load.

question: Plans for a commercial lateral in PVC conduit show 18 inches of cover where it crosses a delivery driveway at a distribution center. Table 300.5 requires 24 inches of cover under driveways in that situation. By how many inches must the cover be increased?

options.A: 0 inches, because the 18 inch cover applies to driveways at one- and two-family dwellings
options.B: 24 inches more, for 42 inches, adding the required cover on top of the cover shown
options.C: 18 inches more, for 36 inches, doubling the existing cover
options.D: 6 inches more, for 24 inches of cover under a commercial driveway

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the dwelling driveway cover to a commercial driveway
distractor_mistakes.B: adds the required cover to the existing cover
distractor_mistakes.C: doubles the existing cover instead of finding the shortfall

explanation: The correct answer is D (6 inches more, for 24 inches of cover under a commercial driveway): Table 300.5 requires 24 inches of cover for nonmetallic raceways under driveways in this situation, and the plans show 18 inches. The shortfall is 24 minus 18, which is 6 inches. The 18 inch figure applies to a different location, so leaving the cover unchanged fails. Adding the requirement to the existing cover, or doubling it, overstates the shortfall.

question: Twelve feet of Type SE cable runs from a service head down to a meter socket, straight along a wall. Section 230.51 requires a support within 12 inches of the head, within 12 inches of the enclosure, and at intervals of no more than 30 inches. What is the minimum number of supports?

options.A: Four supports, dividing the 144 inch run by 36 inches
options.B: Six supports, placing one every 30 inches along the full 144 inch run
options.C: Five supports, placing the end ones 12 inches from each end
options.D: Three supports, one at each end and one at the middle

distractor_mistakes.A: divides by a 36 inch spacing that is not the rule
distractor_mistakes.B: counts 30 inch intervals from the end of the cable instead of from the end supports
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes one mid-run support is enough for 12 feet

explanation: The correct answer is C (Five supports, placing the end ones 12 inches from each end): The run is 144 inches. Supports at 12 inches from each end sit at 12 and 132 inches, leaving 120 inches between them. At no more than 30 inches apart, that gap needs 4 intervals, so 3 intermediate supports, and with the two end supports the total is 5. A 36 inch spacing exceeds the limit, and one mid-run support would leave 60 inch gaps.

question: Handle height is the problem on a troubleshooting walk: a technician measures a service disconnect handle at 84 inches above the floor in its highest position. Section 404.8 limits the handle height to 6 feet 7 inches. By how many inches does the handle exceed the limit?

options.A: 12 inches, comparing against a 6 foot limit of 72 inches
options.B: 6 inches, comparing against a 6 foot 6 inch limit of 78 inches
options.C: 5 inches, because the 6 feet 7 inch limit equals 79 inches above the floor
options.D: Zero inches, since 84 inches is within a 7 foot limit

distractor_mistakes.A: uses a 6 foot limit
distractor_mistakes.B: misreads the limit as 6 feet 6 inches
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a 7 foot limit

explanation: The correct answer is C (5 inches, because the 6 feet 7 inch limit equals 79 inches above the floor): The limit of 6 feet 7 inches equals 6 times 12 plus 7, which is 79 inches. The handle is at 84 inches, so it exceeds the limit by 84 minus 79, or 5 inches. A 6 foot or 6 foot 6 inch limit changes the answer to 12 or 6 inches, and a 7 foot limit is not the value in the section.

question: Every storm leaves water collected in a house's meter socket. The inspector notes that the service head sits below the point where the drop attaches to the building, and the conductors have no drip loops. Which correction is the best fix for the problem?

options.A: Keep the head where it is and form drip loops on every service conductor
options.B: Seal the conduit joints with listed compound and add a second raintight coupling below the head
options.C: Relocate the service head above the service drop attachment point, per 230.54, and form drip loops
options.D: Replace the head with a listed raintight meter socket hub and keep the existing location

distractor_mistakes.A: fixes drip loops but leaves the head below the attachment point
distractor_mistakes.B: treats joint sealing as fixing the water path
distractor_mistakes.D: swaps hardware without correcting the head location

explanation: The correct answer is C (Relocate the service head above the service drop attachment point, per 230.54, and form drip loops): Section 230.54 requires the service head to be located above the point of attachment of the service drop, and drip loops keep water from running along the conductors into the raceway. With the head below the attachment, water follows the conductors in. Drip loops alone leave the head in the wrong place. Sealing joints or changing hardware does not correct the water path.

question: Locked inside an electrical closet, a main service disconnect is reachable only with a key that the occupant keeps. The inspector tests the location against the Article 100 definition of readily accessible. Which condition does that definition allow for reaching the equipment?

options.A: Reaching it only after removing a panel cover or other fixed barrier
options.B: Reaching it quickly with a key, without climbing or using portable ladders
options.C: Reaching it only with a portable ladder placed by the occupant
