options.D: 8 AWG, since the 45 ampere adjusted load is under 50 amperes at 75 degrees

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the 90 degree column and skips the continuous load factor
distractor_mistakes.B: reads the 60 degree column when the terminals are marked 75 degrees
distractor_mistakes.C: applies 125 percent twice and then reads the 60 degree column

explanation: The correct answer is D (8 AWG, since the 45 ampere adjusted load is under 50 amperes at 75 degrees): A continuous load requires conductor ampacity of at least 125 percent of the load, so 36 times 1.25 is 45 amperes. With 75 degree terminals, the 75 degree column of the copper ampacity table gives 8 AWG as 50 amperes, which covers 45 amperes. A 10 AWG conductor is only 35 amperes at 75 degrees and fails the load. Using the 90 degree column to satisfy a terminal that is limited to 75 degrees would overstate what the conductor may carry.

question: Wiring a new electric water heater, an installer runs a 30 ampere two-pole breaker through a two-conductor cable with a white conductor, a black conductor and a bare ground. There is no neutral and the load is 240 volts only. The inspector notes the white conductor connects to the second breaker pole. What correction does the code require?

options.A: Leave the white conductor unmarked, since no neutral exists anywhere on a straight 240 volt circuit
options.B: Permanently reidentify the white conductor as ungrounded at each visible location using paint or tape
options.C: Reidentify the white conductor with green tape so it is recognized as a protective conductor
options.D: Reidentify the white conductor at the panelboard end only, since other locations are concealed

distractor_mistakes.A: claims no marking is needed because the circuit has no neutral
distractor_mistakes.C: marks the conductor green, which is reserved for equipment grounding
distractor_mistakes.D: marks only one end of the conductor instead of every visible location

explanation: The correct answer is B (Permanently reidentify the white conductor as ungrounded at each visible location using paint or tape): A white conductor in a cable assembly may serve as an ungrounded conductor on a 240 volt circuit only when it is permanently reidentified, with paint, tape or another effective means, at each location where the conductor is visible and accessible. Leaving it unmarked invites someone to treat it as a grounded conductor. Green marking is reserved for equipment grounding conductors. Marking only the panelboard end misses the splices and terminations the rule names.

question: Several duplex receptacles sit on a general-use 20 ampere, 120 volt branch circuit in a warehouse office. Staff will plug in cord-and-plug equipment that can run for hours at a time. According to the load limit for circuits with more than one outlet, what is the maximum total cord-and-plug load allowed?

options.A: 20 amperes, which is the full rating of the circuit and of the duplex receptacles
options.B: 16 amperes, 80 percent of the 20 ampere circuit rating under Section 210.21(B)(2)
options.C: 12 amperes, which is the maximum permitted load for a 15 ampere circuit
options.D: 25 amperes, which is 125 percent of the circuit rating for cord-and-plug loads

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the whole circuit rating as usable cord-and-plug load
distractor_mistakes.C: reads the 15 ampere circuit row of the load table
distractor_mistakes.D: applies a 125 percent factor in the wrong direction

explanation: The correct answer is B (16 amperes, 80 percent of the 20 ampere circuit rating under Section 210.21(B)(2)): The maximum load on a circuit with two or more receptacles or outlets for cord-and-plug loads is 80 percent of the circuit rating. Twenty amperes times 0.80 is 16 amperes. The 12 ampere figure belongs to a 15 ampere circuit, and the full 20 amperes is the breaker rating, not the permitted load. The 125 percent factor is used to size circuits for continuous loads, not to raise a receptacle load limit.

question: Measuring a straight dwelling kitchen wall countertop five feet long, with no sink, range or appliance interrupting it, an inspector finds one receptacle at the far left end. The inspector asks how far along the wall line any point on the counter may be from a receptacle. What is the maximum distance?

options.A: 6 feet, measured along the wall at the floor line like ordinary room wall spacing
options.B: 48 inches, measured from the end of the counter to the nearest receptacle outlet
options.C: 24 inches, measured horizontally along the wall line from a receptacle outlet
options.D: 36 inches, measured from the front edge of the counter to the nearest receptacle

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the 6 foot room-wall floor-line rule to a kitchen counter
distractor_mistakes.B: doubles the countertop spacing distance to 48 inches
distractor_mistakes.D: measures 36 inches from the counter edge instead of along the wall line

explanation: The correct answer is C (24 inches, measured horizontally along the wall line from a receptacle outlet): For kitchen wall countertop spaces, no point along the wall line may be more than 24 inches horizontally from a receptacle outlet in that space. With a receptacle only at the left end of a five foot counter, the far end is well over 24 inches away, so another outlet is needed. The 6 foot figure applies to habitable room walls at the floor line. A kitchen counter is held to the tighter spacing because appliances are used right on the counter.

question: Ten hours at a time, from dusk until after midnight each night, a lighted display stays on, and the sign shop owner asks the electrician to label its feeder. Which definition correctly classifies this load as a continuous load under the Article 100 definition?

options.A: A load whose maximum current is expected to continue for two hours or more
options.B: A load whose maximum current is expected to continue for three hours or more
options.C: A load whose maximum current is expected to continue for four hours or more
options.D: A load that operates on a timer or photocell for more than one full hour

distractor_mistakes.A: uses a two hour duration instead of three hours
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a four hour duration instead of three hours
distractor_mistakes.D: treats any automatically controlled load as continuous after one hour

explanation: The correct answer is B (A load whose maximum current is expected to continue for three hours or more): Article 100 defines a continuous load as one where the maximum current is expected to continue for three hours or more. A display running about ten hours easily meets that definition, so the 125 percent sizing rules apply to its conductors and overcurrent protection. Shorter or longer thresholds are not part of the definition. Control by a timer or photocell has no bearing on whether the load is classed as continuous.

question: Nine feet from the nearest sink, a kitchen remodel places a receptacle on a peninsula countertop. The electrician argues that GFCI protection applies only within six feet of a sink, yet the inspector fails the outlet. Which resolution matches the code for dwelling unit kitchens?

options.A: Skip GFCI, since the outlet is farther than six feet from the nearest kitchen sink
options.B: Provide GFCI protection, since all dwelling kitchen countertop receptacles need it wherever the sink sits
options.C: Provide arc-fault protection only, since that protection alone covers every receptacle serving a countertop
options.D: Provide GFCI protection only if the peninsula countertop is wider than twelve inches at the edge

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the sink-distance rule from other locations to a kitchen counter
distractor_mistakes.C: substitutes arc-fault protection for ground-fault protection
distractor_mistakes.D: adds an invented counter-width condition

explanation: The correct answer is B (Provide GFCI protection, since all dwelling kitchen countertop receptacles need it wherever the sink sits): In dwelling unit kitchens, receptacles that serve countertop surfaces must have GFCI protection, and the distance from the sink does not change that. The six foot sink-distance idea belongs to other location rules, not to kitchen countertops. Arc-fault protection is a separate requirement and does not replace ground-fault protection. No counter-width exception removes the GFCI requirement from a peninsula outlet.

question: An electrician is quoting a lighted storefront sign that is connected to a dedicated 20 ampere circuit. The estimator needs the article of the Code that contains the specific installation rules for electric signs and outline lighting. Which article should the electrician open first?

options.A: Article 410, which covers luminaires, lampholders and lamps in general
options.B: Article 680, which covers swimming pools, fountains and similar installations
options.C: Article 600, which covers electric signs and outline lighting
options.D: Article 422, which covers appliances connected to branch circuits

distractor_mistakes.A: picks the general luminaire article instead of the sign article
distractor_mistakes.B: picks the pool article by confusing it with outdoor lighting
distractor_mistakes.D: picks the appliance article because a sign is a connected load

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 600, which covers electric signs and outline lighting): Article 600 is the specific article for electric signs and outline lighting, including disconnects, branch circuits and field wiring. Article 410 covers general luminaires, and a specific article takes precedence over a general rule where both could apply. Article 680 deals with pools and fountains, and Article 422 deals with appliances. A sign is not treated as either of those.

question: Three 2-wire 120 volt circuits are pulled into one conduit by an electrician, giving three ungrounded and three grounded conductors. Each grounded conductor carries the current of its own circuit. For the ampacity adjustment table, what adjustment factor applies to these conductors?

options.A: 80 percent, the factor for four through six current-carrying conductors in a raceway
options.B: 70 percent, the factor for seven through nine current-carrying conductors in a raceway
options.C: 50 percent, the factor for ten through twenty current-carrying conductors in a raceway
options.D: 100 percent, since circuit neutrals do not count when adjusting conductor ampacity

distractor_mistakes.B: uses the seven through nine conductor row instead of the four through six row
distractor_mistakes.C: jumps to the ten through twenty conductor row
distractor_mistakes.D: does not count the grounded conductors that carry current

explanation: The correct answer is A (80 percent, the factor for four through six current-carrying conductors in a raceway): Each grounded conductor here carries its own circuit current, so it counts as current-carrying. The raceway holds six current-carrying conductors, and the adjustment table gives 80 percent for four through six. The 70 percent row starts at seven conductors, and the 50 percent row starts at ten. Leaving the neutrals out would give three conductors and no adjustment, which understates the heating.

question: Feeder sizing under Article 120 for a single-phase 120/240 volt dwelling includes a household electric range with a calculated demand of 8,000 volt-amperes. The electrician now sizes the feeder neutral. How may the range load be treated when calculating the neutral conductor?

options.A: The neutral load may be taken as 70 percent of the range demand load
options.B: The neutral load must be taken as 100 percent, because ranges include 120 volt loads
options.C: The neutral load may be taken as 50 percent of the range demand load
options.D: The neutral load may be omitted, since the range is supplied by a 240 volt circuit

distractor_mistakes.B: carries the full range demand on the neutral
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a 50 percent reduction that the code does not give for ranges
distractor_mistakes.D: omits the neutral even though the range has 120 volt elements

explanation: The correct answer is A (The neutral load may be taken as 70 percent of the range demand load): For a household electric range on a 120/240 volt feeder, the neutral demand may be reduced to 70 percent of the range demand load. Part of a range load is 120 volt, so a neutral is needed and cannot be dropped. Using 100 percent would size the neutral larger than the rule requires. A 50 percent factor has no basis in the range neutral provision.

question: A homeowner asks an electrician where a branch circuit starts and ends, so a new wall clock outlet can be labeled correctly on the panel directory. By the Article 100 definition, what does the term branch circuit describe in this situation?

options.A: The circuit conductors between the final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlets it serves
options.B: The circuit conductors between the service equipment and the final branch-circuit overcurrent device
options.C: The circuit conductors between the final overcurrent device and the utilization equipment's own internal wiring
options.D: The circuit conductors between the service point and the first overcurrent device in the premises

distractor_mistakes.B: describes a feeder instead of a branch circuit
distractor_mistakes.C: extends the branch circuit past the outlet into the equipment
distractor_mistakes.D: describes service conductors instead of a branch circuit

explanation: The correct answer is A (The circuit conductors between the final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlets it serves): Article 100 defines a branch circuit as the circuit conductors between the final overcurrent device protecting the circuit and the outlets it serves. Conductors between the service equipment and that final device are feeders, so the service-to-device description names the wrong segment. Service conductors run from the service point to the service disconnecting means. The branch circuit ends at the outlet and does not include wiring inside the equipment.

question: Reading the 2026 NEC load calculation rules for a dwelling, a designer asks what the 3 volt-ampere per square foot unit load is still used for. Which statement matches how Article 120 treats 3 volt-amperes and 2 volt-amperes per square foot?

options.A: Three volt-amperes is used for feeders and services, while two volt-amperes sets the number of circuits
options.B: Two volt-amperes applies only to the optional method, while three sizes feeders in the standard method
options.C: Both values apply to feeders and services, with three used for the first 3,000 volt-amperes only
options.D: Three volt-amperes sets the minimum circuit count, while two volt-amperes sizes feeders and services

distractor_mistakes.A: swaps which unit load serves which purpose
distractor_mistakes.B: confines the 2 volt-ampere value to the optional method
distractor_mistakes.C: blends the unit loads with the old demand factor tiers

explanation: The correct answer is D (Three volt-amperes sets the minimum circuit count, while two volt-amperes sizes feeders and services): In the 2026 edition the 3 volt-ampere per square foot value is kept only to determine the minimum number of branch circuits. Standard-method feeder and service calculations in dwellings use 2 volt-amperes per square foot. The roles are not swapped, and the 2 volt-ampere figure is not confined to the optional method. The first 3,000 volt-amperes demand tier is a separate step and does not select a unit load.

question: Shared neutral hot to the touch, with discolored insulation, appears on a multiwire branch circuit with two ungrounded conductors feeding two kitchen counters. Both circuits are on 20 ampere breakers, and neither ungrounded conductor is overloaded. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The shared neutral is spliced with an undersized wire nut rated for smaller conductors
options.B: The breakers lack a handle tie, which lets one circuit remain energized during service work
options.C: The neutral conductor is a different color than the ungrounded conductors it serves in the cable
options.D: Both ungrounded conductors land on breakers fed from the same phase leg, so neutral currents add

distractor_mistakes.A: blames a wire nut instead of the phase arrangement
distractor_mistakes.B: blames a missing handle tie, a different code problem
distractor_mistakes.C: blames conductor color, which does not heat a neutral

explanation: The correct answer is D (Both ungrounded conductors land on breakers fed from the same phase leg, so neutral currents add): On a multiwire branch circuit the ungrounded conductors must connect to opposite phase legs so their neutral currents partly cancel. If both land on the same leg, the neutral carries the sum of the two loads, which can exceed its rating even though each ungrounded conductor is within limits. A missing handle tie is a separate rule about simultaneous disconnection and does not heat the neutral. Conductor color has no effect on heating.

question: Fourteen risers make up a dwelling interior stairway that connects a first-floor hallway to an upstairs bedroom floor. An inspector finds one wall switch controlling the stair light, located at the bottom only. What correction does the lighting outlet rule for dwellings require?

options.A: Add a switch at the midpoint landing so the light is controlled from the center
options.B: Replace the bottom switch with a timer that turns the stair light off automatically
options.C: Add a second switch at the top floor level so lighting is controlled from each level
options.D: Add a switch at the garage entrance so the stair light is controlled from there

distractor_mistakes.A: places the extra switch at a midpoint landing instead of each floor level
distractor_mistakes.B: substitutes a timer for the required switch locations
distractor_mistakes.D: adds a switch at a different entry that the stairway rule does not name

explanation: The correct answer is C (Add a second switch at the top floor level so lighting is controlled from each level): Interior stairways with six or more risers need lighting controlled by a wall switch at each floor level where the stairway has an entry. The stair here has fourteen risers, so a switch must be available at the upper level as well as the lower one, normally with three-way switches. A switch at a midpoint landing does not meet the floor-level requirement. A timer alone does not provide the required control at each level.

question: Single continuous-duty motor on a branch circuit: the motor table gives a full-load current of 16 amperes. An electrician sizing the branch-circuit conductors applies the standard motor rule for a single motor. What minimum conductor ampacity is required before any temperature or bundling adjustments?

options.A: 16 amperes, which is 100 percent of the table full-load current for the motor
options.B: 18.4 amperes, which is 115 percent of the table full-load current for the motor
options.C: 20 amperes, which is 125 percent of the 16 ampere full-load current
options.D: 24 amperes, which is 150 percent of the table full-load current for the motor

distractor_mistakes.A: uses 100 percent of the full-load current with no motor factor
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the 115 percent factor used for certain other rules
distractor_mistakes.D: applies a 150 percent factor from a different motor rule

explanation: The correct answer is C (20 amperes, which is 125 percent of the 16 ampere full-load current): Conductors for a single motor used in continuous duty are sized at not less than 125 percent of the motor full-load current from the table. Sixteen times 1.25 is 20 amperes. Using 100 percent ignores the motor rule, and 115 percent is a factor used for other motor applications. The 150 percent figure does not apply to a single continuous-duty motor conductor.

question: Landed on a disconnect whose terminal markings read CU only, 6 AWG aluminum branch-circuit conductors draw the inspector's attention. The installer says the conductors are the right ampacity for the load. What corrective action satisfies the termination rule for these conductors?

options.A: Keep the terminals and apply listed antioxidant joint compound at the lug before tightening to torque
options.B: Keep the terminals and upsize the aluminum conductors to 4 AWG so ampacity exceeds the load
options.C: Keep the terminals because 6 AWG aluminum is allowed on equipment rated 60 amperes or less
options.D: Replace the terminals with devices listed and marked for aluminum, such as AL or CU-AL markings

distractor_mistakes.A: uses joint compound as a substitute for aluminum-rated terminals
distractor_mistakes.B: treats larger ampacity as a fix for terminal marking
distractor_mistakes.C: wrongly extends an equipment size allowance to CU only terminals

explanation: The correct answer is D (Replace the terminals with devices listed and marked for aluminum, such as AL or CU-AL markings): Section 110.14 requires terminals to be identified for the conductor material, so aluminum conductors need terminals marked AL or CU-AL. A CU only marking excludes aluminum. Compound helps at a terminal already listed for aluminum but cannot replace the marking. Larger conductors do not change what the lug is marked for, and no equipment rating permits aluminum on a copper-only terminal.

question: Supplying a lighting panelboard with no receptacle branch circuits, a 4 AWG THWN copper feeder with 75 degree terminations has an ampacity of 85 amperes. The installer asks for the largest standard overcurrent device the next-size-up rule permits for this feeder. What rating is permitted?

options.A: 90 amperes, the next standard size above the 85 ampere conductor ampacity
options.B: 80 amperes, the standard size below the 85 ampere conductor ampacity
options.C: 100 amperes, the standard size two steps above the 85 ampere conductor ampacity
options.D: 95 amperes, the 90 degree column ampacity of the conductor used directly

distractor_mistakes.B: rounds down to the smaller standard size instead of using the allowed next size up
distractor_mistakes.C: jumps two standard sizes above the ampacity
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the 95 ampere 90 degree value, which is not a standard rating

explanation: The correct answer is A (90 amperes, the next standard size above the 85 ampere conductor ampacity): When conductor ampacity does not match a standard overcurrent device size, the next higher standard size may be used for conductors that are not part of a multioutlet receptacle circuit and for ratings up to 800 amperes. The standard sizes around 85 amperes are 80, 90 and 100, so 90 is the next size up. The 95 ampere value is the 90 degree ampacity and is not a standard size. A 100 ampere device skips a size and would leave the conductor underprotected.

question: A 20 ampere, 120 volt general-use branch circuit will serve several receptacles in a school classroom. The installer has both 15 ampere and 20 ampere duplex receptacles on the truck. According to the receptacle rating table, which receptacle ratings are permitted on this circuit?

options.A: Only 20 ampere receptacles, because every receptacle must match the circuit rating exactly
options.B: Only 15 ampere receptacles, because receptacle ratings are limited to the lowest standard size
options.C: Either 20 ampere or 30 ampere receptacles, because larger ratings give extra capacity margin
options.D: Either 15 ampere or 20 ampere receptacles, because the table allows both on that circuit

distractor_mistakes.A: requires an exact match between receptacle and circuit rating
distractor_mistakes.B: limits the receptacles to 15 amperes
distractor_mistakes.C: allows a 30 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit

explanation: The correct answer is D (Either 15 ampere or 20 ampere receptacles, because the table allows both on that circuit): The receptacle rating table permits 15 or 20 ampere receptacles on a 20 ampere circuit that serves two or more receptacles. A single receptacle on an individual branch circuit has a different rule, so the exact-match idea does not apply here. A 30 ampere receptacle would exceed what the 20 ampere circuit may supply under the table. Limiting the circuit to 15 ampere devices is not required either.

question: A 10 AWG copper THHN conductor with a 90 degree rating is installed in a conduit with five current-carrying conductors. The terminals are rated 75 degrees. Applying the adjustment factor correctly, what allowable ampacity may the installer use for this conductor?

options.A: 32 amperes, found by adjusting the 90 degree value of 40 amperes by 80 percent
options.B: 28 amperes, found by adjusting the 75 degree value of 35 amperes by 80 percent
options.C: 35 amperes, found by using the 75 degree value with no bundling adjustment
options.D: 40 amperes, found by using the 90 degree value with no bundling adjustment

distractor_mistakes.B: adjusts the 75 degree column value instead of the 90 degree value
distractor_mistakes.C: ignores the bundling adjustment and uses the 75 degree value
distractor_mistakes.D: ignores the bundling adjustment and uses the 90 degree value

explanation: The correct answer is A (32 amperes, found by adjusting the 90 degree value of 40 amperes by 80 percent): Adjustment factors are applied to the 90 degree column value, and the result is then compared with the termination limit. Forty amperes times 0.80 is 32 amperes, which is below the 35 ampere 75 degree value, so 32 amperes governs. Applying 80 percent to the 75 degree value gives 28 amperes and needlessly penalizes the conductor. Using 35 or 40 amperes ignores the five-conductor adjustment that the installation requires.

question: Every time a toaster is plugged in, a dwelling kitchen countertop receptacle circuit trips its GFCI device, yet the toaster works on a neighbour's circuit. The electrician finds the circuit's neutral is tied to another circuit's neutral at a junction box. What is the cause of the repeated trips?

options.A: The toaster draws more than the 20 ampere circuit rating, so the GFCI trips on overload
options.B: The GFCI is wired with its line and load terminals reversed, so it trips under load
options.C: The shared neutral lets some return current bypass the GFCI sensor, creating an imbalance
options.D: An open equipment grounding conductor lets leakage current flow, so the GFCI senses a fault

distractor_mistakes.A: blames overload for a trip that the breaker would handle
distractor_mistakes.B: blames reversed line and load terminals
distractor_mistakes.D: blames an open equipment grounding conductor

explanation: The correct answer is C (The shared neutral lets some return current bypass the GFCI sensor, creating an imbalance): A GFCI compares the current on the hot and neutral conductors it protects. A neutral tied to another circuit's neutral lets part of the return current flow outside the device, so the GFCI sees an imbalance when a load starts. An overload would trip the breaker rather than the GFCI. Reversed terminals on a GFCI do not cause a trip under load, and an open grounding conductor is not sensed by the GFCI.

question: Display lighting running 14 amperes continuously and a separate 8 ampere noncontinuous receptacle load share one branch circuit. The electrician selects the smallest standard overcurrent device allowed by the rule for a mixed load. Which rating does the calculation require?

options.A: 25 amperes, because adding the two loads at 100 percent gives 22, rounded up
options.B: 20 amperes, because 125 percent of the continuous load alone is 17.5, rounded up
options.C: 35 amperes, because the continuous load is 17.5 and the noncontinuous load is doubled
options.D: 30 amperes, since 125 percent of 14 plus 8 is 25.5, rounded to the next size

distractor_mistakes.A: adds the loads at 100 percent with no continuous load factor
distractor_mistakes.B: applies 125 percent to only the continuous load and drops the other load
distractor_mistakes.C: doubles the noncontinuous load and adds it to the factored continuous load

explanation: The correct answer is D (30 amperes, since 125 percent of 14 plus 8 is 25.5, rounded to the next size): The OCPD must be rated for the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load. Fourteen times 1.25 is 17.5, and adding 8 gives 25.5 amperes. The next standard size above 25.5 is 30 amperes. A 25 ampere device is below the calculated value, and 20 amperes ignores the noncontinuous load. Doubling the noncontinuous load is not part of the rule.

question: Optional method calculations apply to a homeowner's addition on a dwelling under the 2026 NEC. General loads total 18,000 volt-amperes. What demand load results when the first 8 kilovolt-amperes is taken at 100 percent and the remainder at 40 percent?

options.A: 12,000 volt-amperes, which is 8,000 plus 40 percent of the remaining 10,000
options.B: 13,200 volt-amperes, which is 10,000 plus 40 percent of the remaining 8,000
options.C: 7,200 volt-amperes, which is 40 percent applied to the full 18,000
options.D: 18,000 volt-amperes, which is all general loads taken at face value

distractor_mistakes.B: uses the 2023 threshold of the first 10 kilovolt-amperes
distractor_mistakes.C: applies 40 percent to the entire general load
distractor_mistakes.D: takes no demand reduction at all

explanation: The correct answer is A (12,000 volt-amperes, which is 8,000 plus 40 percent of the remaining 10,000): Under the 2026 optional method, the first 8 kilovolt-amperes of general loads is taken at 100 percent and the remainder at 40 percent. The remainder is 18,000 minus 8,000, or 10,000, and 40 percent of that is 4,000, for a demand of 12,000 volt-amperes. The 13,200 figure uses the older 10 kilovolt-ampere threshold. Applying 40 percent to the entire load ignores the 100 percent block.

question: Section 210.11(C)(2) calls for at least one 20 ampere branch circuit for the laundry in a dwelling unit. A homeowner asks the electrician whether the circuit may also supply other outlets in the house. Which statement describes what the laundry circuit may supply?

options.A: Only the laundry receptacle outlets, since this 20 ampere circuit may have no other outlets
options.B: The laundry outlets and the receptacles in the adjoining basement bathroom on the same circuit
options.C: The laundry outlets and the dining room small-appliance receptacles on the same circuit
options.D: The laundry outlets and the general lighting in the adjoining hallway on the same circuit

distractor_mistakes.B: adds a bathroom to the laundry circuit
distractor_mistakes.C: adds small-appliance receptacles to the laundry circuit
distractor_mistakes.D: adds hallway lighting to the laundry circuit

explanation: The correct answer is A (Only the laundry receptacle outlets, since this 20 ampere circuit may have no other outlets): The required laundry circuit is a 20 ampere branch circuit that supplies the laundry receptacle outlets and has no other outlets. It cannot be shared with bathroom receptacles, which have their own circuit rule, or with small-appliance receptacles, which must stay on their own circuits. Hallway lighting would also be another outlet, which the rule does not allow.

question: Three 20 ampere small-appliance branch circuits serve the kitchen and dining areas of a dwelling, instead of the minimum two. For the feeder load calculation under the standard method, how is the small-appliance load counted before demand factors are applied?

options.A: 1,500 volt-amperes for two circuits only, treating the third as a spare circuit
options.B: 2,400 volt-amperes for each circuit, using the full rating of each circuit
options.C: Excluded from the feeder, since small-appliance circuits are not general loads
options.D: 1,500 volt-amperes for each circuit, giving 4,500 volt-amperes added to the lighting load

distractor_mistakes.A: counts only two circuits and ignores the third
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the full 2,400 volt-ampere rating of each circuit
distractor_mistakes.C: omits the small-appliance load from the feeder calculation

explanation: The correct answer is D (1,500 volt-amperes for each circuit, giving 4,500 volt-amperes added to the lighting load): Each small-appliance branch circuit is counted at 1,500 volt-amperes in the dwelling feeder calculation, and the result is added to the general lighting load before demand factors apply. With three circuits the total is 4,500 volt-amperes. Counting only two ignores a circuit that exists. The 2,400 volt-ampere figure is the circuit capacity, not the load value the calculation assigns, and omitting the load would understate the feeder.

question: Workshop air compressor gets one dedicated 20 ampere, 120 volt branch circuit supplying a single receptacle, installed by a contractor. The supplier has 15 ampere and 20 ampere receptacles in stock. What is the minimum receptacle rating allowed for this individual branch circuit?

options.A: 20 amperes, because a single receptacle on an individual circuit must rate at least the circuit
options.B: 15 amperes, because any standard receptacle is acceptable on a 20 ampere branch circuit
options.C: 30 amperes, because a dedicated circuit needs a receptacle rated above its overcurrent device
options.D: 10 amperes, because the compressor load is below the circuit rating by a wide margin

distractor_mistakes.B: applies the multiple-receptacle rule to a single receptacle
distractor_mistakes.C: raises the receptacle rating above the circuit rating
distractor_mistakes.D: sizes the receptacle to the load instead of the circuit

explanation: The correct answer is A (20 amperes, because a single receptacle on an individual circuit must rate at least the circuit): A single receptacle on an individual branch circuit must have an ampere rating not less than that of the circuit. With a 20 ampere circuit, the receptacle must be rated at least 20 amperes. The 15 ampere allowance exists only for circuits serving two or more receptacles. A 30 ampere receptacle is not required, and sizing to the load instead of the circuit would break the rule.

question: An electrician wires a dwelling multiwire branch circuit with two single-pole breakers feeding two devices from one shared neutral. The inspector asks how the ungrounded conductors must be disconnected at the point the circuit starts. Which method satisfies the requirement?

options.A: Use two independent single-pole breakers, since each ungrounded conductor serves its own device
options.B: Use one single-pole breaker with a GFCI on the second leg to open the circuit
options.C: Use two single-pole breakers fed from the same phase bus leg to keep the neutral balanced
options.D: Use a two-pole breaker or a handle tie so both ungrounded conductors open simultaneously

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the two legs as independent circuits that need no common disconnect
distractor_mistakes.B: thinks a GFCI on one leg replaces a simultaneous disconnect
distractor_mistakes.C: puts both legs on the same phase, which overloads the neutral

explanation: The correct answer is D (Use a two-pole breaker or a handle tie so both ungrounded conductors open simultaneously): A multiwire branch circuit must disconnect all its ungrounded conductors simultaneously at the point where the circuit originates, normally with a two-pole breaker or an approved handle tie. Independent single-pole breakers leave one leg energized while the other is off, which endangers someone working on the shared neutral. A GFCI does not provide a simultaneous disconnect. Putting both legs on the same phase leg also overloads the neutral.

question: Dryer nameplate reads 4,500 watts for a tenant's electric clothes dryer, and an estimator is sizing a dwelling feeder under the standard method for the building. What load should be used for the dryer in the feeder calculation, according to the dwelling dryer load rule?

options.A: 4,500 volt-amperes, since the nameplate rating is the load used for every appliance
options.B: 5,000 volt-amperes, since the dryer minimum is 5,000 or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger
options.C: 3,150 volt-amperes, since 70 percent of the nameplate rating is the feeder dryer load value
options.D: 5,625 volt-amperes, since the nameplate rating is increased by 125 percent for dryers in dwellings

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the nameplate rating even though it is below the minimum
distractor_mistakes.C: applies a 70 percent factor that belongs to neutral calculations
distractor_mistakes.D: applies a 125 percent factor that is not part of the dryer rule

explanation: The correct answer is B (5,000 volt-amperes, since the dryer minimum is 5,000 or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger): For an electric dryer in a dwelling feeder calculation, the load is 5,000 volt-amperes or the nameplate rating, whichever is larger. With a nameplate of 4,500 watts, the 5,000 volt-ampere minimum applies. Using the nameplate would undercount the load. The 70 percent figure belongs to feeder neutral reductions rather than the dryer load, and there is no 125 percent increase in the dryer rule.

question: A small office building has 40 general-purpose duplex receptacles on standard 20 ampere branch circuits, with no other receptacle loads. For the feeder calculation, what load is assigned to these receptacles when each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke counts at 180 volt-amperes?

options.A: 7,200 volt-amperes, at 180 volt-amperes for each of the 40 duplex receptacles
options.B: 14,400 volt-amperes, at 180 volt-amperes for each of the 80 receptacle outlets
options.C: 4,000 volt-amperes, at 100 volt-amperes for each of the 40 duplex receptacles
options.D: 5,760 volt-amperes, at 80 percent of the 7,200 volt-ampere receptacle load

distractor_mistakes.B: counts each half of a duplex as a separate receptacle
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a 100 volt-ampere value from a different rule
distractor_mistakes.D: applies an 80 percent factor that does not belong here

explanation: The correct answer is A (7,200 volt-amperes, at 180 volt-amperes for each of the 40 duplex receptacles): Each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke is counted at not less than 180 volt-amperes in nondwelling occupancies. A duplex receptacle is one yoke, so 40 duplex receptacles give 40 times 180, or 7,200 volt-amperes. Counting each half as its own receptacle would double the load. The 100 volt-ampere value does not apply, and the 80 percent factor is a continuous-load idea that is not applied here.

question: Continuous nameplate draw of 16 amperes comes from one fixed heater on a dedicated 20 ampere branch circuit, and an apprentice questions whether the circuit is adequate for continuous use in a small shop. Which conclusion is correct for this single fixed appliance?

options.A: Inadequate, because the breaker must exceed 125 percent of 16 amperes, which is 20 amperes
options.B: Adequate, because 125 percent of 16 amperes is 20 amperes, equal to the breaker rating
options.C: Inadequate, because 16 amperes exceeds 12 amperes, which is 80 percent of a 15 ampere circuit
options.D: The circuit is inadequate, because 125 percent is applied twice, requiring a 25 ampere breaker

distractor_mistakes.A: requires the breaker to exceed 125 percent of the load
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a 15 ampere circuit rating for the 80 percent check
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the 125 percent continuous factor twice

explanation: The correct answer is B (Adequate, because 125 percent of 16 amperes is 20 amperes, equal to the breaker rating): A continuous load may be as large as 80 percent of the OCPD rating because the OCPD must be at least 125 percent of that load. Sixteen times 1.25 is 20 amperes, which equals the 20 ampere breaker, so the circuit is adequate. The rule is that the OCPD is not less than 125 percent, so an equal value passes. Using a 15 ampere base or applying the factor twice gives numbers that do not belong to this circuit.

question: Floor area used for the general lighting load comes under review as a building inspector checks a dwelling plan. Which spaces are excluded from the floor area, based on the rule for dwelling units, when the plan lists porches, a garage and finished rooms?

options.A: Computed from outside dimensions, excluding open porches, garages, and unused spaces not adaptable for future use
options.B: Open porches, garages, and unfinished basements are excluded whether or not they are adaptable for use
options.C: Open porches, garages, and attached sunrooms are excluded because none are habitable space
options.D: Garages and unfinished spaces are excluded, but open porches are counted at half area

distractor_mistakes.B: excludes unfinished basements even when adaptable
distractor_mistakes.C: treats attached sunrooms as excluded space
distractor_mistakes.D: counts open porches at half area

explanation: The correct answer is A (Computed from outside dimensions, excluding open porches, garages, and unused spaces not adaptable for future use): The floor area for the dwelling lighting load comes from outside dimensions and excludes open porches, garages, and unused or unfinished spaces not adaptable for future use. A basement that can be finished is counted, so excluding all basements is wrong. Heated sunrooms are habitable and are counted. Open porches are excluded outright, with no half-area treatment for any floor.

question: An electrician plans a 60 ampere, 240 volt outdoor receptacle for a welder on the side of a dwelling and wants to know what changed between the 2023 and 2026 editions for dwelling outdoor outlets. Which statement matches the 2026 NEC?

options.A: GFCI protection still applies only to outdoor outlets rated 50 amperes or less, as in 2023
options.B: GFCI protection now covers outdoor dwelling outlets rated 60 amperes or less, up from 50 amperes
options.C: GFCI protection now applies only to outdoor outlets within six feet of the dwelling wall
options.D: GFCI protection for outdoor outlets was moved entirely to Article 625 for vehicle charging

distractor_mistakes.A: keeps the 2023 threshold of 50 amperes
distractor_mistakes.C: adds a six foot distance condition that is not in the rule
distractor_mistakes.D: claims the outdoor rule moved to the vehicle charging article

explanation: The correct answer is B (GFCI protection now covers outdoor dwelling outlets rated 60 amperes or less, up from 50 amperes): The 2026 edition raises the outdoor GFCI threshold for dwelling units from 50 amperes to 60 amperes, so a 60 ampere outdoor receptacle now needs protection. Keeping the 2023 limit would leave this welder outlet unprotected. There is no distance condition in the rule, and Article 625 covers charging equipment but does not take over the general outdoor outlet rule.

question: Ampacity comes up when a foreman asks an apprentice to explain the term while selecting conductors for a mixed office and shop wiring job. Which definition matches Article 100 for the ampacity of a conductor, as used when choosing conductor sizes?

options.A: The maximum current a conductor carries for a few minutes before its insulation begins to fail
options.B: The maximum current a conductor carries continuously under conditions of use without exceeding its rated temperature
options.C: The maximum voltage a conductor may be exposed to under conditions of use in normal service
options.D: The maximum current an overcurrent device allows to flow before the device opens the circuit

distractor_mistakes.A: describes a short-time overload instead of continuous capacity
distractor_mistakes.C: describes a voltage rating instead of current capacity
distractor_mistakes.D: describes the trip rating of a protective device instead of conductor capacity

explanation: The correct answer is B (The maximum current a conductor carries continuously under conditions of use without exceeding its rated temperature): Ampacity is the maximum current, in amperes, that a conductor can carry continuously under the conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating. It is not a short-time overload value, and it is not a voltage rating. The trip level of an overcurrent device is a different quantity, because the device is selected to protect the conductor rather than define its capacity.

question: Flickering lights at the end of a 100 foot, 120 volt circuit in a barn appear when a 16 ampere load starts. The circuit uses 12 AWG copper, 100 feet one way. Using K equal to 12.9 and 6,530 circular mils for 12 AWG, what is the voltage drop at 16 amperes?

options.A: 3.2 volts, using only the one-way length of 100 feet in the formula
options.B: 6.3 volts, using twice the one-way length in the two-wire circuit formula
options.C: 7.9 volts, using the 20 ampere breaker rating instead of the 16 ampere load
options.D: 12.6 volts, using twice the one-way length counted two times in the formula

distractor_mistakes.A: uses only the one-way length and halves the drop
distractor_mistakes.C: substitutes the breaker rating for the actual load current
distractor_mistakes.D: counts the round-trip length twice

explanation: The correct answer is B (6.3 volts, using twice the one-way length in the two-wire circuit formula): For a two-wire circuit the drop is 2 times K times current times one-way length divided by circular mils. That is 2 times 12.9 times 16 times 100 divided by 6,530, or 41,280 divided by 6,530, about 6.3 volts. Using only one-way length gives 3.2 volts. Using 20 amperes gives 7.9 volts, which is the breaker rating rather than the actual load, and doubling the round trip again gives 12.6 volts.

question: Ambient temperature of 40 degrees Celsius surrounds a 6 AWG THHN copper conductor rated 90 degrees. It carries a noncontinuous load and terminates on 75 degree rated lugs, with three current-carrying conductors. The 90 degree correction factor at 40 degrees is 0.91. What is its allowable ampacity?

options.A: 75 amperes, since the 90 degree column value applies without correction at the terminals
options.B: 59 amperes, since the 75 degree column value is reduced by the 0.91 correction factor
options.C: 65 amperes, since the corrected value of 68.25 amperes exceeds the 75 degree termination limit
options.D: 68 amperes, since the corrected 90 degree value is used with no termination limit

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the uncorrected 90 degree value at the terminals
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the correction factor to the 75 degree value instead of the 90 degree value
distractor_mistakes.D: ignores the termination limit after correcting the 90 degree value

explanation: The correct answer is C (65 amperes, since the corrected value of 68.25 amperes exceeds the 75 degree termination limit): The correction factor is applied to the 90 degree value of 75 amperes, giving 75 times 0.91, or 68.25 amperes. That result must not exceed the 75 degree termination value of 65 amperes, so 65 amperes governs. Using 75 amperes ignores the ambient correction. Correcting the 75 degree value gives 59 amperes, which is too low, and using 68 amperes ignores the terminal limit.

question: Wet raceway to a pump house carries 6 AWG copper conductors marked only THWN along a trench. The electrician needs the highest temperature rating used to find ampacity for this conductor in a wet location. What temperature rating applies in the ampacity table?

options.A: 90 degrees Celsius, because the conductor insulation is thermoplastic with a nylon jacket
options.B: 75 degrees Celsius, the rating for a THWN conductor installed in a wet location
options.C: 60 degrees Celsius, the limit for terminations on circuits rated 100 amperes or less
options.D: 90 degrees Celsius, the rating of any conductor listed for both wet and dry locations

distractor_mistakes.A: assumes the nylon jacket raises the wet rating to 90 degrees
distractor_mistakes.C: applies the termination limit to the conductor rating
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes dual wet and dry listing gives the 90 degree wet rating

explanation: The correct answer is B (75 degrees Celsius, the rating for a THWN conductor installed in a wet location): A conductor marked only THWN is rated 75 degrees Celsius in a wet location, so the 75 degree column applies. A 90 degree wet rating needs a marking such as THWN-2, and a nylon jacket alone does not provide it. The 60 degree limit is a termination matter for small circuits and does not set this conductor's rating. Dual wet and dry listing does not by itself raise the wet rating.

question: Final inspection brings a dispute: a contractor challenges the inspector's reading of a Code rule and wants a decision on whether the installation is acceptable. The inspector says only one person or office holds that authority. Which party holds the authority to interpret the Code and approve equipment?

options.A: The equipment manufacturer, whose installation instructions override any Code requirement in the field
options.B: The electrical contractor, whose licence allows final interpretation of any installation rule on site
options.C: The authority having jurisdiction, the organization or individual responsible for enforcing the Code
options.D: The testing laboratory, whose listing decides whether an installation passes inspection or not

distractor_mistakes.A: gives the manufacturer authority over Code enforcement
distractor_mistakes.B: gives the licensed contractor final interpretive authority
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses product listing with enforcement authority

explanation: The correct answer is C (The authority having jurisdiction, the organization or individual responsible for enforcing the Code): The authority having jurisdiction is the organization, office or individual responsible for enforcing the Code and for approving equipment and installations. Manufacturer instructions must be followed but cannot override the Code. A contractor does not hold final interpretive authority. A testing laboratory lists products but does not decide whether an installation passes inspection.

question: Before sizing a feeder for a small workshop, a new apprentice needs the article that gives the general requirements for conductors used in wiring, including ampacity tables and insulation types. Which article of the Code contains Table 310.16 and the general conductor rules?

options.A: Article 300, which covers general wiring methods and installation requirements
options.B: Article 250, which covers grounding and bonding of electrical systems
options.C: Article 310, which covers conductors for general wiring, including Table 310.16
options.D: Article 110, which covers requirements for electrical installations in general

distractor_mistakes.A: picks the general wiring methods article instead of the conductor article
distractor_mistakes.B: picks the grounding article because conductors are bonded
distractor_mistakes.D: picks the general requirements article instead of the conductor article

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 310, which covers conductors for general wiring, including Table 310.16): Article 310 holds the general requirements for conductors, including insulation types and the allowable ampacity tables. Article 300 covers wiring methods, Article 250 covers grounding and bonding, and Article 110 covers general installation requirements. Because conductor ampacity tables sit in Article 310, that is where the apprentice should look.

question: Chapter 2 holds a general rule that permits an installation, but Chapter 6 has a special rule for the same marina installation that is more restrictive, an electrician finds. Which statement describes how the Code treats the two rules when they differ in this way?

options.A: Chapter 2 governs, since Chapters 1 through 4 apply to all installations and cannot be modified
options.B: Chapters 5 through 7 supplement or modify Chapters 1 through 4, so the special rule governs
options.C: Chapters 5 through 7 modify Chapters 1 through 4 only where the general article cross-references them
options.D: Chapters 5 through 7 apply only in hazardous locations, so the Chapter 2 rule governs

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the general chapters as unmodifiable
distractor_mistakes.C: requires a cross-reference for the special chapters to apply
distractor_mistakes.D: limits chapters 5 through 7 to hazardous locations

explanation: The correct answer is B (Chapters 5 through 7 supplement or modify Chapters 1 through 4, so the special rule governs): Chapters 5, 6 and 7 supplement or modify the general rules in Chapters 1 through 4, so a special rule governs where it differs. No cross-reference is needed for that to apply. The general chapters can be modified, so the Chapter 2 rule does not override the special one. Chapters 5 through 7 cover special occupancies, equipment and conditions, not only hazardous locations.

question: Listed equipment rated for 60 amperes, with terminals that have no temperature marking, is wired with copper THHN conductors for a 40 ampere noncontinuous heater load. The AHJ asks for the smallest conductor that satisfies the 60 degree termination presumption. Which size is correct?

options.A: 10 AWG, which is rated 40 amperes in the 90 degree column
options.B: 6 AWG, which is rated 55 amperes in the 60 degree column after applying 125 percent
options.C: 4 AWG, rated 70 amperes in the 60 degree column after applying 125 percent twice
options.D: 8 AWG, which is rated 40 amperes in the 60 degree column

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the 90 degree column value for unmarked terminals
distractor_mistakes.B: applies 125 percent to a load that is noncontinuous
distractor_mistakes.C: applies 125 percent twice and then reads the 60 degree column

explanation: The correct answer is D (8 AWG, which is rated 40 amperes in the 60 degree column): With unmarked terminals on equipment of 100 amperes or less, the 60 degree column limits the ampacity. In that column 8 AWG is 40 amperes, which equals the noncontinuous load, so 8 AWG is the smallest size. Using the 90 degree value of 10 AWG exceeds what the terminal may carry. The 125 percent factor applies only to continuous loads, so sizing up to 6 AWG or 4 AWG is not required.

question: Only when a space heater runs does the cover plate on a warm duplex receptacle get hot in a bedroom fed by 14 AWG copper cable from a 20 ampere breaker. The electrician finds no loose terminations. What is the code problem causing the overheating?

options.A: The receptacle is a 15 ampere type installed on a 20 ampere circuit with multiple outlets
options.B: The 14 AWG conductor is protected by a 20 ampere breaker, exceeding its 15 ampere limit
options.C: The cover plate is made of metal and traps heat from the space heater
options.D: The bedroom circuit lacks arc-fault protection, which causes receptacle heating

distractor_mistakes.A: thinks a 15 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit causes heating
distractor_mistakes.C: blames the cover plate material
distractor_mistakes.D: blames missing arc-fault protection for heating

explanation: The correct answer is B (The 14 AWG conductor is protected by a 20 ampere breaker, exceeding its 15 ampere limit): Small copper conductors have fixed overcurrent limits, and 14 AWG copper is limited to a 15 ampere device. A 20 ampere breaker lets the conductor carry more current than it can handle, so it overheats under a heater load. A 15 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit is permitted when several outlets are served. The cover plate material and arc-fault protection are not the cause.

question: Box fill: six 12 AWG circuit conductors, two 12 AWG grounding conductors, one duplex receptacle on a standard yoke and internal cable clamps are counted by a contractor installing a box on a residential lighting circuit. Using 2.25 cubic inches per 12 AWG conductor, what minimum box volume is required?

options.A: 20.25 cubic inches, counting six conductors, one grounding allowance and two for the device only
options.B: 24.75 cubic inches, counting both grounding conductors separately along with the other items
options.C: 22.5 cubic inches, counting six conductors, one grounding allowance, two for the device, one for clamps
options.D: 15.75 cubic inches, counting six conductors and one grounding allowance with no device or clamps

distractor_mistakes.A: leaves out the internal cable clamp allowance
distractor_mistakes.B: counts each grounding conductor separately instead of once
distractor_mistakes.D: leaves out both the device and the clamp allowances

explanation: The correct answer is C (22.5 cubic inches, counting six conductors, one grounding allowance, two for the device, one for clamps): Each circuit conductor counts once, all grounding conductors together count once, a device yoke counts twice, and internal clamps together count once. That is 6 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1, or 10 allowances, and 10 times 2.25 is 22.5 cubic inches. Leaving out the clamp allowance gives 9 allowances, or 20.25. Counting the two grounding conductors separately gives 11 allowances, or 24.75, and omitting the device and clamps gives only 7 allowances.

question: Pulling a 10 AWG insulated neutral for a branch circuit, an installer needs the correct way to identify a grounded conductor of 6 AWG or smaller on a residential job. Which identification matches the Code requirement for conductors of that size?

options.A: A continuous green outer finish along the entire length of the conductor
options.B: A continuous green outer finish with one yellow stripe along the whole conductor
options.C: A continuous white or gray outer finish along the entire length of the conductor
options.D: A continuous bare copper finish with a white marking at each termination point

distractor_mistakes.A: uses green, which identifies the equipment grounding conductor
distractor_mistakes.B: uses green with a yellow stripe, a protective conductor identification
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a bare conductor, which is not a grounded circuit conductor identification

explanation: The correct answer is C (A continuous white or gray outer finish along the entire length of the conductor): A grounded conductor of 6 AWG or smaller is identified by a continuous white or gray outer finish, or by three continuous white or gray stripes on other than green insulation. Green and green with a yellow stripe identify equipment grounding conductors. A bare conductor cannot serve as the insulated grounded conductor for a branch circuit, so it is not an acceptable identification.

question: Testing a standard Class A GFCI receptacle in a dwelling bathroom with a calibrated tester, a technician records the trip point. Which leakage current range correctly describes the trip threshold of a Class A GFCI for personnel protection at 50 to 60 hertz?

options.A: 4 to 6 milliamperes of ground-fault current at 50 to 60 hertz
options.B: 15 to 20 milliamperes of ground-fault current at 50 to 60 hertz
options.C: 30 milliamperes of ground-fault current at 50 to 60 hertz
options.D: 100 milliamperes of ground-fault current at 50 to 60 hertz

distractor_mistakes.B: gives the Class C special-purpose GFCI range
distractor_mistakes.C: gives a European residual current device value
distractor_mistakes.D: gives the equipment protection threshold rather than personnel protection

explanation: The correct answer is A (4 to 6 milliamperes of ground-fault current at 50 to 60 hertz): A Class A GFCI is designed to trip when the ground-fault current is between 4 and 6 milliamperes at 50 to 60 hertz. The 15 to 20 milliampere range belongs to the Class C special-purpose GFCI. The 30 milliampere value is a common figure for residual current devices elsewhere, and 100 milliamperes is the level used for equipment protection rather than personnel protection.

question: Loads in a distribution warehouse are being sorted before the branch circuits are sized. Under the Article 100 definition, which load counts as a continuous load that requires the 125 percent factor on the conductors and the overcurrent protective device, given the stated operating times for each?

options.A: Dock door operators that draw full current for forty seconds at a time all shift
options.B: A battery charger that runs at full current for two hours and fifty minutes nightly
options.C: A conveyor motor that cycles ten minutes on and ten minutes off all day
options.D: Aisle lighting running at full current for three hours and ten minutes each shift

distractor_mistakes.A: Treats many short cycles as if they were one long run of current
distractor_mistakes.B: Rounds two hours fifty minutes up to the three hour threshold
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds up total daily on-time instead of judging uninterrupted duration

explanation: The correct answer is D (Aisle lighting running at full current for three hours and ten minutes each shift): Article 100 defines a continuous load as one where the maximum current is expected to continue for three hours or more. Aisle lighting running three hours and ten minutes without interruption meets that test. The battery charger stops short of three hours, and the conveyor and dock operators run in separate short intervals, so the charger and cycling loads do not qualify even though total daily on-time may be long.

question: Plan reviewers at a strip-mall tenant fit-out are checking circuit ratings on the drawings, where the designer lists the ratings intended for general-purpose branch circuits. The reviewer wants each one to be a standard branch-circuit rating from Article 210. Which set lists only standard branch-circuit ratings?

options.A: Branch circuits rated 15, 20, 25, 30, and 40 amperes
options.B: Branch circuits rated 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes
options.C: Branch circuits rated 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60 amperes
options.D: Branch circuits rated 15, 20, 30, 50, and 60 amperes

distractor_mistakes.A: Inserts 25 amperes, a standard OCPD size but not a branch-circuit rating
distractor_mistakes.C: Starts at 20 and adds 60, which is a feeder-type size not listed
distractor_mistakes.D: Skips 40 and adds 60, mixing OCPD sizes into the list

explanation: The correct answer is B (Branch circuits rated 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes): Section 210.3 gives the standard branch-circuit ratings other than individual loads as 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amperes. A rating of 25 amperes exists as a standard overcurrent device size under the 240.6 list, but it is not a branch-circuit rating. Likewise 60 amperes is a standard device size, yet it is not among the listed branch-circuit ratings.

question: Fourteen amperes of noncontinuous load and 24 amperes of continuous load share one circuit fed from a small shop subpanel. The circuit overcurrent device is not listed for operation at 100 percent of its rating. What is the minimum standard overcurrent protective device rating permitted for this circuit?

options.A: 45 amperes, noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of continuous load
options.B: 40 amperes, the plain sum of the two loads rounded to a standard size
options.C: 50 amperes, 125 percent applied to both loads and rounded up
options.D: 30 amperes, 125 percent of the continuous load only

distractor_mistakes.B: Adds both loads at 100 percent and ignores the continuous-load factor
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the 125 percent factor to the noncontinuous load as well
distractor_mistakes.D: Drops the noncontinuous load after applying the factor to the continuous load

explanation: The correct answer is A (45 amperes, noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of continuous load): Section 210.20(A) requires an OCPD rating of at least the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load. That is 14 plus 24 times 1.25, which is 14 plus 30, or 44 amperes. The next standard size from the 240.6 list is 45 amperes. The 40 ampere device falls below the 44 ampere minimum because it carries no continuous-load factor.

question: Three 10 AWG THHN copper conductors are derated by an electrician for a 38 degree Celsius mechanical room, and the corrected value comes out above the 75 degree column ampacity. The equipment terminals are marked for 75 degrees. What is the highest ampacity she may use for the circuit?

options.A: 36.4 amperes, the 90 degree value after ambient temperature correction
options.B: 35 amperes, as the 75 degree terminal rating caps the final value
options.C: 40 amperes, the uncorrected 90 degree column value for 10 AWG
options.D: 30.8 amperes, the 75 degree value with ambient correction applied

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the corrected 90 degree number without checking the terminal temperature
distractor_mistakes.C: Ignores both the ambient factor and the terminal limit
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies the ambient factor a second time to the terminal-limited value

explanation: The correct answer is B (35 amperes, as the 75 degree terminal rating caps the final value): The 90 degree column gives 40 amperes for 10 AWG, and the 36 to 40 degree correction factor of 0.91 gives 36.4 amperes. Under 110.14(C), however, the final ampacity cannot exceed the value in the 75 degree column for 75 degree terminals, which is 35 amperes. The 36.4 ampere figure is useful only as a derating starting point, not as the circuit rating.

question: Run length is 60 feet in conduit for a feeder-fed circuit with 40 amperes of continuous load and 10 amperes of noncontinuous load. Copper THWN conductors land on equipment terminals marked for 75 degrees. Using Table 310.16, which copper size is the smallest permitted?

options.A: 8 AWG, sized from the plain 50 ampere sum at 75 degrees
options.B: 4 AWG, sized from the 60 degree column for 62.5 amperes
options.C: 10 AWG, using the 90 degree column for the 40 ampere continuous load
options.D: 6 AWG, the 75 degree column value of 65 amperes

distractor_mistakes.A: Skips the 125 percent factor and sizes to a 50 ampere total
distractor_mistakes.B: Reads the 60 degree column even though terminals allow 75 degrees
distractor_mistakes.C: Sizes only the continuous load from the 90 degree column

explanation: The correct answer is D (6 AWG, the 75 degree column value of 65 amperes): Minimum conductor ampacity is the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load, which is 10 plus 50, or 60 amperes. With 75 degree terminals, the 75 degree column applies, where 8 AWG gives 50 amperes and 6 AWG gives 65 amperes. So 6 AWG is the smallest size that carries 60 amperes. The 8 AWG choice results from leaving out the continuous-load factor.

question: Article 220 is cited for the service load on a dwelling calculation sheet that an inspector is reviewing. The project is permitted under the 2026 NEC, and the designer asks which article now holds the branch-circuit, feeder, and service load calculation rules for any occupancy, replacing the older numbering?

options.A: Article 210, which covers branch-circuit requirements and not feeder or service loads
options.B: Article 120, which took over the load calculation rules from Article 220
options.C: Article 130, which covers energy management systems and power control systems
options.D: Article 230, which covers services and their disconnecting means

distractor_mistakes.A: Picks the article for branch-circuit rules instead of load calculations
distractor_mistakes.C: Confuses the new energy management article with the relocated calculations
distractor_mistakes.D: Chooses the services article, which sets equipment rules rather than load methods

explanation: The correct answer is B (Article 120, which took over the load calculation rules from Article 220): The 2026 NEC relocated the load calculation rules from Article 220 to Article 120, titled Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations. Article 130 is a separate new article for energy management systems, though it is sometimes referenced from load calculations. Article 210 and Article 230 keep their own scopes and do not contain the calculation methods.

question: Identifying the white conductor correctly at every splice matters to a crew wiring a 120 volt receptacle circuit in a farm shop. Under Article 210, which identification is permitted for the grounded conductor of a branch circuit in this kind of wiring, where each circuit shares a raceway?

options.A: White or gray insulation, or one white stripe on any non-green insulation
options.B: White insulation, or gray only where the system is 277/480 volts
options.C: Any color insulation with white tape applied at terminations, for conductors 6 AWG and smaller
options.D: White or gray insulation, or three white stripes on non-green insulation

distractor_mistakes.A: uses a single white stripe instead of three
distractor_mistakes.B: limits gray to the 277/480 volt system
distractor_mistakes.C: applies the white tape allowance to small conductors

explanation: The correct answer is D (White or gray insulation, or three white stripes on non-green insulation): Section 200.6 identifies the grounded conductor by white or gray insulation, or by three continuous white stripes on other than green insulation. A single stripe does not meet the rule, and gray is not limited to one system voltage. White tape at terminations is allowed only for larger conductors, not 6 AWG and smaller. Green and green with yellow stripes belong to equipment grounding conductors.

question: Plans prepared under the 2023 NEC showed GFCI protection for outdoor dwelling receptacles only up to a certain ampere rating. A contractor asks how the 2026 NEC changed the ampere threshold that decides whether an outdoor outlet at a dwelling needs GFCI protection under Section 210.8?

options.A: The limit fell from outlets rated 60 amperes or less to 50 amperes or less
options.B: The limit rose from outlets rated 20 amperes or less to 30 amperes or less
options.C: The limit rose from outlets rated 50 amperes or less to 60 amperes or less
options.D: The limit was removed so every outdoor outlet needs GFCI protection whatever its rating

distractor_mistakes.A: Reverses the direction of the change and lowers the threshold
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses 20 and 30 ampere ratings from other GFCI lists
distractor_mistakes.D: Assumes the ampere threshold was dropped altogether

explanation: The correct answer is C (The limit rose from outlets rated 50 amperes or less to 60 amperes or less): For dwelling unit outdoor outlets, the 2026 NEC raised the GFCI threshold in 210.8 from 50 amperes to 60 amperes. Outdoor outlets rated 60 amperes or less now need protection, so more large-rated outlets are covered than under the 2023 text. The option that lowers the limit describes the opposite direction of change.

question: Copper conductors on a 120 volt single-phase circuit carry 16 amperes over a one-way distance of 100 feet. The conductors are 10 AWG with 10,380 circular mils, and the constant K for copper is 12.9. The breaker is rated 20 amperes. What is the voltage drop at the load?

options.A: 1.99 volts, using only the one-way length without doubling it
options.B: 3.44 volts, using a three-phase multiplier of 1.732 in place of 2
options.C: 3.98 volts, using two times K times I times L over circular mils
options.D: 6.32 volts, using the 6,530 circular mils of 12 AWG

distractor_mistakes.A: Forgets the return path and uses the one-way distance only
distractor_mistakes.B: Applies the three-phase factor to a single-phase circuit
distractor_mistakes.D: Takes circular mils from the 12 AWG row of the table

explanation: The correct answer is C (3.98 volts, using two times K times I times L over circular mils): For single-phase, voltage drop equals 2 times K times I times L divided by circular mils. That gives 2 times 12.9 times 16 times 100, which is 41,280, divided by 10,380, or 3.98 volts. The breaker rating does not enter the calculation. Using one-way length alone halves the result to 1.99 volts, and using 6,530 circular mils produces a value that belongs to 12 AWG, not the 10 AWG installed.

question: Under the 2026 NEC, a designer laying out a 2,400 square foot dwelling must find the minimum number of 20 ampere, 120 volt circuits for general lighting and receptacles at 3 volt-amperes per square foot. Small-appliance and laundry circuits are counted separately. How many circuits are needed?

options.A: Two circuits, using 2 volt-amperes per square foot for the count
options.B: Four circuits, dividing 7,200 by the 1,800 volt-amperes of a 15 ampere circuit
options.C: Six circuits, counting small-appliance and laundry circuits in the lighting total
options.D: Three circuits, from 7,200 volt-amperes divided by 2,400 volt-amperes per circuit

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the feeder and service unit load for a circuit count
distractor_mistakes.B: Divides by 15 ampere circuit capacity instead of 20 ampere
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds the small-appliance and laundry circuits the stem excludes

explanation: The correct answer is D (Three circuits, from 7,200 volt-amperes divided by 2,400 volt-amperes per circuit): Under the dwelling rule that keeps 3 volt-amperes per square foot for counting branch circuits, 2,400 times 3 is 7,200 volt-amperes. A 20 ampere, 120 volt circuit supplies 2,400 volt-amperes, so 7,200 divided by 2,400 is exactly 3 circuits. The four circuit answer comes from dividing by a 15 ampere circuit, which is not the rating stated.

question: Overcurrent device ratings for several feeders are listed on a panel schedule that the electrician plans to buy against. The inspector asks which group contains only ratings found in the standard list of overcurrent device ampere ratings in Section 240.6(A), so the order matches the Code?

options.A: Standard OCPD ratings of 75, 90, 100, and 125 amperes
options.B: Standard OCPD ratings of 90, 100, 110, and 125 amperes
options.C: Standard OCPD ratings of 80, 90, 100, 120, and 125 amperes
options.D: Standard OCPD ratings of 90, 100, 110, and 130 amperes

distractor_mistakes.A: Includes 75 amperes, which sits between standard sizes
distractor_mistakes.C: Includes 120 amperes, which is not on the standard list
distractor_mistakes.D: Includes 130 amperes, a value read from the 75 degree column instead

explanation: The correct answer is B (Standard OCPD ratings of 90, 100, 110, and 125 amperes): The 240.6(A) list runs 70, 80, 90, 100, 110, 125, 150, and so on, with no 75, 120, or 130 ampere ratings. Only the group of 90, 100, 110, and 125 amperes is made entirely of standard sizes. The others each contain a number that appears in ampacity tables or load calculations but not in the overcurrent device list.

question: Copper 6 AWG conductors with 75 degree insulation and terminals serve a single noncontinuous 58 ampere load. The 6 AWG ampacity in the 75 degree column is 65 amperes. No small-conductor limit applies, and the circuit is not a multioutlet receptacle circuit. What is the maximum standard overcurrent device permitted?

options.A: 70 amperes, the next standard size above the 65 ampere ampacity
options.B: 60 amperes, the standard size next below the conductor ampacity
options.C: 80 amperes, the next size above the 75 ampere 90 degree value
options.D: 90 amperes, the ampacity multiplied by 125 percent and rounded up

distractor_mistakes.B: Believes the device must always step down to the lower size
distractor_mistakes.C: Starts from the 90 degree column instead of the terminal column
distractor_mistakes.D: Multiplies the ampacity by 125 percent before choosing a size

explanation: The correct answer is A (70 amperes, the next standard size above the 65 ampere ampacity): Where the ampacity of a conductor does not match a standard device rating, 240.4(B) permits the next higher standard size, provided it does not exceed 800 amperes. The 6 AWG value is 65 amperes, and the next standard size on the 240.6 list above 65 is 70 amperes. Dropping to 60 amperes is allowed but is not the maximum permitted.

question: Two single-pole breakers on adjacent poles of a 120/240 volt panel feed the shared neutral of a three-wire multiwire branch circuit that an electrician is servicing in a bakery. Which arrangement meets the requirement for disconnecting the ungrounded conductors of this multiwire circuit?

options.A: Separate single-pole breakers with no handle tie, since each conductor has its own device
options.B: Two single-pole breakers on the same phase joined with an identified handle tie
options.C: A handle tie or common-trip breaker that opens every ungrounded conductor together
options.D: Single-pole breakers on different phases with a label warning of the shared neutral

distractor_mistakes.A: Treats separate protection as enough without simultaneous disconnection
distractor_mistakes.B: Joins the breakers but lands both on one phase so neutral current adds
distractor_mistakes.D: Relies on a warning label rather than a simultaneous disconnecting means

explanation: The correct answer is C (A handle tie or common-trip breaker that opens every ungrounded conductor together): Section 210.4(B) requires each multiwire branch circuit to have a means that disconnects all ungrounded conductors simultaneously at the point where the branch circuit originates. A handle tie or a common-trip multipole breaker satisfies this. Separate single-pole breakers without a tie allow a worker to open one conductor and still find the shared neutral energized from the other.

question: Two three-wire multiwire branch circuits on a 120/240 volt single-phase system serving balanced linear loads share a conduit with one equipment grounding conductor. The electrician needs the number of current-carrying conductors for the Article 310 adjustment factor. How many conductors are counted?

options.A: Four, because the neutrals and the grounding conductor are not counted here
options.B: Six, because both neutrals are counted along with the four ungrounded conductors
options.C: Seven, because the neutrals and the grounding conductor all count as current carrying
options.D: Two, because only one circuit is counted at a time in a shared raceway

distractor_mistakes.B: Counts neutrals that carry only unbalanced current
distractor_mistakes.C: Counts neutrals and also the equipment grounding conductor
distractor_mistakes.D: Evaluates one circuit at a time instead of the whole raceway

explanation: The correct answer is A (Four, because the neutrals and the grounding conductor are not counted here): Each three-wire circuit has two ungrounded conductors, giving four. A neutral that carries only the unbalanced current of the other conductors on a single-phase three-wire system is not counted, and equipment grounding conductors are never counted. The count is therefore four, and the 4 to 6 conductor adjustment factor of 80 percent applies.

question: Several receptacles sit on one 20 ampere, 12 AWG branch circuit in a woodworking shop. The inspector asks which receptacle ampere ratings Table 210.21(B)(3) permits on that circuit so that replacement devices match the installation. Which ratings are permitted on this circuit?

options.A: Receptacles rated either 15 amperes or 20 amperes in the table
options.B: Receptacles rated only 20 amperes, matching the breaker rating
options.C: Receptacles rated 20 amperes or 30 amperes in any mix
options.D: Receptacles rated 15, 20, or 30 amperes depending on the load

distractor_mistakes.B: Believes the receptacle rating must equal the breaker rating
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds 30 ampere devices that belong on 30 ampere circuits
distractor_mistakes.D: Allows a 30 ampere device because the wire is 12 AWG
