question: Starting a conveyor motor with a hard-starting load and a table full-load current of 34 amperes keeps tripping its 250 percent inverse-time breaker on every start, and the overload relays are not tripping. The electrician rechecks Table 430.52. What does 430.52(C)(1) allow next for the breaker?

options.A: Raise the inverse-time breaker to at most 300 percent of the full-load current rating
options.B: Replace it with an instantaneous-trip breaker set at up to 800 percent of full-load current
options.C: Replace it with a time-delay fuse at 175 percent of full-load current from the table
options.D: Raise the inverse-time breaker to at most 400 percent of full-load current under Exception No. 2

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the ceiling for motors above 100 amperes
distractor_mistakes.B: takes the 430.52(C)(3) instantaneous-trip limit for a different device
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a fuse percentage that is lower than the present setting

explanation: The correct answer is D (Raise the inverse-time breaker to at most 400 percent of full-load current under Exception No. 2): Exception No. 2 to 430.52(C)(1) lets an inverse-time breaker be increased when it will not carry the starting current, up to 400 percent of full-load current for motors of 100 amperes or less. At 34 amperes this motor is under that line, so 400 percent is the ceiling. The 300 percent limit applies to motors above 100 amperes, and the instantaneous-trip limit belongs to a different device under 430.52(C)(3). A 175 percent fuse setting is lower than the breaker already tripping, so it would not help starting.

question: A contractor picks a general-use switch as the disconnecting means for a 15 hp, 460-volt, three-phase motor with a Table 430.250 current of 21 amperes. The motor has a 25 ampere nameplate and a 52.5 ampere breaker. What minimum ampere rating does 430.110(A) require the disconnect to carry?

options.A: 21.0 amperes, which is the table current with no percentage added
options.B: 26.3 amperes, which is 125 percent of the table current of 21 amperes used for conductors
options.C: 52.5 amperes, which is the 250 percent branch-circuit breaker rating
options.D: 24.2 amperes, which is 115 percent of the table current of 21 amperes

distractor_mistakes.A: leaves out the 115 percent disconnect factor
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the conductor factor from 430.22 for the disconnect
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the breaker rating as the disconnect rating

explanation: The correct answer is D (24.2 amperes, which is 115 percent of the table current of 21 amperes): For a motor disconnecting means, 430.110(A) requires an ampere rating of at least 115 percent of the full-load current from the tables. Twenty-one amperes times 1.15 equals 24.15, which rounds to 24.2 amperes. The 125 percent value is for conductors under 430.22, and the breaker percentage of 250 percent applies to short-circuit protection only.

question: On a farm irrigation project, an estimator needs the conductor sizing current for a 7.5 hp, 208-volt, three-phase squirrel-cage motor driving a well pump. The nameplate shows 22.5 amperes. Under 430.6(A)(1), which value is used for sizing the branch-circuit conductors for this motor?

options.A: 22.5 amperes, which is the motor nameplate current rating shown on the pump
options.B: 22.0 amperes, from the 230 volt column of Table 430.250 for three-phase motors
options.C: 11.0 amperes, from the 460 volt column of Table 430.250
options.D: 24.2 amperes, from the 208 volt column of Table 430.250

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the nameplate where the rule points to the table
distractor_mistakes.B: reads the wrong voltage column of the table
distractor_mistakes.C: reads the 460 volt column for a 208 volt supply

explanation: The correct answer is D (24.2 amperes, from the 208 volt column of Table 430.250): Section 430.6(A)(1) requires the full-load current from Table 430.250 for conductor ampacity, and the 208 volt column for 7.5 hp lists 24.2 amperes. The nameplate current of 22.5 amperes is used for overload protection instead. The 230 volt and 460 volt columns give lower currents that do not match the 208 volt supply.

question: Instructions on a QR code for a pump motor controller include installation instructions on a QR code that call for conductors sized at 125 percent of the nameplate current. Code section 430.22 requires 125 percent of the Table 430.250 current, which is a larger value in this case. Under 110.3(B), which value governs?

options.A: The 430.22 value governs, because instructions may add to the Code but cannot reduce it
options.B: The QR code value governs, because listed instructions replace general Code rules
options.C: The smaller of the two values governs, because both documents are accepted by the inspector
options.D: The QR code is not accepted, so the written Code value governs for that reason

distractor_mistakes.B: treats manufacturer instructions as overriding the Code
distractor_mistakes.C: picks the lower value even though one is a Code minimum
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes a QR code cannot present valid instructions

explanation: The correct answer is A (The 430.22 value governs, because instructions may add to the Code but cannot reduce it): Section 110.3(B) says listed and labeled equipment must be installed per its instructions, and the instructions may be printed, a QR code or a web address. The instructions can exceed Code requirements but cannot reduce them. Because 430.22 asks for a larger conductor, that value governs. The QR code format is acceptable and is not the reason for the outcome.

question: During a discussion of motor protection devices, a reviewer states that a short circuit is the same as an overload because both involve excess current. The Article 100 definition of overload is cited to settle the point. Which statement matches that definition?

options.A: Operation in excess of normal rating that includes short circuits and ground faults too
options.B: A brief starting surge, lasting a few seconds, that does not harm the winding
options.C: Excess current that persists long enough to cause damage; faults are not overloads
options.D: Operation at below rated current for several hours that wastes motor efficiency

distractor_mistakes.A: includes faults that the definition expressly excludes
distractor_mistakes.B: treats normal inrush as the overload
distractor_mistakes.D: describes light loading, not an overload

explanation: The correct answer is C (Excess current that persists long enough to cause damage; faults are not overloads): Article 100 defines overload as operation in excess of normal full-load rating that, if it persists for a sufficient length of time, would cause damage or dangerous overheating. It adds that a short circuit or ground fault is not an overload. That separation explains why Article 430 uses overload relays for running overload and breakers or fuses for faults.

question: At a water treatment plant, the crew installs an adjustable speed drive with a rated input of 40 amperes to run a blower motor. The designer needs the minimum ampacity for the conductors feeding the drive. Under 430.122(A), what percentage of the drive rated input current must those conductors carry?

options.A: 125 percent of the rated input current of the drive
options.B: 115 percent of the rated input current, the factor used for generator conductors
options.C: 100 percent of the rated input current, adding no continuous-duty margin
options.D: 150 percent of the rated input current of the power conversion equipment

distractor_mistakes.B: uses the generator conductor factor on a drive circuit
distractor_mistakes.C: adds no continuous-duty margin
distractor_mistakes.D: invents a margin that no section requires

explanation: The correct answer is A (125 percent of the rated input current of the drive): Section 430.122(A) requires conductors supplying power conversion equipment, including adjustable-speed drive systems, to have an ampacity of not less than 125 percent of the rated input current. Forty amperes times 1.25 equals 50 amperes. The 115 percent factor is the generator output rule in 445.13, and no section asks for 150 percent.

question: On a rooftop unit, there is a hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor and a separate condenser fan motor. The designer finds that one rule in Article 430 about conductor sizing differs from a rule in Article 440 for the compressor circuit. Which article governs where the two differ for that equipment?

options.A: Article 430, because it covers every motor and overrides all other articles
options.B: Whichever rule is less restrictive, because the unit has two kinds of motor
options.C: Article 440, because it adds to or amends Article 430 for such equipment
options.D: Article 422, because the rooftop unit is classed as an appliance only

distractor_mistakes.A: assigns the general motor article priority over the specific one
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the lower requirement instead of the governing one
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the appliance article to a unit covered by Article 440

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 440, because it adds to or amends Article 430 for such equipment): Section 440.3 states that Article 440 provisions are in addition to or amend Article 430 for air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment with hermetic motor-compressors. Where they conflict, the specific rule in Article 440 governs. The fan motor still follows Article 430, but the compressor circuit uses the Article 440 requirements.

question: A one-line diagram note for a small shop shows a portable generator tied to the service panel through a two-position switch labeled normal and generator. The inspector asks which function the switch must provide under 702.5 for an optional standby system. Which function is it?

options.A: Transfer the connected loads to the alternate source within 60 seconds of a failure
options.B: Prevent inadvertent interconnection of the normal and alternate sources
options.C: Provide a bypass isolation path so loads stay energized during switch maintenance
options.D: Be rated for the load it serves and the generator output current it carries

distractor_mistakes.A: assigns a legally required standby timing rule to optional standby
distractor_mistakes.C: adds a bypass feature that 702.5 does not require
distractor_mistakes.D: gives an equipment rating rule instead of the required function

explanation: The correct answer is B (Prevent inadvertent interconnection of the normal and alternate sources): Section 702.5 requires transfer equipment for optional standby systems that prevents inadvertent interconnection of the normal and alternate sources, which keeps generator power from backfeeding the utility. A transfer time limit belongs to legally required and emergency systems, not optional standby. Equipment rating is a true general requirement but it is not the function the section assigns, and a bypass path is a design option rather than a requirement.

question: A grain building panel schedule lists a 70-ampere inverse-time breaker feeding a 5 hp, 230-volt, single-phase motor. The nameplate shows 24 amperes, and Table 430.248 lists 28 amperes. The inspector checks the maximum allowed rating from Table 430.52 and the next standard size. Which maximum breaker rating applies?

options.A: 50 amperes, from 175 percent of the table current rounded to a standard size
options.B: 60 amperes, from 250 percent of the 24 ampere nameplate current
options.C: 70 amperes, from 250 percent of the 28 ampere full-load current in Table 430.248
options.D: 90 amperes, from 300 percent of the table current rounded to a standard size

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the dual-element time-delay fuse column for a breaker
distractor_mistakes.B: uses nameplate current instead of the table current
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the nontime-delay fuse column for a breaker

explanation: The correct answer is C (70 amperes, from 250 percent of the 28 ampere full-load current in Table 430.248): Table 430.52 allows 250 percent of the full-load current for an inverse-time breaker, and 430.6(A)(1) says to use the table current of 28 amperes. Twenty-eight times 2.5 equals 70 amperes, which is a standard size, so the installed breaker is within the limit. The 60 ampere answer comes from the nameplate. The 50 and 90 ampere results apply fuse columns that do not fit a breaker.

question: A 1,200-ampere feeder disconnecting means in a processing plant is a switchboard section more than 6 feet wide, installed in a room used by maintenance staff. The 2023 NEC applied the large-equipment access and egress rule in 110.26(C)(2) to service equipment only. How does the 2026 NEC treat feeder disconnecting means?

options.A: The rule still covers service disconnecting means only, as in the 2023 edition of the Code
options.B: The rule now covers only equipment operating above 1,000 volts alternating current
options.C: The rule now covers feeder disconnecting means as well as service disconnecting means
options.D: The rule now covers dwelling unit panelboards but not industrial switchboards

distractor_mistakes.A: repeats the 2023 scope that the 2026 text removed
distractor_mistakes.B: limits the rule to medium voltage equipment
distractor_mistakes.D: reverses the occupancy the rule is aimed at

explanation: The correct answer is C (The rule now covers feeder disconnecting means as well as service disconnecting means): For 2026, 110.26(C)(2) drops the word service and refers to 225.33(A), so large service and feeder disconnecting means must meet the extra access and egress requirements. The 2023 edition applied the rule only to service equipment, which is why that option is tempting. The change does not limit the rule to over 1,000 volt equipment or to dwellings.

question: Wiring for a new 460-volt, three-phase, 20 hp motor starts from a nameplate current of 24 amperes and a Table 430.250 current of 27 amperes. Conductors are 75 degree C insulated copper on 75 degree C terminals, and the circuit is 100 amperes or less. Using Table 310.16 and 430.22, which conductor size is the smallest permitted?

options.A: 10 AWG copper, rated 35 amperes in the 75 degree column
options.B: 12 AWG copper, rated 30 amperes in the 90 degree column, sized from nameplate current
options.C: 12 AWG copper, rated 25 amperes in the 75 degree column, sized with no percentage
options.D: 8 AWG copper, rated 40 amperes in the 60 degree column

distractor_mistakes.B: sizes from nameplate current and the 90 degree column
distractor_mistakes.C: omits the 125 percent factor and uses nameplate current
distractor_mistakes.D: reads the 60 degree column for 75 degree terminals

explanation: The correct answer is A (10 AWG copper, rated 35 amperes in the 75 degree column): Section 430.22 requires 125 percent of the Table 430.250 current, or 27 times 1.25 equals 33.75 amperes. With 75 degree terminals the 75 degree column applies, and 10 AWG carries 35 amperes, which exceeds 33.75. The 12 AWG choices fall short because they use nameplate current or skip the 125 percent factor. The 8 AWG choice reads the 60 degree column, which is not the governing column here.

question: Comparing two pump motors, a buyer sees a service factor of 1.15 marked on one nameplate and 1.0 on the other. The buyer wants to know what the number means in practical terms. Which statement describes the service factor of a motor?

options.A: A ratio of locked-rotor current to full-load current used to select the starter size
options.B: A multiplier on rated horsepower showing the continuous load the motor can carry
options.C: A percentage of rated voltage the motor tolerates before the winding overheats
options.D: A rating for the number of starts per hour that the motor winding allows

distractor_mistakes.A: confuses service factor with the locked-rotor ratio
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses service factor with voltage tolerance
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses service factor with the duty rating for starting

explanation: The correct answer is B (A multiplier on rated horsepower showing the continuous load the motor can carry): Service factor is a multiplier applied to rated horsepower that shows the permissible loading that can be carried continuously under the conditions on the nameplate. A 1.15 service factor on a 10 hp motor allows about 11.5 hp. It matters in 430.32(A)(1) because a marked service factor of 1.15 or more permits the 125 percent overload setting.

question: After a flood, an inspector finds the branch-circuit conductors and wiring method serving a pump motor exposed to water for two days. The motor is dry and runs, and the owner proposes to re-energize it. What does 300.4(C), in the 2026 NEC, require for conductors and wiring methods no longer suitable after water damage?

options.A: Replace the conductors and wiring methods that are no longer suitable
options.B: Dry them in place and re-energize since the insulation rating is unchanged
options.C: Replace only the damaged conductors and keep the existing raceway and boxes after drying
options.D: Perform an insulation resistance test and re-energize the circuit when the readings look acceptable

distractor_mistakes.B: treats drying as restoring suitability
distractor_mistakes.C: limits replacement to conductors and ignores the wiring method
distractor_mistakes.D: substitutes an insulation test for required replacement

explanation: The correct answer is A (Replace the conductors and wiring methods that are no longer suitable): The 2026 text of 300.4(C) says conductors and wiring methods that are no longer suitable for use, from overheating, fire damage, corrosive influences or water, must be replaced. An informational note points to NEMA GD 1 for water-damaged equipment. Drying in place or passing an insulation test does not make a water-damaged wiring method suitable again, and replacing only the conductors leaves the raceway and boxes that are also covered by the rule.

question: In a quarry, a 10 hp, three-phase, 900 rpm motor shows a nameplate current of 15.4 amperes, while Table 430.250 gives 14 amperes at the same voltage. Under the 430.6(A)(1) exception for low-speed motors, what minimum conductor ampacity is required by 430.22?

options.A: 17.5 amperes, which is 125 percent of the 14 ampere Table 430.250 current
options.B: 19.3 amperes, which is 125 percent of the 15.4 ampere nameplate current
options.C: 16.1 amperes, which is 115 percent of the 14 ampere Table 430.250 current
options.D: 17.7 amperes, which is 115 percent of the 15.4 ampere nameplate current

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the table value instead of the nameplate for a low-speed motor
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the generator factor and the table current
distractor_mistakes.D: uses nameplate current with the wrong percentage

explanation: The correct answer is B (19.3 amperes, which is 125 percent of the 15.4 ampere nameplate current): Section 430.6(A)(1) has exceptions for motors built for low speeds, under 1,200 rpm, and for high torque or multispeed motors, which require the nameplate current to size conductors. Then 430.22 applies the 125 percent factor, so 15.4 times 1.25 equals 19.25, rounded to 19.3 amperes. The table-based answers ignore the low-speed exception, and the 115 percent factor is not used for motor conductors.

question: Reading a motor nameplate, the technician sees a NEMA Design letter B beside the horsepower and speed. The shop is deciding between two similar motors for a fan and wants to know what the Design letter communicates. Which statement describes the NEMA design letter on a nameplate?

options.A: It classifies the motor by the temperature class of its winding insulation
options.B: It classes the motor by its starting torque and locked-rotor current traits
options.C: It classifies the motor by the degree of enclosure protection around the frame and bearings
options.D: It classifies the motor by the voltage range that the winding accepts

distractor_mistakes.A: confuses the design letter with the insulation class
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses the design letter with the enclosure type
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses the design letter with the voltage rating

explanation: The correct answer is B (It classes the motor by its starting torque and locked-rotor current traits): The NEMA Design letter, such as B, groups induction motors by their torque and locked-rotor current characteristics. Table 430.52 refers to Design B when it sets the maximum protective device ratings, which is why the nameplate entry matters. Insulation class, enclosure type and voltage are separate nameplate entries.

question: A commissioning inspector finds a 25 hp, 460-volt motor served by a controller marked 20 hp at 460 volts, with a continuous rating of 40 amperes. Table 430.250 lists 34 amperes for the 25 hp motor, and no exception applies. What finding does the inspector record under 430.83?

options.A: The controller horsepower rating is lower than the motor horsepower, so it fails
options.B: The controller is acceptable since its 40 ampere rating exceeds the 34 ampere table current
options.C: The controller is too large because its rating exceeds the motor full-load current
options.D: The controller is acceptable because its rating exceeds 115 percent of the motor current

distractor_mistakes.B: relies on ampere rating where the rule requires a horsepower rating
distractor_mistakes.C: treats a higher rating as a violation
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the disconnect factor to a controller

explanation: The correct answer is A (The controller horsepower rating is lower than the motor horsepower, so it fails): Section 430.83(A) requires a controller, other than an inverse-time breaker or molded-case switch, to have a horsepower rating not lower than the motor horsepower. A 20 hp controller on a 25 hp motor fails that test even though its 40 ampere continuous rating exceeds 34 amperes. Over-rating the controller is not a violation, and the 115 percent factor is for disconnect ampere ratings.

question: Arc flash data are written by a crew on a motor control center in a plant, with a permanent marker on a strip of tape applied to the enclosure door. The data are correct and readable. The inspector rejects it under the 2026 NEC rules for field-applied hazard markings. What is the basis for rejection?

options.A: The marking must be permanently affixed, and 110.21(B) does not allow handwriting
options.B: The marking must be applied by the manufacturer, because field-applied labels are not recognized for equipment
options.C: The marking must be an engraved metal plate, since printed labels are not durable enough
options.D: The marking must sit inside the enclosure behind the door, not on the outside face

distractor_mistakes.B: treats field-applied markings as not allowed
distractor_mistakes.C: requires engraved plates where durable printed labels qualify
distractor_mistakes.D: puts the marking where a qualified person cannot see it first

explanation: The correct answer is A (The marking must be permanently affixed, and 110.21(B) does not allow handwriting): The 2026 110.16 marking must be permanently affixed and clearly visible to a qualified person, and 110.21(B) does not allow handwritten field-applied markings. Correct data written in marker on tape therefore fails on the method of marking. Field-applied markings are recognized when they are durable and not handwritten, an engraved plate is not required, and a marking placed behind the door would not be visible before the equipment is opened.

question: A plans reviewer cites an informational note that follows 430.32 and insists the contractor install a specific overload relay trip class, because the note uses a recommendation about relay classes. The contractor disagrees. How does the Code treat an informational note in this situation?

options.A: As an enforceable requirement, because it appears in the body of Article 430 text
options.B: Explanatory material only, which is not an enforceable requirement under 90.5(C)
options.C: As enforceable once the plans reviewer cites it in a written correction notice to the owner
options.D: As enforceable only when the note contains the word shall or must

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the note as mandatory text
distractor_mistakes.C: lets the reviewer convert a note into a rule
distractor_mistakes.D: looks for mandatory wording in a note that is explanatory

explanation: The correct answer is B (Explanatory material only, which is not an enforceable requirement under 90.5(C)): Section 90.5(C) says informational notes are explanatory material and are not requirements of the Code. A reviewer cannot make a note enforceable by citing it. Mandatory rules use shall in the numbered text. The relay class recommendation therefore cannot be required on the strength of the note alone.

question: Walk-in coolers and point-of-sale terminals are the only loads a restaurant owner wants a new generator to carry, and no code or authority requires it. Which article governs the wiring of this installation, and what makes it the correct choice instead of the life safety or legally required articles?

options.A: Article 700, because any generator that restores power to an occupied building is an emergency system.
options.B: Article 702, because the system is optional and protects property rather than mandated safety loads.
options.C: Article 701, because a health inspector expects refrigerated food to stay protected during outages.
options.D: Article 705, because a generator located beside the utility service is an interconnected power source.

distractor_mistakes.A: treats every backup generator as an emergency system
distractor_mistakes.C: assumes health expectations make the load legally required
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses a standby source with an interconnected source

explanation: The correct answer is B (Article 702, because the system is optional and protects property rather than mandated safety loads.): Optional standby systems are installed voluntarily to protect property or keep a business operating, and Article 702 covers them. Article 700 applies to loads required for life safety, and Article 701 applies to loads a governmental body requires by rule. Nothing here is mandated by an authority, so a food-safety preference does not move the system into the legally required class. Article 705 would apply only if the generator operated in parallel with the utility.

question: Bonded at its own terminals as a separately derived system, a standby generator connects through an automatic transfer switch to a service equipped with ground-fault protection of equipment. To prevent a second neutral-to-ground path and nuisance ground-fault trips during transfer, which transfer switch arrangement does the designer select?

options.A: A four-pole switch that transfers the neutral conductor together with the phase conductors.
options.B: A three-pole switch with a solid neutral carried straight through to both power sources.
options.C: A switch that bonds the neutral to ground inside the enclosure for each source in turn.
options.D: A three-pole switch with the ground-fault sensing function disabled while the generator carries load.

distractor_mistakes.B: applies the non-separately-derived arrangement to a bonded generator
distractor_mistakes.C: adds a second bond that creates parallel neutral paths
distractor_mistakes.D: defeats the protection instead of correcting the neutral path

explanation: The correct answer is A (A four-pole switch that transfers the neutral conductor together with the phase conductors.): When the generator is a separately derived system with its own neutral-to-ground bond, the neutral must be switched so the two sources do not share a neutral path through the service bond. A four-pole transfer switch does this by opening and closing the neutral with the phase poles. A solid neutral is the right choice only when the generator is not bonded, because then the service bond is the only one. Disabling ground-fault protection removes a required safeguard and does not fix the double path.

question: Marked 24 volts and 100 volt-amperes maximum, a listed Class 2 transformer feeds a thermostat circuit in a school wing. The transformer primary is connected at 120 volts, and the secondary conductors are 18 AWG. What maximum secondary current does the marking allow the circuit to draw?

options.A: 0.83 amperes, dividing 100 volt-amperes by the 120 volt primary connection.
options.B: 3.33 amperes, dividing 100 volt-amperes by the 30 volt Class 2 voltage limit.
options.C: 4.17 amperes, dividing 100 volt-amperes by the marked 24 volt secondary rating.
options.D: 5.21 amperes, dividing by 24 volts and then adding a 25 percent continuous margin.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the primary voltage for a secondary current
distractor_mistakes.B: divides by the Class 2 voltage ceiling instead of the marking
distractor_mistakes.D: adds a continuous load margin to a marked rating

explanation: The correct answer is C (4.17 amperes, dividing 100 volt-amperes by the marked 24 volt secondary rating.): Current equals volt-amperes divided by volts on the same side of the transformer. The secondary marking gives 100 volt-amperes at 24 volts, so 100 / 24 = 4.17 amperes. Using 120 volts gives 0.83 amperes, which is the primary side. Using the 30 volt Class 2 limit gives 3.33, and adding 25 percent gives 5.21, but neither belongs to the marking. The 18 AWG conductor size and the school location do not change the calculation.

question: Two listed 24-volt Class 2 supplies, each marked 60 volt-amperes, are mounted in a warehouse office. Zone 1 draws 40 volt-amperes and zone 2 draws 35 volt-amperes. The installer may not parallel the outputs, so each zone gets its own supply. What current does the supply feeding zone 2 carry?

options.A: 3.13 amperes, from both zones totalling 75 volt-amperes on one supply at 24 volts.
options.B: 5.00 amperes, from the combined 120 volt-ampere rating of two paralleled supplies at 24 volts.
options.C: 1.46 amperes, from 35 volt-amperes at 24 volts on its own separate supply.
options.D: 0.29 amperes, from 35 volt-amperes divided by the 120 volt primary voltage.

distractor_mistakes.A: puts both zones on one supply
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes paralleled supplies add their ratings
distractor_mistakes.D: divides by the primary voltage instead of the secondary

explanation: The correct answer is C (1.46 amperes, from 35 volt-amperes at 24 volts on its own separate supply.): Listed Class 2 power sources must not have their outputs paralleled unless they are listed for that interconnection. Each zone therefore stays on its own supply, and zone 2 carries 35 volt-amperes divided by 24 volts, which is 1.46 amperes. That is within the 60 volt-ampere rating of its supply. Adding the two zones together would overload one 60 volt-ampere supply, and adding the two supply ratings relies on a parallel connection the rules do not allow.

question: Pushbuttons 60 feet from a 480-volt pump motor start it through a magnetic contactor, which is wired to the pushbutton station with small control conductors. Which part of this arrangement carries the motor load current and opens that circuit when the coil de-energizes?

options.A: The pushbutton station contacts, since they issue the start and stop commands for the pump.
options.B: The coil winding of the contactor, which conducts motor current while the contactor is closed.
options.C: The overload relay trip contacts, which sit in series with each pump motor lead.
options.D: The power contacts of the magnetic contactor, installed in the motor circuit between line and load.

distractor_mistakes.A: confuses a command device with a load-carrying device
distractor_mistakes.B: thinks the coil carries the motor current
distractor_mistakes.C: places overload trip contacts in the power circuit

explanation: The correct answer is D (The power contacts of the magnetic contactor, installed in the motor circuit between line and load.): A contactor uses a small coil circuit to close heavy power contacts that carry the motor current. When the coil de-energizes, those power contacts open and interrupt the motor circuit. The pushbutton contacts and the coil handle only control current, and the overload relay trip contacts also sit in the control circuit, where they open the coil circuit rather than the motor leads.

question: Servicing a 480-volt starter, a maintenance electrician finds a control transformer marked 480 volts primary, 120 volts secondary, 250 volt-amperes, supplying the coil circuit. Before judging whether added pilot lights overload it, the electrician needs the rated current of the secondary winding. What is that current?

options.A: 0.52 amperes, from 250 volt-amperes divided by the 480 volt primary.
options.B: 2.08 amperes, from 250 volt-amperes divided by the 120 volt secondary.
options.C: 2.60 amperes, from the secondary rated current increased by a 25 percent margin.
options.D: 8.33 amperes, from the 0.52 ampere primary current multiplied by 4 squared.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the primary voltage for a secondary rating
distractor_mistakes.C: adds a margin to a nameplate rating
distractor_mistakes.D: squares the voltage ratio when converting primary to secondary current

explanation: The correct answer is B (2.08 amperes, from 250 volt-amperes divided by the 120 volt secondary.): The secondary current rating is the volt-ampere rating divided by the secondary voltage, so 250 / 120 = 2.08 amperes. The 0.52 ampere figure is the primary rated current at 480 volts. Converting primary current to secondary current uses the voltage ratio of 4 once, giving 0.52 x 4 = 2.08, so squaring it to 16 overstates the current. Adding 25 percent produces a number that is not on the nameplate.

question: Feeders at 480 volts already run in a cable tray on a plant mezzanine, and the HVAC contractor wants to add Class 2 control cables in the same tray. The tray has no dividers today. Which installation method does the NEC accept for placing the Class 2 cables in this tray?

options.A: Space the Class 2 cables 300 mm (12 inches) away from the feeders with no barrier.
options.B: Space the Class 2 cables 6 mm (1/4 inch) from the feeders with no barrier.
options.C: Mark the Class 2 cables orange and run them in the same open compartment.
options.D: Install a solid fixed barrier in the tray between the feeders and the Class 2 cables.

distractor_mistakes.A: relies on a large gap in place of a barrier
distractor_mistakes.B: relies on a small air gap in place of a barrier
distractor_mistakes.C: relies on marking in place of separation

explanation: The correct answer is D (Install a solid fixed barrier in the tray between the feeders and the Class 2 cables.): Class 2 cables may share a cable tray with power conductors only when separated by a solid fixed barrier. A small air gap does not keep the cables from touching the feeders over the length of a tray, and a colour marking identifies cables but gives no physical separation.

question: Selecting a 225-ampere automatic transfer switch, a contractor sized it for a standby generator nameplated 100 kilowatts at 208 volts, three-phase, at unity power factor. The inspector questions the switch size. What full-load generator current should the switch rating be checked against?

options.A: 481 amperes, from 100,000 watts divided by 208 volts as a single-phase load.
options.B: 120 amperes, from 100,000 watts divided by 1.732 times 480 volts.
options.C: 347 amperes, from the three-phase calculation also divided by a 0.8 power factor.
options.D: 278 amperes, from 100,000 watts divided by 1.732 times 208 volts.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the single-phase formula for a three-phase generator
distractor_mistakes.B: uses a voltage that is not the generator voltage
distractor_mistakes.C: applies a power factor the nameplate does not state

explanation: The correct answer is D (278 amperes, from 100,000 watts divided by 1.732 times 208 volts.): Three-phase current is watts divided by 1.732 times line voltage. Here 100,000 / (1.732 x 208) = 277.6, or about 278 amperes. That exceeds the 225-ampere switch rating, so the inspector is right to question it. The single-phase formula and the 480 volt figure do not describe this generator, and the nameplate states unity power factor, so no 0.8 factor applies.

question: Class 1 remote-control conductors for a motor starter come from a control transformer, and a Chapter 7 rule on those conductors differs from a general Chapter 3 wiring rule. Under the way Article 90 organizes the code chapters, how does the inspector treat this conflict?

options.A: Chapter 3 governs, since wiring method rules outrank the special condition rules of later chapters.
options.B: Chapter 1 governs, since general requirements outrank every other chapter of the code.
options.C: Chapter 7 stands alone like Chapter 8, so Chapters 1 through 4 are not applied.
options.D: Chapter 7 supplements or modifies Chapters 1 through 4, so its rule governs for that circuit.

distractor_mistakes.A: thinks wiring methods override special conditions
distractor_mistakes.B: thinks general rules override all later chapters
distractor_mistakes.C: treats Chapter 7 as an independent chapter

explanation: The correct answer is D (Chapter 7 supplements or modifies Chapters 1 through 4, so its rule governs for that circuit.): Article 90 explains that Chapters 1 through 4 apply generally, while Chapters 5, 6 and 7 supplement or modify them for special occupancies, equipment and conditions. A Chapter 7 rule for Class 1 conductors therefore governs where it differs from a general rule. Chapter 8 is the chapter that stands on its own, which is why treating Chapter 7 the same way fails here.

question: Nurse call wiring at 24 volts carries 1.2 amperes over a run of 150 feet one way to the remote station. The two conductors have a resistance of 6.5 ohms per 1,000 feet each. What is the voltage drop in the conductors for the full loop?

options.A: 1.17 volts, using only the 150 foot outgoing conductor and ignoring the return.
options.B: 4.68 volts, doubling the loop length a second time for the two conductors.
options.C: 2.34 volts, using 300 feet of total loop length at 6.5 ohms per 1,000 feet.
options.D: 1.95 volts, using the loop resistance without multiplying by the circuit current.

distractor_mistakes.A: counts only the outgoing conductor
distractor_mistakes.B: doubles the length twice
distractor_mistakes.D: reports resistance as if it were volts

explanation: The correct answer is C (2.34 volts, using 300 feet of total loop length at 6.5 ohms per 1,000 feet.): The current flows out on one conductor and back on the other, so the loop is 2 x 150 = 300 feet. Resistance is 300 x 6.5 / 1,000 = 1.95 ohms. The voltage drop is 1.2 amperes x 1.95 ohms = 2.34 volts. Counting one conductor halves the answer, and stopping at 1.95 leaves a resistance in ohms that has not been multiplied by the current.

question: Drawing more current than any listed Class 2 power source can supply, an access control door strike cannot be treated as a Class 2 circuit. A damaged cable to the strike must be replaced. Which approach applies to the replacement circuit?

options.A: Keep the CL2 cable and increase the rating of the overcurrent device on the supply.
options.B: Use CL3 cable instead, since it tolerates the higher current that this strike requires.
options.C: Install it as a Class 1 circuit or as a general power circuit with matching methods.
options.D: Treat it as a communications circuit and use communications cable instead.

distractor_mistakes.A: raises the protection but keeps a low-energy classification
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes Class 3 allows unlimited current
distractor_mistakes.D: applies communications rules to a power load

explanation: The correct answer is C (Install it as a Class 1 circuit or as a general power circuit with matching methods.): Class 2 and Class 3 circuits are defined by the power limits of their listed sources. A load above those limits cannot be treated as Class 2 or Class 3 and must follow Class 1 or general power wiring rules instead. A larger overcurrent device does not change the classification, and Class 3 has its own power limit. A door strike is not a communications circuit, so those rules do not apply.

question: Refrigeration at 18 amperes, point-of-sale equipment at 4 amperes and lighting at 8 amperes make up the 240-volt single-phase loads on a restaurant standby generator that no code requires. The owner asks for the minimum kilovolt-ampere rating to carry these loads together. What is it?

options.A: 3.6 kilovolt-amperes, from 30 amperes multiplied by 120 volts.
options.B: 12.5 kilovolt-amperes, from 30 amperes multiplied by 240 volts and 1.732.
options.C: 7.2 kilovolt-amperes, from 30 amperes multiplied by 240 volts.
options.D: 9.0 kilovolt-amperes, from the 7.2 total increased by 25 percent for all loads.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses 120 volts for 240-volt loads
distractor_mistakes.B: applies a three-phase factor to single-phase loads
distractor_mistakes.D: adds a 25 percent factor to every load

explanation: The correct answer is C (7.2 kilovolt-amperes, from 30 amperes multiplied by 240 volts.): The connected load is 18 + 4 + 8 = 30 amperes at 240 volts single-phase. Volt-amperes equal 30 x 240 = 7,200, or 7.2 kilovolt-amperes. Using 120 volts halves the result, and the 1.732 factor belongs only to three-phase systems. A 25 percent increase applies to continuous motor loads in certain rules, not to every load in a simple optional standby sizing.

question: A 120-volt motor control circuit has one conductor grounded, and a remote pushbutton station is wired with long runs. An installer asks how to arrange the circuit so a ground fault in the remote wiring cannot start the motor. Which arrangement does the control circuit rule accept?

options.A: Connect the coil to the grounded conductor and place all control contacts in the ungrounded conductor.
options.B: Place the start pushbutton in the grounded conductor and connect the coil to the ungrounded conductor
options.C: Connect the coil to the ungrounded conductor and all control contacts in the grounded conductor
options.D: Place the stop contacts in the grounded conductor and start contacts in the ungrounded conductor

distractor_mistakes.B: puts the start contact in the grounded side where a fault bypasses it
distractor_mistakes.C: reverses the coil and contact positions fully
distractor_mistakes.D: splits the contacts so the stop device can be bypassed by a fault

explanation: The correct answer is A (Connect the coil to the grounded conductor and place all control contacts in the ungrounded conductor.): With the coil connected directly to the grounded conductor, a ground fault in the wiring to the contacts cannot complete a path through the coil. All control contacts sit in the ungrounded conductor, where a fault cannot bypass them. Any contact placed in the grounded conductor can be shorted around by a ground fault in the remote wiring, which is exactly the start or stop failure the arrangement rule is written to prevent.

question: Hospital egress lighting must be restored within 10 seconds of a normal source outage, while a nearby sewage lift pump is a legally required standby load. A test shows 7.5 seconds for the generator to reach rated voltage and 1.2 seconds for the transfer switch to operate. What margin does the egress lighting have?

options.A: 51.3 seconds of margin, measured against the 60 second legally required standby limit.
options.B: 2.5 seconds of margin, counting only the generator start time against the 10 second limit.
options.C: 8.7 seconds of margin, reading the total time of both steps as the margin.
options.D: 1.3 seconds of margin, measured against the 10 second emergency limit for egress lighting

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the wrong system's time limit
distractor_mistakes.B: leaves out the transfer switch time
distractor_mistakes.C: reads total elapsed time as the margin

explanation: The correct answer is D (1.3 seconds of margin, measured against the 10 second emergency limit for egress lighting): The total restoration time is 7.5 + 1.2 = 8.7 seconds. Egress lighting is an emergency system load with a 10 second limit, so the margin is 10 - 8.7 = 1.3 seconds. The 60 second limit belongs to the legally required standby pump, not to egress lighting. Counting only the generator start leaves out the time the transfer switch takes to move the load.

question: Inspectors walking a mechanical room find a fire pump controller's remote-control conductors pulled through the same conduit as unrelated general building power wiring, and nothing in the plans explains the sharing. During the walk-through, the inspector writes a correction. Which NEC requirement does this installation violate?

options.A: Control conductors for fire pumps must be 12 AWG and carry a separate overcurrent device.
options.B: Fire pump control wiring must be supplied from the emergency system instead of the pump circuit.
options.C: Fire pump control conductors must be kept entirely independent of all other building wiring.
options.D: Fire pump circuits may share a raceway with Class 1 wiring only when insulation ratings match.

distractor_mistakes.A: invents a minimum size and protection rule
distractor_mistakes.B: confuses the pump source with an emergency system supply
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes matching insulation allows shared raceways

explanation: The correct answer is C (Fire pump control conductors must be kept entirely independent of all other building wiring.): The fire pump article requires that the control wiring for the pump be kept entirely independent of other wiring so a fault elsewhere in the building cannot disable the pump. Sharing a conduit with general power wiring breaks that independence. The other options describe requirements that do not appear in the rule, so they would not cure the violation even if they were met.

question: Plans for a warehouse show wiring for remote control switches and signaling devices that is not power limited and operates at no more than 600 volts. The electrician must choose the circuit classification before selecting the wiring methods. Which classification fits this wiring?

options.A: Class 2 circuit, since all remote control wiring is treated as a low energy circuit.
options.B: Class 3 circuit, since the voltage is above the Class 2 limit but still low.
options.C: Power-limited fire alarm circuit, since signaling devices are covered by the fire alarm article.
options.D: Class 1 remote-control and signaling circuit, not power limited and rated up to 600 volts.

distractor_mistakes.A: treats every control circuit as Class 2
distractor_mistakes.B: uses Class 3 for a circuit that is not power limited
distractor_mistakes.C: applies fire alarm rules to ordinary signaling

explanation: The correct answer is D (Class 1 remote-control and signaling circuit, not power limited and rated up to 600 volts.): A remote-control or signaling circuit that is not power limited and operates up to 600 volts is a Class 1 circuit. Class 2 and Class 3 circuits depend on listed power sources that limit available energy, which this circuit lacks. The fire alarm article covers circuits for fire alarm systems, not general remote control and signaling in a warehouse.

question: Life safety branch loads in a hospital must be restored automatically after a normal power failure, and the electrician is choosing the transfer equipment. The hospital also has an optional standby generator for office areas. What type of transfer equipment applies to the life safety branch?

options.A: Automatic transfer equipment identified for emergency use and approved by the authority having jurisdiction.
options.B: Manual transfer equipment rated for the generator load and operated by trained facility staff.
options.C: Any listed transfer switch rated for optional standby service under the optional standby article.
options.D: A double-throw switch with a mechanical interlock set by the maintenance department.

distractor_mistakes.B: accepts manual operation for a life safety load
distractor_mistakes.C: uses an optional standby transfer switch for emergency loads
distractor_mistakes.D: treats an interlocked switch as emergency equipment

explanation: The correct answer is A (Automatic transfer equipment identified for emergency use and approved by the authority having jurisdiction.): Emergency system loads must transfer automatically, and the transfer equipment must be identified for emergency use and approved by the authority having jurisdiction. Manual operation would leave life safety loads dark until someone arrived, and a transfer switch listed only for optional standby service is not identified for emergency use. The optional standby generator for the offices is a separate system and does not affect this choice.

question: Several contactors, overload relays and terminal blocks go into an enclosure that a panel builder assembles for a conveyor system in a bottling plant. The assembly will carry a short-circuit current rating marking. Which article covers the construction and marking requirements for this assembly?

options.A: Article 430, which covers motor circuits and controllers installed in the field.
options.B: Article 408, which covers switchboards, switchgear and panelboards for power distribution.
options.C: Article 409, which covers industrial control panels and their construction requirements.
options.D: Article 450, which covers transformers and their vaults in industrial plants.

distractor_mistakes.A: picks the motor article for a panel assembly
distractor_mistakes.B: picks the distribution equipment article
distractor_mistakes.D: picks the transformer article

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 409, which covers industrial control panels and their construction requirements.): Article 409 applies to industrial control panels, which are assemblies of motor controllers, relays and similar devices rated at 600 volts or less, and it includes the short-circuit current rating marking. Article 430 covers how motor circuits and controllers are installed rather than how the assembly is built. Articles 408 and 450 cover distribution equipment and transformers, which are not what this panel is.

question: Stairwell emergency luminaires in a hospital use unit equipment with a 12-volt battery. The lamps draw a total of 24 watts, and the unit must operate the load for the full code duration after a power outage. What minimum battery capacity does the load require?

options.A: 2.0 ampere-hours, from 2 amperes carried for only one hour of operation.
options.B: 3.0 ampere-hours, from 2 amperes carried for the 90 minute required duration.
options.C: 4.0 ampere-hours, from 2 amperes carried for two hours of operation.
options.D: 0.3 ampere-hours, from 24 watts divided by 120 volts and carried for 90 minutes.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses one hour instead of 90 minutes
distractor_mistakes.C: uses two hours instead of 90 minutes
distractor_mistakes.D: divides by the 120 volt supply instead of the battery voltage

explanation: The correct answer is B (3.0 ampere-hours, from 2 amperes carried for the 90 minute required duration.): Emergency unit equipment must operate for at least 1 1/2 hours, which is 90 minutes. Battery current is 24 watts divided by 12 volts, or 2 amperes. Over 1.5 hours that requires 2 x 1.5 = 3.0 ampere-hours. Using the 120 volt supply gives the wrong current, because the lamps run from the battery during the outage.

question: Planning a permanent optional standby generator tied in at a building's service location, the installer asks what must be marked at the service equipment. The owner wants the generator on the wall beside the utility meter. Which marking must the installer provide at the service equipment for this system?

options.A: A sign showing the type and location of the optional standby power source.
options.B: A sign showing the type and location of the legally required standby power source.
options.C: A sign showing the location of the transfer equipment and the generator main breaker.
options.D: A label showing the generator kilowatt rating and the available fault current at the service.

distractor_mistakes.B: names the wrong class of standby system
distractor_mistakes.C: marks equipment locations instead of the power source type
distractor_mistakes.D: mixes in the fault current marking from a different rule

explanation: The correct answer is A (A sign showing the type and location of the optional standby power source.): Optional standby systems require a sign at the service equipment identifying the type and location of the on-site optional standby power source. That sign tells firefighters and other workers that a second source can energize the building after the utility is disconnected. A sign for legally required standby belongs to a different system, available fault current marking is a separate service rule, and equipment locations do not name the source.

question: Citing an Informational Note under a control circuit rule as a mandatory requirement, a designer draws an objection from the inspector. The note recommends spacing Class 2 cables away from power conductors in a panel. How does the NEC treat an Informational Note?

options.A: As enforceable text only when it cites a specific section number elsewhere in the Code
options.B: As enforceable once the adopting jurisdiction fails to amend or delete the note.
options.C: As a permissive rule, so the installer may follow it or skip the related requirement
options.D: As explanatory material only, which is not enforceable as a code requirement.

distractor_mistakes.A: ties enforceability to a cross reference
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes silence by the jurisdiction makes a note enforceable
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses notes with permissive rules

explanation: The correct answer is D (As explanatory material only, which is not enforceable as a code requirement.): Informational Notes provide explanatory or advisory information and are not part of the enforceable requirements of the code. Only text written as a mandatory or permissive rule can be enforced. A cross reference does not turn a note into a rule, a jurisdiction's failure to amend a note does not convert it either, and a note is not a permissive rule. The inspector is right that spacing cannot be enforced from the note alone.

question: At a rooftop unit, a 24-volt control relay needs at least 21.6 volts to pull in and draws 0.8 amperes. The 18 AWG thermostat cable has 6.5 ohms per 1,000 feet per conductor, and the transformer supplies 24 volts. What is the maximum one-way run length?

options.A: 461 feet, ignoring that the return conductor doubles the length of the loop.
options.B: 230 feet, halving the 461 feet of total conductor length for the loop.
options.C: 115 feet, halving the one-way length a second time.
options.D: 2,308 feet, allowing the whole 24 volts to be dropped in the conductors.

distractor_mistakes.A: forgets the return conductor
distractor_mistakes.C: halves the length twice
distractor_mistakes.D: allows the entire supply voltage as drop

explanation: The correct answer is B (230 feet, halving the 461 feet of total conductor length for the loop.): The allowed drop is 24 - 21.6 = 2.4 volts. At 0.8 amperes the maximum loop resistance is 2.4 / 0.8 = 3.0 ohms. At 6.5 ohms per 1,000 feet that allows 3.0 / 6.5 x 1,000 = 461 feet of conductor in the loop. The run is out and back, so the cable can be about 230 feet one way.

question: Wiring two listed Class 2 transformers in parallel to feed one 24-volt control loop is a technician's idea for doubling the available current. Both transformers carry identical ratings and each has its own primary overcurrent device. What does the NEC say about this connection?

options.A: It is permitted when both transformers carry identical ratings and the same polarity marking.
options.B: It is permitted when each transformer has its own primary overcurrent protection device.
options.C: It is not permitted unless the sources are specifically listed for such parallel interconnection.
options.D: It is permitted when the combined volt-ampere rating stays within 100 volt-amperes.

distractor_mistakes.A: thinks matching ratings qualify parallel use
distractor_mistakes.B: treats primary protection as enough
distractor_mistakes.D: applies a combined limit instead of the interconnection rule

explanation: The correct answer is C (It is not permitted unless the sources are specifically listed for such parallel interconnection.): Class 2 sources are limited by their individual listing, and their outputs may not be paralleled or interconnected unless they are listed for that use. Identical ratings, separate primary protection and a combined volt-ampere total do not change the listing. Only a source marked as suitable for parallel interconnection may be connected this way.

question: Low-voltage cable above a ceiling plenum in an office feeds a 16-volt, 30 volt-ampere access control unit, and the old CL2 cable is being replaced with plenum-rated cable. The electrician records the unit's rated current for the work order. What is it?

options.A: 1.88 amperes, from 30 volt-amperes divided by the 16 volt rating.
options.B: 1.50 amperes, from the rated current reduced to 80 percent for continuous operation.
options.C: 0.25 amperes, from 30 volt-amperes divided by the 120 volt supply.
options.D: 2.34 amperes, from the rated current also divided by an 80 percent factor.

distractor_mistakes.B: reduces a marked rating by an 80 percent factor
distractor_mistakes.C: divides by the primary supply voltage
distractor_mistakes.D: adds a continuous load factor to a nameplate rating

explanation: The correct answer is A (1.88 amperes, from 30 volt-amperes divided by the 16 volt rating.): The unit's rated current equals its volt-ampere rating divided by its operating voltage: 30 / 16 = 1.875, or 1.88 amperes. Reducing that to 80 percent gives 1.50, and dividing by 0.8 gives 2.34, but neither factor applies to a rated current. The 120 volt supply is on the other side of the power supply and does not set the unit's current. The plenum rating affects cable selection only.

question: Holding a large motor starter coil energized, an industrial 120-volt control circuit draws 6 amperes continuously. The circuit is fed from a 500 volt-ampere control transformer in the control cabinet. At what percentage of the transformer's volt-ampere rating is the transformer operating?

options.A: 69 percent, from the 500 volt-ampere rating divided by the 720 volt-ampere load.
options.B: 1.2 percent, from the 6 ampere load divided by the 500 volt-ampere rating.
options.C: 180 percent, from 720 volt-amperes divided by 400 volt-amperes, 80 percent of the rating.
options.D: 144 percent, from 720 volt-amperes divided by the 500 volt-ampere rating.

distractor_mistakes.A: inverts the load and the rating
distractor_mistakes.B: divides amperes by volt-amperes without converting units
distractor_mistakes.C: derates the transformer by 80 percent before dividing

explanation: The correct answer is D (144 percent, from 720 volt-amperes divided by the 500 volt-ampere rating.): The load is 6 amperes x 120 volts = 720 volt-amperes. Dividing by the 500 volt-ampere rating gives 720 / 500 = 1.44, which is 144 percent. The transformer is overloaded and would overheat, so the coil circuit needs a larger transformer. Inverting the ratio hides the overload, dividing amperes by volt-amperes mixes units, and an 80 percent derate of the rating is not part of this comparison.

question: Feeding a pilot light panel through a 16 AWG home run and an 18 AWG tap, a power-limited Class 1 circuit has both conductor sizes sharing one overcurrent device at the source. What is the maximum overcurrent device rating the circuit may have?

options.A: 10 amperes, the limit that applies only to the 16 AWG home run.
options.B: 7 amperes, the limit that applies to the 18 AWG conductors in the circuit.
options.C: 15 amperes, the limit that applies to 14 AWG conductors under the small conductor rule.
options.D: 20 amperes, the standard rating for a general lighting branch circuit.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the larger conductor's limit
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the small conductor rule for 14 AWG
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a general branch circuit rating

explanation: The correct answer is B (7 amperes, the limit that applies to the 18 AWG conductors in the circuit.): For power-limited Class 1 circuits, 18 AWG conductors may be protected at not more than 7 amperes and 16 AWG conductors at not more than 10 amperes. When both sizes share one device, the smaller conductor sets the limit, so the device cannot exceed 7 amperes. Fifteen and twenty amperes are limits for larger conductors in ordinary branch circuits.

question: Derived from a 480-volt branch circuit through a step-down transformer with a 120-volt secondary, a Class 1 remote-control circuit feeds six relay coils at 18 volt-amperes each and two pilot lights at 4.8 volt-amperes each. What total current does the secondary carry?

options.A: 0.24 amperes, from 117.6 volt-amperes divided by the 480 volt primary.
options.B: 1.70 amperes, from the secondary current also multiplied by 1.732.
options.C: 0.90 amperes, from the six relay coils alone divided by 120 volts.
options.D: 0.98 amperes, from 117.6 volt-amperes divided by 120 volts.

distractor_mistakes.A: divides by the primary voltage
distractor_mistakes.B: applies a three-phase factor
distractor_mistakes.C: leaves out the pilot lights

explanation: The correct answer is D (0.98 amperes, from 117.6 volt-amperes divided by 120 volts.): The load is 6 x 18 = 108 volt-amperes for the coils plus 2 x 4.8 = 9.6 volt-amperes for the lights, for 117.6 total. The secondary is 120 volts, so the current is 117.6 / 120 = 0.98 amperes. Dividing by 480 volts gives the primary current, and the pilot lights must be counted because they are on the same secondary.

question: Markings of 30 volts maximum and 1,000 volt-amperes maximum appear on a power-limited Class 1 source installed in a control panel for a packaging line. The panel builder records the maximum current rating that the markings imply on the drawing. What is that current?

options.A: 33.3 amperes, from 1,000 volt-amperes divided by 30 volts.
options.B: 41.7 amperes, from 1,000 volt-amperes divided by 30 volts and increased by 25 percent.
options.C: 3.33 amperes, from the 100 volt-ampere Class 2 limit divided by 30 volts.
options.D: 25.0 amperes, from 1,000 volt-amperes divided by 30 volts and reduced to 75 percent.

distractor_mistakes.B: adds a 25 percent margin to a marked limit
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the Class 2 power limit for a Class 1 source
distractor_mistakes.D: applies a 75 percent reduction to a marked limit

explanation: The correct answer is A (33.3 amperes, from 1,000 volt-amperes divided by 30 volts.): Current is volt-amperes divided by volts, so 1,000 / 30 = 33.3 amperes. The 3.33 ampere result comes from the 100 volt-ampere limit used for Class 2 sources, and a Class 1 power-limited source allows 1,000 volt-amperes instead. Adding 25 percent gives 41.7 and cutting to 75 percent gives 25.0, but neither factor changes what the markings imply.

question: Installation of a new emergency system in a commercial building is finished, and the contractor says the work is complete. The system must be tested before it is accepted for use. Who must conduct or witness the acceptance test of the completed emergency system?

options.A: The manufacturer's representative, who certifies the equipment after startup.
options.B: The installing contractor's foreman, who signs a completion statement.
options.C: The engineer of record, who reviews the system drawings before installation.
options.D: The authority having jurisdiction, who conducts or witnesses the acceptance test.

distractor_mistakes.A: lets the manufacturer replace the inspector
distractor_mistakes.B: accepts the contractor's own sign-off
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses design review with an acceptance test

explanation: The correct answer is D (The authority having jurisdiction, who conducts or witnesses the acceptance test.): The code requires that the authority having jurisdiction conduct or witness an acceptance test of a completed emergency system on installation. A manufacturer's startup, a contractor's signed statement and an engineer's design review are all useful, but none replaces the test by the authority. The test confirms that the installed system actually performs as required.

question: Under the 2026 NEC, an inspector reviews a 400-ampere feeder-supplied motor control center in a warehouse. The arc flash marking lists nominal voltage, arc flash boundary and incident energy, but its only date is the day the label was applied. What makes the marking incomplete?

options.A: The 2026 marking must show the date the arc flash assessment was completed.
options.B: The 2026 marking must also show the name of the qualified person who made the assessment.
options.C: The 2026 marking must show the available short-circuit current at the equipment line terminals.
options.D: Equipment under 1,000 amperes is exempt from marking, so no label is needed.

distractor_mistakes.B: adds a signer name that the list does not include
distractor_mistakes.C: swaps in the fault current marking from a different rule
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the removed 1,000 ampere threshold

explanation: The correct answer is A (The 2026 marking must show the date the arc flash assessment was completed.): The 2026 NEC requires the marking to show the nominal system voltage, the arc flash boundary, the available incident energy or minimum PPE level, and the date the assessment was completed. The 2023 edition asked only for the date the label was applied. Available fault current is a separate marking rule, no signer name is listed, and the old amperage threshold was removed, so this 400-ampere control center needs the marking.

question: Ventilation fans at 12 kilowatts, smoke control equipment at 8 kilowatts and a sewage pump at 5 kilowatts are required by the authority having jurisdiction and share one generator at 208 volts, three-phase, unity power factor. What full-load current do the three loads draw together?

options.A: 120.2 amperes, from 25,000 watts divided by 208 volts as a single-phase load.
options.B: 69.4 amperes, from 25,000 watts divided by 1.732 times 208 volts.
options.C: 77.1 amperes, from the three-phase result divided by a 0.9 power factor.
options.D: 30.1 amperes, from 25,000 watts divided by 1.732 times 480 volts.

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the single-phase formula
distractor_mistakes.C: applies a power factor that is not stated
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a voltage that is not the system voltage

explanation: The correct answer is B (69.4 amperes, from 25,000 watts divided by 1.732 times 208 volts.): Legally required standby loads add directly: 12 + 8 + 5 = 25 kilowatts, or 25,000 watts. Three-phase current is watts divided by 1.732 times line voltage, so 25,000 / (1.732 x 208) = 69.4 amperes. The single-phase formula overstates the current, the stem states unity power factor so no factor of 0.9 belongs in the calculation, and 480 volts is not this system's voltage.

question: Routing an emergency lighting feeder through a mechanical room, an electrician wants to pull it in the same raceway as the normal lighting circuits. All conductors are the same size. What does the NEC require for emergency system wiring in this situation?

options.A: Keep it entirely independent of normal wiring, in its own raceway, except for the listed exceptions.
options.B: Allow it to share a raceway with normal circuits when all conductors are the same size.
options.C: Allow it to share a raceway when both circuits are fed through the same transfer switch.
options.D: Allow it to share a raceway when each circuit has a 20 ampere device or less.

distractor_mistakes.B: thinks matching conductor size allows sharing
distractor_mistakes.C: treats a common transfer switch as an exception
distractor_mistakes.D: applies an invented overcurrent limit

explanation: The correct answer is A (Keep it entirely independent of normal wiring, in its own raceway, except for the listed exceptions.): Emergency system wiring must be kept entirely independent of all other wiring and equipment, so a fault in normal wiring cannot take out the emergency feeder. The exceptions are narrow, such as wiring inside the transfer equipment and circuits for emergency luminaires fed from the same circuit. Matching conductor sizes, a shared transfer switch or a 20 ampere device do not qualify.

question: Locked out and tagged, the disconnect for a 480-volt starter is open, but the control circuit is supplied from a separate source in another panel. The next task is replacing the contactor coil. What is the next step before touching the conductors?

options.A: Begin work immediately, since lockout and tagging have made the equipment electrically safe.
options.B: Verify absence of voltage on all conductors using a rated tester proven on a known source.
options.C: Test only the line terminals of the contactor, since control wiring cannot carry voltage now.
options.D: Close the control circuit disconnect to see whether the coil drops out, then start work.

distractor_mistakes.A: skips verification after locking out
distractor_mistakes.C: tests only the power terminals and misses the separate control source
distractor_mistakes.D: re-energizes the circuit as a check

explanation: The correct answer is B (Verify absence of voltage on all conductors using a rated tester proven on a known source.): After locking and tagging out, the electrical safety process requires verifying that the circuit is de-energized with a properly rated voltage tester that has been checked on a known live source. The control circuit comes from a separate source, so it can still be energized after the main disconnect opens. Closing a disconnect to see what happens re-energizes the equipment, which is the hazard the lockout was meant to remove.

question: Rated 20 kilowatts, an optional standby generator at a restaurant is meant to carry connected loads the owner says total 32 kilowatts. The generator has no way to select loads. Which provision lets the installation keep the connected load within the generator's capacity?

options.A: Connect every load and rely on the built-in generator overcurrent protection to disconnect any excess load
options.B: Install a larger transfer switch rated for the full 32 kilowatt connected load
options.C: Size the generator output conductors at 125 percent of the 32 kilowatt connected load
options.D: Add load management that selects or sheds loads to keep the total within the rating.

distractor_mistakes.A: relies on an overload breaker as the control method
distractor_mistakes.B: thinks a larger switch increases the source capacity
distractor_mistakes.C: treats conductor sizing as a way to raise generator capacity

explanation: The correct answer is D (Add load management that selects or sheds loads to keep the total within the rating.): Where an optional standby source cannot carry the whole connected load, the installation needs manual or automatic load selection so the generator is not overloaded. A breaker only trips after an overload develops. A larger transfer switch and larger output conductors are properly sized equipment, but neither raises the 20 kilowatt output of the generator, so the 32 kilowatt total would still overload it.

question: Hydronic heating in a house uses a listed 24-volt, 40 volt-ampere transformer feeding three zone valves at 12 volt-amperes each and one relay at 10 volt-amperes. The homeowner reports the transformer running hot. What total secondary current does the connected load draw?

options.A: 1.50 amperes, from the three zone valves alone at 36 volt-amperes.
options.B: 1.92 amperes, from 46 volt-amperes divided by the 24 volt secondary.
options.C: 0.38 amperes, from 46 volt-amperes divided by the 120 volt primary.
options.D: 3.83 amperes, from 46 volt-amperes divided by a 12 volt valve coil rating.

distractor_mistakes.A: leaves out the relay
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the primary voltage
distractor_mistakes.D: divides by a coil voltage that is not the secondary

explanation: The correct answer is B (1.92 amperes, from 46 volt-amperes divided by the 24 volt secondary.): The connected load is 3 x 12 = 36 volt-amperes for the valves plus 10 for the relay, which makes 46 volt-amperes. Dividing by the 24 volt secondary gives 46 / 24 = 1.92 amperes. That is 6 volt-amperes above the 40 volt-ampere rating, which explains the heat, so a larger transformer is needed. Leaving out the relay hides the overload.

question: During acceptance testing of emergency luminaire unit equipment in a school, the facility manager finds the battery carried the load for only 72 minutes against the 90 minute code requirement. What percentage of the required runtime did the battery achieve?

options.A: 80 percent, from the 72 minutes achieved divided by the 90 minute requirement.
options.B: 20 percent, from the 18 minute shortfall reported as if it were the achieved runtime.
options.C: 125 percent, from the 90 minute requirement divided by the 72 minute result.
options.D: 72 percent, from reading the measured minutes directly as a percentage.

distractor_mistakes.B: reports the shortfall instead of the achieved runtime
distractor_mistakes.C: inverts the required and measured runtime ratio
distractor_mistakes.D: reads minutes as a percentage

explanation: The correct answer is A (80 percent, from the 72 minutes achieved divided by the 90 minute requirement.): The achieved runtime as a share of the requirement is 72 / 90 = 0.80, or 80 percent. The battery fell 18 minutes, or 20 percent, short, so it fails the 90 minute requirement and must be replaced or repaired. Inverting the ratio suggests it exceeded the requirement, which it did not.

question: Wiring a manual transfer switch to connect a portable generator to the branch circuits of a small shop, an electrician must prevent the generator from feeding power back into the utility lines when the utility is restored. What does the NEC require of the transfer equipment?

options.A: It must prevent inadvertent interconnection of the normal source and the generator source.
options.B: It must contain a neutral-to-ground bond that is made whenever the generator source is selected.
options.C: It must be located within sight of the utility meter and be marked as service equipment.
options.D: It must switch the grounded conductor along with the ungrounded conductors at every transfer.

distractor_mistakes.B: thinks the switch must make a neutral bond
distractor_mistakes.C: adds a location and service equipment marking rule
distractor_mistakes.D: treats a switched neutral as a requirement

explanation: The correct answer is A (It must prevent inadvertent interconnection of the normal source and the generator source.): Transfer equipment for standby sources must be arranged so the normal supply and the alternate supply cannot be connected to the loads at the same time. This protects utility workers from backfeed and the generator from the utility. Neutral bonding and switching the grounded conductor depend on how the system is derived and are design choices, not the transfer equipment rule, and a meter location is not required.

question: Three 12 AWG motor conductors of 0.0133 square inches each share trade size 3/4 EMT with two functionally associated 14 AWG Class 1 control conductors of 0.0097 square inches each, where 40 percent fill is 0.213 square inches. How much fill area remains in the conduit?

options.A: 0.194 square inches, from 0.213 minus only the two control conductors.
options.B: 0.173 square inches, from 0.213 minus only the three motor conductors.
options.C: 0.474 square inches, from the 0.533 total conduit area minus the conductors.
options.D: 0.154 square inches, from 0.213 minus the 0.0593 total conductor area.

distractor_mistakes.A: leaves out the power conductors
distractor_mistakes.B: leaves out the control conductors
distractor_mistakes.C: uses total area instead of the 40 percent limit

explanation: The correct answer is D (0.154 square inches, from 0.213 minus the 0.0593 total conductor area.): Class 1 conductors may share a raceway with the power conductors of the motor they control. The conductor area is 3 x 0.0133 = 0.0399 plus 2 x 0.0097 = 0.0194, for 0.0593 square inches. Subtracting from the 40 percent fill area gives 0.213 - 0.0593 = 0.154 square inches. The total conduit area is not the limit, because the fill rule applies to 40 percent of it.

question: At a bakery, a 24-volt control relay drops out during starting loads. With the circuit energized, the electrician measures 20.6 volts at the coil, while the supply side reads 24 volts. What percentage voltage drop exists in the circuit conductors?

options.A: 14.2 percent, from the 3.4 volt loss divided by the 24 volt source voltage drop.
options.B: 16.5 percent, from the 3.4 volt loss divided by the 20.6 volt coil voltage.
options.C: 3.4 percent, from reading the volts of drop directly as a percentage.
options.D: 7.1 percent, from taking half the loss for only one of the two conductors.

distractor_mistakes.B: divides by the load voltage
distractor_mistakes.C: reads volts as percent
distractor_mistakes.D: halves the drop for one conductor

explanation: The correct answer is A (14.2 percent, from the 3.4 volt loss divided by the 24 volt source voltage drop.): The loss is 24 - 20.6 = 3.4 volts. Percentage drop is measured against the source voltage, so 3.4 / 24 = 0.142, or 14.2 percent. That is far above any normal design target and explains the relay dropout. The electrician should look for undersized conductors, a long run or a loose termination, since the measurement already covers both conductors of the loop.

question: Powering a 24-volt thermostat circuit from a generic doorbell transformer that carries no Class 2 marking, a technician uses CL3 cable and wiring practices meant for Class 2 circuits. Why does the installation not qualify as a Class 2 circuit?

options.A: The power source must be listed and marked Class 2, and this transformer is not.
options.B: It qualifies because the secondary is 30 volts or less, whatever the marking says.
options.C: It qualifies because the transformer primary has its own overcurrent protective device.
options.D: It qualifies because the cable is CL3, which makes the whole circuit Class 2.

distractor_mistakes.B: thinks voltage alone sets the class
distractor_mistakes.C: treats primary protection as the qualifier
distractor_mistakes.D: believes the cable type sets the circuit class

explanation: The correct answer is A (The power source must be listed and marked Class 2, and this transformer is not.): A Class 2 circuit gets its classification from a listed power source marked Class 2, which limits the available energy. A secondary voltage under 30 volts says nothing about how much current the transformer can deliver. Primary protection and cable type do not make a power source Class 2 either, so the installation must be treated under rules for a higher energy circuit until the source is replaced.
