The system is divided into an emergency system and an equipment system, and the emergency system itself contains branches. Which pair of branches makes up the emergency system?

options.A: The life safety branch together with the critical branch, restored within ten seconds
options.B: The critical branch together with the equipment system, which connects after a delay or manually
options.C: The life safety branch together with the equipment system, both fed from one transfer switch
options.D: The normal system together with the equipment system, supplied through separate utility service connections

distractor_mistakes.B: Pairs the critical branch with the delayed equipment system
distractor_mistakes.C: Pairs the life safety branch with the equipment system
distractor_mistakes.D: Names the normal utility system as part of the emergency system

explanation: The correct answer is A (The life safety branch together with the critical branch, restored within ten seconds): Section 517.30 divides the essential electrical system into the emergency system and the equipment system. The emergency system is made up of the life safety branch and the critical branch, which are restored within ten seconds. The equipment system is separate and connects with a delay or manually. Pairing the equipment system with either branch mixes the two systems.

question: Hospital feeder ground fault protective device clears a fault in 0.2 second on a 60 hertz system. The main service ground fault device must be coordinated by adding the six cycle minimum separation between tripping curves. What minimum clearing time results for the main device, in cycles?

options.A: 6 cycles, using only the minimum separation and dropping the feeder clearing time entirely
options.B: 12 cycles, matching the feeder clearing time with no separation added to it
options.C: 24 cycles, doubling the feeder clearing time instead of adding the separation
options.D: 18 cycles, adding the six cycle minimum separation to the twelve cycle feeder clearing time total

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the separation alone and drops the feeder clearing time
distractor_mistakes.B: Matches the feeder time and adds no separation
distractor_mistakes.C: Doubles the feeder time instead of adding six cycles

explanation: The correct answer is D (18 cycles, adding the six cycle minimum separation to the twelve cycle feeder clearing time total): The feeder device clears in 0.2 second, which is 0.2 times 60, or 12 cycles. Section 517.17 requires a minimum of six cycles of separation between the tripping curves of the main and feeder ground fault devices. Adding gives 12 plus 6, or 18 cycles for the main device. Matching the feeder time leaves no separation, so both devices could open together.

question: Metal stanchions that animals touch stand on the concrete milking floor of a dairy barn, and the contractor cites a general bonding rule from Article 250 to skip the equipotential plane. Article 547 differs from that general rule. Which statement correctly settles the conflict?

options.A: Article 547 governs, since Chapter 5 rules supplement or modify Chapters 1 through 4
options.B: Article 250 governs, since Chapter 2 grounding rules apply to all special occupancies first
options.C: The less restrictive of the two rules governs once the inspector approves the plan
options.D: Article 547 governs only for wiring methods and does not affect bonding or grounding

distractor_mistakes.B: puts the general grounding article above special occupancies
distractor_mistakes.C: believes the less strict rule wins with inspector approval
distractor_mistakes.D: limits Article 547 to wiring methods

explanation: The correct answer is A (Article 547 governs, since Chapter 5 rules supplement or modify Chapters 1 through 4): Section 90.3 explains that Chapters 5, 6 and 7 apply to special occupancies and supplement or modify the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4. Article 547 is a Chapter 5 article, and its equipotential plane requirement for livestock areas is a bonding rule, so it is not limited to wiring methods. The general bonding rules still apply except where Article 547 changes them, and an inspector cannot choose the less strict rule.

question: Grain elevator conveyor motor planning: combustible grain dust is routinely suspended in air in ignitible quantities during normal operation. The planner must set the classification before choosing any equipment for the structure. Which classification applies to this area of the elevator?

options.A: Class I, Division 1, because dust and flammable vapor hazards are grouped together in one class
options.B: Class II, Division 2, because grain dust suspended in air appears only during equipment malfunction
options.C: Class III, Division 1, because grain fibers are easily ignitible and settle on equipment surfaces
options.D: Class II, Division 1, because ignitible dust concentrations exist in normal operation

distractor_mistakes.A: Groups dust with flammable vapors under Class I
distractor_mistakes.B: Chooses Division 2 although dust is present during normal operation
distractor_mistakes.C: Treats grain dust as fibers belonging to Class III

explanation: The correct answer is D (Class II, Division 1, because ignitible dust concentrations exist in normal operation): Class II locations involve combustible dust. Division 1 applies where ignitible concentrations of dust are present in the air under normal operating conditions. That matches an elevator where dust is routinely suspended. Division 2 would apply only where such concentrations occur under abnormal conditions. Class I covers gases and vapors, not dust.

question: One branch circuit from the emergency system serves every receptacle at a critical care bed location in a new hospital wing, and the inspector cites it. What does the code require for the branch circuits supplying a critical care patient bed location?

options.A: At least two circuits, both from the emergency system on separate transfer switches
options.B: At least two circuits, one from the emergency system and one from the normal system
options.C: A single circuit from the emergency system with a spare breaker installed
options.D: At least three circuits, one each from the life safety, critical and equipment systems

distractor_mistakes.A: Takes both circuits from the emergency system only
distractor_mistakes.C: Accepts a lone emergency circuit with a spare breaker
distractor_mistakes.D: Requires three circuits, one from each essential system

explanation: The correct answer is B (At least two circuits, one from the emergency system and one from the normal system): Section 517.19 requires each critical care patient bed location to be served by at least two branch circuits, with one or more from the emergency system and one or more from the normal system. That arrangement keeps some outlets live if either source fails. A single emergency circuit supplying everything does not meet it. Two emergency circuits also fail because the normal system is missing.

question: Holiday decorative lighting at a shopping plaza is energized on a temporary installation on November 15. The code limits temporary power for such lighting to a fixed number of days. On what date must it be removed at the latest, counting November 15 as day zero?

options.A: February 28, using a flat three month period instead of counting days
options.B: February 13, which is 90 days after the November 15 start
options.C: January 14, using a 60 day limit for holiday decorative lighting
options.D: March 16, using a 120 day limit for holiday decorative lighting

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses a calendar quarter instead of 90 days
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses a 60 day limit that the code does not give
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses a 120 day limit that the code does not give

explanation: The correct answer is B (February 13, which is 90 days after the November 15 start): Section 590.3(B) permits temporary power and lighting for holiday decorative lighting for no more than 90 days. Counting from November 15, 15 days reach November 30, 31 more reach December 31, 31 more reach January 31, and 13 more reach February 13. That totals 90 days. A three month period would run past the limit by about two weeks.

question: Bed 3 feet wide in a hospital room layout: receptacle placement near it is governed by the patient care vicinity, which extends 6 feet beyond the normal bed position on each side. What total width in feet does the vicinity cover across the bed and both sides?

options.A: 9 feet, adding 6 feet on one side only to the bed width
options.B: 12 feet, counting only the two 6 foot extensions without the bed
options.C: 18 feet, adding the 6 foot extension three times
options.D: 15 feet, adding 6 feet beyond each side to the 3 foot bed width

distractor_mistakes.A: Extends the vicinity on only one side of the bed
distractor_mistakes.B: Leaves out the width of the bed itself
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the 6 foot extension three times

explanation: The correct answer is D (15 feet, adding 6 feet beyond each side to the 3 foot bed width): The patient care vicinity extends 6 feet beyond the normal location of the bed on every side. Across the width, the vicinity is 6 feet, plus the 3 foot bed, plus 6 feet, or 15 feet. Counting one side only or omitting the bed width gives a smaller figure than the code area. Adding three extensions creates distance the definition does not include.

question: Branch circuits are being wired to a hospital patient room, and the inspector requires an effective ground fault current path with built-in redundancy, not just a single path. Which wiring method satisfies this requirement for circuits serving patient care spaces?

options.A: Nonmetallic sheathed cable with a bare copper equipment grounding conductor inside the cable sheath
options.B: Rigid nonmetallic conduit with insulated phase conductors and a bare copper grounding wire
options.C: Electrical metallic tubing alone, relying on the raceway as the only grounding path
options.D: Metal raceway or armored cable, plus an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses nonmetallic cable that has no metallic armor or sheath
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses nonmetallic conduit and a bare wire instead of an insulated conductor
distractor_mistakes.C: Relies on the raceway as the only grounding path

explanation: The correct answer is D (Metal raceway or armored cable, plus an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor): Section 517.13 requires branch circuits serving patient care spaces to run in a metal raceway or a cable with a metallic armor or sheath, which gives one ground path. It also requires an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor sized under 250.122, which gives the second, redundant path. Nonmetallic wiring lacks the metallic path. Metal tubing alone lacks the insulated conductor.

question: Underground PVC conduit already reaches a gasoline dispenser, and the contractor cites the general rule that PVC is allowed below grade. The motor fuel dispensing article adds a specific requirement for the end of the run. What must the last portion rising to the dispenser be?

options.A: PVC conduit all the way to the dispenser, since the general underground rule applies
options.B: Threaded rigid metal or threaded steel intermediate metal conduit for the last 2 feet
options.C: Electrical metallic tubing with setscrew fittings that are sealed against moisture and fuel
options.D: Liquidtight flexible nonmetallic conduit, because it tolerates settling at dispenser islands

distractor_mistakes.A: Applies the general PVC permission to the entire run
distractor_mistakes.C: Chooses tubing with setscrew fittings that the article does not allow
distractor_mistakes.D: Chooses flexible nonmetallic conduit that the article does not allow

explanation: The correct answer is B (Threaded rigid metal or threaded steel intermediate metal conduit for the last 2 feet): Section 514.8 permits nonmetallic conduit underground with 2 feet of cover, but it requires threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel IMC for the last 2 feet of the run where it emerges from the ground and connects to the dispenser. The specific rule in Article 514 overrides the general permission for PVC. Tubing with setscrew fittings is not an allowed method in that classified space.

question: Any listed grounding receptacle satisfies the general receptacle article, and a designer cites it for a general care bed location. A specific rule in the health care article changes the choice. Which receptacle type must be installed at the bed location?

options.A: Any tamper-resistant receptacle, since the general rule already covers listed devices
options.B: Listed GFCI receptacles, since patient bed locations are treated as wet locations
options.C: Hospital grade receptacles, listed and identified as such under the specific rule
options.D: Any listed 20 ampere receptacle, since patient care equipment draws more current than general loads

distractor_mistakes.A: accepts any listed or tamper-resistant device under the general rule
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes GFCI replaces the hospital grade requirement
distractor_mistakes.D: selects by ampere rating instead of the hospital grade rule

explanation: The correct answer is C (Hospital grade receptacles, listed and identified as such under the specific rule): Section 517.18 requires receptacles at general care patient bed locations to be listed hospital grade and so identified. Under 90.3, special occupancy rules modify the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4, so the stricter hospital grade requirement applies. Tamper resistance, GFCI protection and a higher ampere rating are separate features that do not replace the hospital grade listing.

question: Electrical metallic tubing with setscrew fittings carries circuits into a Class I, Division 1 solvent pump room, and a new break room sits next door. The inspector flags it. What correction does the code require for the wiring method in the pump room?

options.A: Add listed seals at every fitting, since seals make the existing tubing acceptable here
options.B: Swap setscrew fittings for compression fittings, since the tubing itself is otherwise acceptable
options.C: Replace it with threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel IMC using listed fittings
options.D: Replace it with PVC conduit, since nonmetallic raceways avoid any possible ignition source

distractor_mistakes.A: Believes seals make an unacceptable raceway acceptable
distractor_mistakes.B: Changes only the fitting type and keeps the tubing
distractor_mistakes.D: Selects nonmetallic conduit that is not permitted in Division 1

explanation: The correct answer is C (Replace it with threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel IMC using listed fittings): Section 501.10(A) requires threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel IMC, along with specific cable types, as the wiring methods in Class I, Division 1 locations. Electrical metallic tubing is not permitted there, and changing its fittings or adding seals does not change that. Nonmetallic conduit is also not an accepted method in this room. The break room has no classified area and does not affect the answer.

question: Airframe inspection will last a week for an aircraft towed into a hangar, and an electrician is asked about the plane's own battery and wiring. Under the hangar article, when must the aircraft electrical systems be de-energized while it remains inside the hangar?

options.A: Only while fuel is being added to or removed from the aircraft fuel tanks
options.B: While the aircraft is stored and, where possible, during maintenance
options.C: Only while the aircraft is stored, and not during maintenance work in the hangar
options.D: Only during fuel tank repair or other work involving the aircraft fuel system

distractor_mistakes.A: limits de-energizing to fueling operations
distractor_mistakes.C: drops the maintenance condition
distractor_mistakes.D: limits de-energizing to fuel system work

explanation: The correct answer is B (While the aircraft is stored and, where possible, during maintenance): Section 513.10 requires aircraft electrical systems in hangars to be de-energized while the aircraft is stored in the hangar and, whenever possible, during maintenance. That reduces the chance of arcing near fuel vapors. The week-long inspection here is maintenance, so the second condition applies. Limiting the rule to fueling, fuel system work or storage alone would leave systems energized during the work this question describes.

question: Fixed wiring for a new reception hall seating 350 guests is being planned by the electrician, who wonders about the wiring method rule. For assembly occupancies of this size, which statement describes the general rule for wiring methods in permanent installations?

options.A: Any Chapter 3 wiring method is acceptable for fixed wiring, with no limits tied to occupancy
options.B: Metal raceway or armored cable, with nonmetallic cable only in some construction types
options.C: Nonmetallic sheathed cable throughout the hall, since the hall has no classified locations
options.D: Flexible cords hard wired to ceiling outlets serve as the permanent lighting circuits

distractor_mistakes.A: Believes every Chapter 3 method is allowed in an assembly hall
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses nonmetallic cable throughout because nothing is classified
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats hard wired flexible cord as permanent wiring

explanation: The correct answer is B (Metal raceway or armored cable, with nonmetallic cable only in some construction types): Section 518.4 requires fixed wiring in assembly occupancies to be in metal raceways, armored cable or metal-clad cable. Nonmetallic wiring is allowed only in limited cases tied to the type of building construction. The hall is not classified, but that does not remove the assembly rule. Flexible cords are not a substitute for fixed wiring.

question: Hospital isolated power systems run at 120 volts nominal with an alarm threshold of 5 milliamperes of total hazard current. The line isolation monitor must be designed so the largest internal current is 1 milliampere when any point is grounded. What minimum monitor impedance results, in ohms?

options.A: 24,000 ohms, using the 5 milliampere alarm threshold in place of 1 milliampere
options.B: 120 ohms, using 1 ampere by dropping the milli prefix
options.C: 120,000 ohms, found by dividing 120 volts by 0.001 ampere
options.D: 240,000 ohms, using a 240 volt line to line value for the system

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the alarm threshold current instead of the internal current limit
distractor_mistakes.B: Drops the milli prefix and gets an impedance 1,000 times too small
distractor_mistakes.D: Substitutes a 240 volt value for the stated 120 volt system

explanation: The correct answer is C (120,000 ohms, found by dividing 120 volts by 0.001 ampere): Section 517.160 requires the monitor to limit internal current to 1 milliampere when a point of the system is grounded. Impedance equals voltage divided by current, so 120 volts divided by 0.001 ampere gives 120,000 ohms. The 5 milliampere figure is the alarm threshold for hazard current and is not the monitor's internal current limit. Dropping the milli prefix gives a value 1,000 times too small.

question: Permanently connected EVSE at an office parking garage, which is not a dwelling, has an emergency disconnect planned 12 feet from the equipment, within sight and readily accessible. The 2026 rule sets a minimum distance of 20 feet and a maximum of 100 feet. How much farther must the disconnect be moved at minimum?

options.A: 88 feet farther, subtracting 12 feet from the 100 foot maximum
options.B: 20 feet farther, applying the minimum distance as added distance
options.C: 8 feet farther, since the minimum distance is 20 feet from the equipment
options.D: No move is needed, because being within sight satisfies every distance rule

distractor_mistakes.A: Subtracts from the maximum distance instead of the minimum
distractor_mistakes.B: Adds the full minimum distance to the current distance
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats within sight as replacing the distance range

explanation: The correct answer is C (8 feet farther, since the minimum distance is 20 feet from the equipment): Section 625.43(D) requires the emergency disconnect for non-dwelling EVSE to be at least 20 feet and no more than 100 feet from the equipment. At 12 feet it is too close, so it must move 20 minus 12, or 8 feet farther. Moving it 88 feet would use the maximum as a target. Within sight is a separate requirement that does not replace the distance range.

question: Main floor capacity of 64 persons plus balcony capacity of 38 persons describes a municipal hall whose owner asks the electrician whether the assembly occupancy article applies to the building. What is the total capacity, and what is the result?

options.A: 64 persons, because a balcony is not counted, so the article does not apply here
options.B: 102 persons, which falls below the 300 person threshold, so the article does not apply
options.C: 102 persons in total, meeting the 100 person threshold in Section 518.2, so Article 518 applies
options.D: 102 persons, but the article applies only to buildings with fixed seating and a stage

distractor_mistakes.A: leaves the balcony out of the total
distractor_mistakes.B: uses a 300 person threshold the article does not set
distractor_mistakes.D: adds a seating and stage condition to the scope

explanation: The correct answer is C (102 persons in total, meeting the 100 person threshold in Section 518.2, so Article 518 applies): Section 518.2 applies the assembly occupancy article to buildings or portions of buildings designed or intended for the gathering of 100 or more persons. Adding the main floor and the balcony gives 64 plus 38, or 102 persons. That meets the threshold, so the article applies. The balcony counts toward the total, there is no 300 person threshold, and the article does not require fixed seating or a stage.

question: New bulk storage plant inspection finds a luminaire in a classified area carrying only a general purpose listing mark, while office luminaires nearby are fine. What must the inspector require for equipment in the classified location, given what the Code says about identification?

options.A: Equipment listed for general use with a drip cover installed over the lens glass
options.B: Equipment rated for the circuit voltage and the ampacity of its supply conductors
options.C: Equipment in a gasketed enclosure rated for protection against water and dust entry
options.D: Equipment identified for the class, group and temperature class of the location

distractor_mistakes.A: Accepts a general listing with a cosmetic cover
distractor_mistakes.B: Checks only electrical ratings of the luminaire
distractor_mistakes.C: Substitutes a water protection rating for hazardous location identification

explanation: The correct answer is D (Equipment identified for the class, group and temperature class of the location): Section 500.8 requires equipment in hazardous locations to be identified for the class of location and for the ignitible properties present. Markings show the class, division or zone, group and temperature class or operating temperature. A general purpose listing does not show any of these. Voltage rating, drip covers and water protection do not address ignition hazards.

question: Major repair garage work on fuel systems takes place at a facility that also has a separate multilevel deck used only to park customer vehicles, with no repairs there. The owner asks how the deck floor space is treated under the commercial garage article. What applies?

options.A: The whole deck is Class I, Division 2 up to 18 inches above every floor level
options.B: Parking areas with no repair work are unclassified, while repair bays receive the classification
options.C: The deck is Class I, Division 1 at every ramp and stair opening between levels
options.D: The classification depends on the gallons of fuel carried in all the parked vehicles

distractor_mistakes.A: Applies the repair garage 18 inch layer to the whole parking deck
distractor_mistakes.C: Invents a Division 1 area at ramp and stair openings
distractor_mistakes.D: Bases classification on fuel quantity in parked vehicles

explanation: The correct answer is B (Parking areas with no repair work are unclassified, while repair bays receive the classification): Article 511 classifies areas where repair or service is performed, but parking and storage areas where no repair work occurs are not classified. The repair garage is treated separately and receives the 18 inch Class I, Division 2 layer. The fuel in a parked vehicle's tank does not create a classified space. Ramps and stairs of a parking deck are also unclassified.

question: Health care facilities have their own article in the Code, and the electrician is told this building falls under it. Which of these buildings is within that article's scope as a facility where patients are examined, treated or cared for, rather than only visited?

options.A: A dental office where patients receive examination and treatment
options.B: The business offices and waiting rooms of a clinic, where no patients are treated
options.C: An office building tenant space leased to a medical billing and records company
options.D: A hotel with a first aid cabinet kept at the front desk

distractor_mistakes.B: treats non-patient areas of a clinic as covered spaces
distractor_mistakes.C: treats a medical-related business as patient care
distractor_mistakes.D: treats a first aid cabinet as enough to make a hotel a health care facility

explanation: The correct answer is A (A dental office where patients receive examination and treatment): Article 517 covers wiring in health care facilities, including hospitals, nursing homes, clinics and medical and dental offices where patients are examined or treated. A dental office fits that scope. Business offices and waiting rooms of a clinic are excluded from the patient care requirements, a billing company handles records and treats no one, and a first aid cabinet does not make a hotel a health care facility.

question: Construction site temporary power from the building service panel feeds 125 volt, 20 ampere receptacles used for cord-connected hand tools at the building site, and the inspector rejects the setup. Which correction does the temporary wiring article require for these receptacle outlets?

options.A: Install arc fault circuit interrupter protection on the temporary branch circuits feeding those receptacles
options.B: Provide GFCI protection for workers on those temporary 125 volt receptacle outlets at each construction site
options.C: Use tamper-resistant weather-resistant receptacles in listed in-use covers at each temporary outlet location
options.D: Provide an assured equipment grounding conductor program with written test records for each cord set

distractor_mistakes.A: Substitutes arc fault protection for ground fault shock protection
distractor_mistakes.C: Treats device ratings as a substitute for GFCI tripping
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies the assured grounding program meant for other receptacles

explanation: The correct answer is B (Provide GFCI protection for workers on those temporary 125 volt receptacle outlets at each construction site): Section 590.6 requires ground fault circuit interrupter protection for personnel on 125 volt, 15, 20 and 30 ampere receptacle outlets used on construction sites. Workers hold the tools while standing on damp ground, so shock protection is the hazard addressed. Arc fault protection targets fire from arcing and does not protect people. An assured equipment grounding conductor program is an alternative only for receptacles outside this group, and weather-resistant tamper-resistant devices do not trip on a ground fault.

question: Vent opening for a gasoline storage tank discharges above grade, and plans place a junction box 4 feet from the open end of the vent. Division 1 ends 3 feet from the opening and Division 2 ends 5 feet from it. How much farther must the box be moved to clear the classified space?

options.A: 2 feet farther, measuring from the 3 foot Division 1 boundary instead of the outer limit
options.B: 3 feet farther, using the Division 1 radius as the added distance to move
options.C: 1 foot farther, since the outer Division 2 boundary sits 5 feet from the vent
options.D: 5 feet farther, applying the full Division 2 radius as extra distance to move

distractor_mistakes.A: Measures from the Division 1 boundary instead of the outer limit
distractor_mistakes.B: Adds the Division 1 radius as extra distance
distractor_mistakes.D: Adds the full Division 2 radius to the existing distance

explanation: The correct answer is C (1 foot farther, since the outer Division 2 boundary sits 5 feet from the vent): Table 514.3 gives Class I, Division 1 within 3 feet of the open end of a tank vent and Class I, Division 2 from 3 to 5 feet. The box at 4 feet is inside the Division 2 band. To clear the classified space it must sit beyond 5 feet, so it needs to move 5 minus 4, or 1 foot. The other values use the wrong boundary or add a whole radius.

question: Marina feeder supplies 12 shore power receptacles, each rated 30 amperes at 125 volts, and the owner plans to add more docks later. The demand factor table gives 80 percent for 9 to 14 receptacles. What feeder load in volt-amperes results?

options.A: 45,000 volt-amperes, taking every receptacle at its full rating with no demand factor
options.B: 69,120 volt-amperes, using 240 volts instead of 125 volts for each receptacle
options.C: 9,000 volt-amperes, applying 20 percent instead of the 80 percent demand factor
options.D: 36,000 volt-amperes, which is 80 percent of the 45,000 connected load

distractor_mistakes.A: Skips the demand factor and uses the connected load
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses 240 volts for a 125 volt receptacle rating
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the complement of the demand factor

explanation: The correct answer is D (36,000 volt-amperes, which is 80 percent of the 45,000 connected load): Section 555.12 calculates shore power receptacle load from the receptacle ratings with a demand factor. Each receptacle is 30 times 125, or 3,750 volt-amperes, and 12 of them give 45,000 volt-amperes. At 80 percent the calculated load is 36,000 volt-amperes. Using full ratings ignores the demand factor, and a 240 volt basis overstates the load.

question: Fairground circuit at 125 volts feeds three booth appliances during an evening event, and each appliance cord leaks 2.5 milliamperes to ground. The Class A GFCI protecting the circuit trips when ground fault current reaches 6 milliamperes. What does the total leakage do?

options.A: The total is 2.5 milliamperes, since leakage does not add between cords, so no trip
options.B: The total is 7.5 milliamperes, but a Class A device trips only above 30 milliamperes
options.C: The total is 5 milliamperes, counting two cords, below the trip level so it stays closed
options.D: The total is 7.5 milliamperes, above the 6 milliampere level, so the device trips

distractor_mistakes.A: Assumes leakage from separate cords does not add
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses a 30 milliampere trip level for a Class A device
distractor_mistakes.C: Counts only two of the three cords

explanation: The correct answer is D (The total is 7.5 milliamperes, above the 6 milliampere level, so the device trips): The leakage from each cord returns to the source through the grounding path rather than the neutral, so the GFCI sees the sum: 3 times 2.5 is 7.5 milliamperes. A Class A GFCI trips at about 6 milliamperes, so the device opens. Counting only one or two cords understates the current. A trip level of 30 milliamperes belongs to equipment protection devices, not Class A personnel protection.

question: The tallest aircraft stored in a hangar has a wing upper surface 11 feet above the floor. A fixed luminaire that is not totally enclosed must be at least 10 feet above wings and engine enclosures. What minimum mounting height above the floor results?

options.A: 21 feet above the floor, adding the 10 foot clearance to the wing height
options.B: 11 feet above the floor, using the wing height alone as the mounting height
options.C: 12.5 feet above the floor, adding 18 inches to the 11 foot wing height
options.D: 16 feet above the floor, adding the 5 foot vicinity distance to the wing height

distractor_mistakes.B: Uses the wing height without adding the clearance
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses the 18 inch floor layer in place of the 10 foot clearance
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the 5 foot vicinity distance in place of the 10 foot clearance

explanation: The correct answer is A (21 feet above the floor, adding the 10 foot clearance to the wing height): Section 513.7 requires fixed luminaires less than 10 feet above wings and engine enclosures to be totally enclosed, so an open luminaire must sit at least 10 feet above the wing surface. The wing is 11 feet above the floor, so the minimum height is 11 plus 10, or 21 feet. Using the wing height alone ignores the required clearance above it. The 18 inch and 5 foot figures belong to the rules that classify hazardous areas around aircraft, not to luminaire clearance.

question: Conduit run leaves an explosionproof enclosure with arcing contacts in a Class I, Division 1 mixing area. The installed seal sits 26 inches from the enclosure, and the code allows a maximum of 18 inches. How many inches closer must it move?

options.A: 8 inches closer, since 26 inches less the 18 inch limit leaves 8 inches
options.B: 18 inches closer, treating the 18 inch code limit as the distance the seal must move
options.C: 44 inches closer, adding the 26 inch distance to the 18 inch limit
options.D: 26 inches closer, placing the seal directly at the enclosure conduit hub

distractor_mistakes.B: Uses the limit itself as the distance to move
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds the installed distance to the limit
distractor_mistakes.D: Moves the seal all the way to the enclosure

explanation: The correct answer is A (8 inches closer, since 26 inches less the 18 inch limit leaves 8 inches): Section 501.15 requires a seal in each conduit entry of an enclosure housing arcing or sparking devices in Division 1, located within 18 inches of the enclosure. The seal is at 26 inches, so it is 26 minus 18, or 8 inches too far away. Moving it 8 inches puts it exactly at the limit. Moving it 18 inches treats the limit as the correction, and adding the two numbers to get 44 inches confuses a distance with a sum.

question: Low voltage signal wiring will run beside 120 volt power wiring in the control system of a permanently installed amusement attraction at a theme park. The electrician asks which article covers control circuits for permanent attractions, not traveling rides. Which article applies?

options.A: Article 522, covering control systems for permanent amusement attractions and rides
options.B: Article 525, covering carnivals, circuses and similar portable temporary events
options.C: Article 551, covering recreational vehicles and recreational vehicle parks
options.D: Article 520, covering theaters, audience areas and similar stage performance spaces

distractor_mistakes.B: Chooses the temporary event article for a permanent attraction
distractor_mistakes.C: Chooses the recreational vehicle article
distractor_mistakes.D: Chooses the theater article because of public audiences

explanation: The correct answer is A (Article 522, covering control systems for permanent amusement attractions and rides): Article 522 covers control systems for permanent amusement attractions, including the circuits that control ride operation. Article 525 applies to portable rides and temporary events. A permanent attraction falls under Article 522 for its controls. Articles 520 and 551 cover theaters and recreational vehicles.

question: Prefabricated building sections with factory installed wiring arrive on flatbeds and will be set on a foundation and joined on site. They have no chassis for towing. The electrician is unsure whether the manufactured home article or another article applies. Which article governs?

options.A: Article 550, because any factory built dwelling counts as a manufactured home under the Code
options.B: Article 551, because transport on flatbeds makes the sections vehicle mounted equipment
options.C: Article 545, because closed sections without a towing chassis are manufactured buildings
options.D: Article 547, because the sections will later be used for farm structures and barns

distractor_mistakes.A: Treats every factory built dwelling as a manufactured home
distractor_mistakes.B: Treats flatbed transport as making them recreational vehicles
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats intended farm use as making the agricultural article apply

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 545, because closed sections without a towing chassis are manufactured buildings): Article 545 covers manufactured buildings, which are closed construction buildings made in a factory and installed on a building site, other than manufactured homes, mobile homes, park trailers or recreational vehicles. The sections here have no towing chassis. Article 550 covers manufactured and mobile homes, and Article 551 covers recreational vehicles. Farm use does not matter without agricultural classification.

question: Utility power fails at a hospital, and the generator reaches rated voltage in 6 seconds while the transfer switch adds 3 seconds. The code gives 10 seconds to restore the life safety branch. How much margin remains once both delays are counted?

options.A: 4 seconds, counting only the generator start time against the 10 second limit
options.B: 1 second, since 6 plus 3 is 9 seconds against the 10 second limit
options.C: 7 seconds, counting only the transfer switch delay against the 10 second limit
options.D: 51 seconds, using the 60 second limit that applies to the delayed equipment system branch

distractor_mistakes.A: Counts only the generator start delay
distractor_mistakes.C: Counts only the transfer switch delay
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the longer delayed equipment branch limit

explanation: The correct answer is B (1 second, since 6 plus 3 is 9 seconds against the 10 second limit): Section 517.31 requires the life safety and critical branches to be restored within 10 seconds of loss of normal power. The generator and transfer switch times add: 6 plus 3 is 9 seconds. That leaves 10 minus 9, or 1 second of margin. Counting a single delay overstates the margin at 4 or 7 seconds. The 60 second figure belongs to a delayed connection that does not apply to the life safety branch, so subtracting 9 from 60 to get 51 seconds uses the wrong limit.

question: Flour mill motor runs hotter after a month, and the inspector finds a thick layer of flour dust on its housing. The motor is identified for Class II, Division 1. Why does the dust layer still create an ignition hazard?

options.A: The layer conducts electricity across the motor terminals and shorts out the windings quickly
options.B: The layer makes the motor draw excess current and trips the overload on the next start
options.C: The layer lowers the winding insulation rating until the identification marking becomes void
options.D: The layer insulates the housing, so surface temperature can exceed the dust ignition temperature

distractor_mistakes.A: Blames conduction of dust across terminals instead of heat buildup
distractor_mistakes.B: Blames an overload trip instead of heat buildup
distractor_mistakes.C: Invents an insulation rating loss that does not exist

explanation: The correct answer is D (The layer insulates the housing, so surface temperature can exceed the dust ignition temperature): Class II equipment is marked with a maximum surface temperature that must stay below the ignition temperature of the dust. A thick layer of dust on the housing blocks heat loss, so the surface can climb above the marked temperature and ignite the dust. Electrical shorting and insulation rating changes are not the mechanism. Housekeeping to remove dust accumulation is part of the safeguard.

question: Fixed pier deck sits 28 inches above the water at the highest expected level. The code requires shore power receptacles to be at least 12 inches above the deck and at least 24 inches above the water. What minimum height above the water results?

options.A: 24 inches above the water, using the water clearance alone
options.B: 52 inches above the water, adding both clearances to the deck height
options.C: 40 inches above the water, because 12 inches above the deck governs
options.D: 12 inches above the water, using the deck clearance as the water height

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses only the water clearance and ignores the deck rule
distractor_mistakes.B: Adds both clearances to the deck height
distractor_mistakes.D: Confuses the deck clearance with a height above the water

explanation: The correct answer is C (40 inches above the water, because 12 inches above the deck governs): Section 555.33 requires receptacles to be at least 12 inches above the deck surface and at least 24 inches above the water level. The deck is 28 inches above the water, so 12 inches above the deck puts the receptacle 28 plus 12, or 40 inches above the water. That is higher than 24 inches, so the deck rule governs. Adding both clearances double counts them.

question: Traveling carnival food booths plug into portable 125 volt, 15 and 20 ampere receptacle outlets that the public can reach during evening hours, and an inspector asks about GFCI protection for those outlets at the fairground. Which article requires it, and why?

options.A: Article 525, because it covers carnivals and requires GFCI protection for such receptacles
options.B: Article 590, because its 90 day limit on temporary wiring governs every outdoor event
options.C: Article 210, because the general GFCI rule applies only to dwelling unit outdoor receptacles
options.D: Article 518, because crowds make the whole fairground an assembly occupancy by definition

distractor_mistakes.B: Believes temporary wiring rules override the special article
distractor_mistakes.C: Misreads the general GFCI rule as limited to dwellings
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats outdoor crowds as an assembly occupancy

explanation: The correct answer is A (Article 525, because it covers carnivals and requires GFCI protection for such receptacles): Article 525 covers carnivals, circuses and similar events, and section 525.23 requires GFCI protection for 125 volt, 15 and 20 ampere receptacle outlets readily accessible to the public. Under 90.3 a Chapter 5 article supplements the general rules, so its requirement governs here. Article 590 sets time limits on temporary wiring and does not displace the carnival rule. The general GFCI rule is not limited to dwellings, so that reasoning fails, and a fairground does not become an assembly occupancy.

question: Under the 2023 edition, a marina designer specified ground-fault protection of equipment on docking facility feeders only, relying on receptacle GFCIs for branch circuits. The same marina will now be inspected under the 2026 NEC. What does Article 555 now require for ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) on the docks and piers?

options.A: Equipment ground-fault protection tripping at 100 mA or less on both feeders and branch circuits
options.B: Equipment ground-fault protection tripping at 30 mA or less applied to branch circuits only
options.C: Class A GFCI protection tripping at 6 mA applied to every feeder and branch circuit
options.D: Equipment ground-fault protection tripping at 100 mA or less on feeders only, as in 2023

distractor_mistakes.B: confuses the 100 mA GFPE limit with a 30 mA personnel limit
distractor_mistakes.C: substitutes personnel-level GFCI for equipment protection on feeders
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the older 2023 feeder-only scope to the new edition

explanation: The correct answer is A (Equipment ground-fault protection tripping at 100 mA or less on both feeders and branch circuits): Section 555.35 in the 2026 NEC extends GFPE with a trip current not exceeding 100 milliamperes to both feeders and branch circuits on docking facilities and piers. The 2023 approach covered the feeders and left the branch circuits to receptacle GFCIs, so a designer carrying that habit forward under-protects the branch circuits. The 6 milliampere Class A GFCI is a personnel device and does not replace equipment protection on the feeder. A 30 milliampere limit is also not the GFPE trip value.

question: Article 547 covers agricultural buildings where manure vapors and moisture attack metal parts. A farm electrician must choose a wiring method for a poultry house with this corrosive atmosphere, and the owner asks for the cheapest option. Which wiring method suits the corrosive environment described in Article 547?

options.A: Type NM cable in its plastic sheath stapled exposed to the ceiling joists
options.B: Electrical metallic tubing with steel set-screw fittings and galvanized boxes
options.C: Type AC armored cable with zinc-coated steel armor on the bare steel surfaces
options.D: Rigid PVC conduit with PVC fittings and listed corrosion-resistant enclosures

distractor_mistakes.A: picks the cheapest cable although it is not listed for corrosive agricultural use
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes galvanizing alone resists ammonia and moisture
distractor_mistakes.C: treats zinc-coated armor as corrosion resistant in manure vapors

explanation: The correct answer is D (Rigid PVC conduit with PVC fittings and listed corrosion-resistant enclosures): Section 547.5 steers wiring in corrosive agricultural atmospheres toward nonmetallic or corrosion-resistant methods such as rigid nonmetallic conduit with nonmetallic fittings and boxes. Plastic conduit does not rust when exposed to ammonia, moisture, and cleaning chemicals. Type NM cable is not among the methods accepted for this environment, so its low cost does not make it compliant. Galvanized steel tubing and zinc-coated armor corrode in these vapors and are the tempting but wrong choices.

question: Dairy cows in a concrete-floored milking parlor flinch when touching metal stanchions and waterers, although every metal part is already bonded to the equipment grounding conductor. Voltage is measured between a stanchion and the floor where an animal stands. Which corrective action best addresses this stray-voltage complaint under Article 547?

options.A: Isolate the stanchions from the equipment grounding conductor so fault current cannot reach the animals
options.B: Add an equipotential plane in the concrete floor, bonded to the metal equipment and grounding system
options.C: Replace the branch circuit breakers with GFCI breakers on every circuit in the parlor
options.D: Drive another ground rod beside the parlor and bond it only to the neutral conductor

distractor_mistakes.A: removes the bond and leaves the stanchion floating above the floor potential
distractor_mistakes.C: treats a touch-voltage gradient as if it were a ground-fault trip problem
distractor_mistakes.D: bonds a new rod to the neutral only, creating a parallel return path

explanation: The correct answer is B (Add an equipotential plane in the concrete floor, bonded to the metal equipment and grounding system): Section 547.10 requires an equipotential plane in concrete floor areas where livestock stand near metal equipment, bonded to the metal equipment and the equipment grounding system. The plane holds the floor and the metal at the same potential, so the animal sees no voltage difference when it touches both. Disconnecting the stanchions from the grounding conductor makes them energized objects and increases the hazard. A GFCI breaker looks for current imbalance and does not remove a small touch-voltage gradient.

question: Rigid metal conduit enters an explosion-proof enclosure that houses a motor starter with arcing contacts, inside a Class I, Division 1 area at a solvent plant. The inspector asks where the sealing fitting must be placed on the conduit. How close to the enclosure must the seal be installed?

options.A: At least 24 inches from the enclosure the conduit enters
options.B: Between 24 and 36 inches from the enclosure the conduit enters
options.C: Between 3 and 10 feet from the enclosure along the conduit run
options.D: Within 18 inches of the enclosure the conduit enters, in each conduit run entering it

distractor_mistakes.A: places the seal past the 18 inch limit
distractor_mistakes.B: doubles the allowed distance and more
distractor_mistakes.C: reads a general conduit support spacing as the seal distance

explanation: The correct answer is D (Within 18 inches of the enclosure the conduit enters, in each conduit run entering it): Section 501.15 requires a seal in each conduit entering an enclosure for arcing or sparking equipment in a Class I, Division 1 location, placed within 18 inches of the enclosure. The seal limits the passage of flames and gases through the conduit into the enclosure. Placing it 24 inches or more away leaves a long volume where an explosion could build up inside the conduit.

question: At a marina, a 240-volt single-phase pedestal feeds a 24-ampere load through 150 feet of 10 AWG copper, one way. Dockhands report dim lights at the far end. Using K of 12.9 and 10,380 circular mils for 10 AWG, what voltage drop does the run produce at 24 amperes?

options.A: 4.47 volts, leaving out the factor of two for the return conductor
options.B: 7.75 volts, using 1.732 instead of two for a single-phase run
options.C: 8.95 volts, using two times K times current times length over circular mils
options.D: 14.2 volts, using the 6,530 circular mils of 12 AWG

distractor_mistakes.A: omits the factor of two for the round trip
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the three-phase multiplier to a single-phase circuit
distractor_mistakes.D: reads the circular mils of 12 AWG instead of 10 AWG

explanation: The correct answer is C (8.95 volts, using two times K times current times length over circular mils): For a single-phase circuit, voltage drop equals 2 times K times current times one-way length divided by circular mils. That is 2 x 12.9 x 24 x 150 = 92,880, divided by 10,380, which gives 8.95 volts or about 3.7 percent of 240 volts. Dropping the factor of two halves the answer to 4.47 volts. Using 1.732 belongs to a three-phase circuit, and 6,530 circular mils belongs to 12 AWG, so both give wrong results here.

question: Rigid metal conduit carries conductors from a Class I, Division 1 pump room through its wall into an unclassified control room. An inspector finds one sealing fitting inside the control room, 10 feet past the wall, with several couplings between it and the wall. Where must the seal be located?

options.A: Inside the control room at the far end of the run near the first device
options.B: Anywhere along the run provided it is within 10 feet of the wall
options.C: At the classified boundary, with no union, coupling, or box between the seal and the wall
options.D: Only at the pump-room device end, since the wall needs no seal

distractor_mistakes.A: places the seal well beyond the boundary where gases can travel
distractor_mistakes.B: allows a loose distance instead of a seal at the boundary
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes only the device end needs sealing

explanation: The correct answer is C (At the classified boundary, with no union, coupling, or box between the seal and the wall): Section 501.15 requires a seal where a conduit leaves a Class I, Division 1 location for an unclassified one, and the seal goes at the boundary. No union, coupling, box, or fitting other than a listed reducer may sit between the seal and the boundary. A seal 10 feet beyond the wall lets gases migrate through the couplings into the control room. Sealing only at the device end does not stop vapors from traveling along the conduit through the wall.

question: Inside the enclosed spray booth of a collision shop, flammable finishes are atomized and applied to vehicles during normal operation. The electrician must pick luminaires and wiring suited to the interior of that booth. Which classification applies to the interior of a spray booth under Article 516?

options.A: Class I, Division 1, so equipment must be identified for that location
options.B: Class I, Division 2, because the exhaust fan dilutes vapors during normal operation
options.C: Class II, Division 1, because overspray residue is treated as a combustible dust
options.D: Unclassified, as long as the booth fan interlock keeps airflow running

distractor_mistakes.B: assumes ventilation lowers the booth interior to Division 2
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses finish vapors with a combustible dust classification
distractor_mistakes.D: treats an interlocked fan as removing the classification

explanation: The correct answer is A (Class I, Division 1, so equipment must be identified for that location): The interior of a spray booth where flammable finishes are applied is a Class I, Division 1 location, because ignitible vapors are present during normal operation. Equipment inside must be identified for that classification. Ventilation and fan interlocks control the hazard but do not lower the classification of the booth interior. Overspray residue may be a fire concern, yet the governing vapor hazard makes the interior Class I.

question: On a sound stage, a raceway of 3/4-inch EMT will carry 12 AWG THHN conductors of one size, more than two in number. Table 1 sets a 40 percent fill limit, Table 4 gives 0.213 square inch at that limit, and Table 5 lists 0.0133 square inch per conductor. What is the maximum number of conductors?

options.A: 9 conductors, using the smaller one-half inch EMT fill area
options.B: 21 conductors, using the 14 AWG area of 0.0097 square inch
options.C: 16 conductors, from 0.213 divided by 0.0133 rounded down
options.D: 40 conductors, using the full 0.533 total area without the fill limit

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the one-half inch trade size area instead of three-quarter inch
distractor_mistakes.B: reads the 14 AWG conductor area by mistake
distractor_mistakes.D: skips the 40 percent fill limit and uses the total area

explanation: The correct answer is C (16 conductors, from 0.213 divided by 0.0133 rounded down): With more than two conductors the limit is 40 percent of the conduit area, which Table 4 lists as 0.213 square inch for 3/4-inch EMT. Dividing 0.213 by the 0.0133 square inch of a 12 AWG THHN conductor gives 16.01, and the count is rounded down to 16. Using the 0.0097 square inch of 14 AWG would allow 21 conductors, but those are not the conductors in this raceway. Using the full conduit area ignores the fill limit.

question: An inspector reviews a junction box in a Class I, Division 1 solvent room and finds a nameplate showing only manufacturer, catalog number, and voltage. The installer says that is enough for hazardous location equipment. Which additional information must the marking carry under the hazardous location rules of Article 500?

options.A: Class, division, voltage and current rating, and the maximum ambient temperature range for the enclosure
options.B: Class, material group, enclosure type number, and the date of manufacture of the equipment
options.C: Class, division or zone, material group, and operating temperature or temperature class
options.D: Division, explosion pressure rating, ingress protection rating, and the listing laboratory mark

distractor_mistakes.A: Lists circuit ratings instead of group and temperature class
distractor_mistakes.B: Swaps temperature class for enclosure type and date
distractor_mistakes.D: Lists construction ratings and omits class and group

explanation: The correct answer is C (Class, division or zone, material group, and operating temperature or temperature class): Equipment for hazardous locations must be marked with the class, the division or zone, the material group, and the operating temperature or temperature class under section 500.8. These items let the inspector match the equipment to the atmosphere and to the ignition temperature of the material. Voltage, current and ambient range describe the circuit but not suitability for the atmosphere. Enclosure type numbers, pressure ratings and listing marks do not replace the required group and temperature marking.

question: For a manufactured home with 1,200 square feet of floor area by outside dimensions, a designer sizes the feeder demand for lighting, two small-appliance circuits, and one laundry circuit, using 3 volt-amperes per square foot and 1,500 volt-amperes per circuit. Applying 100 percent to the first 3,000 and 35 percent to the rest, what is the demand?

options.A: 2,835 volt-amperes, applying 35 percent to the entire 8,100 total
options.B: 8,100 volt-amperes, applying no demand factor to the connected load
options.C: 3,000 volt-amperes, ignoring all load above the first 3,000
options.D: 4,785 volt-amperes, with 35 percent applied only above the first 3,000

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the 35 percent factor to the first 3,000 as well
distractor_mistakes.B: skips the demand factor entirely
distractor_mistakes.C: drops the load above the first 3,000

explanation: The correct answer is D (4,785 volt-amperes, with 35 percent applied only above the first 3,000): The connected load is 1,200 x 3 = 3,600 for lighting, plus 3,000 for two small-appliance circuits and 1,500 for laundry, a total of 8,100 volt-amperes. The first 3,000 counts at 100 percent. The remaining 5,100 counts at 35 percent, which is 1,785, and the sum is 4,785 volt-amperes. Applying 35 percent to the whole 8,100 gives 2,835 and understates the demand.

question: Along a tidal shoreline, a designer is locating equipment at a boat basin, where the electrical datum plane controls how high certain equipment must sit above the water. For land areas subject to tidal fluctuation, where does Article 555 place the electrical datum plane?

options.A: A horizontal plane 12 inches above the highest water level during storms
options.B: A horizontal plane 2 feet above the highest high tide under normal circumstances
options.C: A horizontal plane 2 feet above mean sea level on an average day
options.D: A horizontal plane 3 feet above the deck surface of the nearest pier

distractor_mistakes.A: uses a 12 inch height and storm level that does not match the definition
distractor_mistakes.C: references mean sea level instead of the highest high tide
distractor_mistakes.D: measures from the pier deck instead of the water level

explanation: The correct answer is B (A horizontal plane 2 feet above the highest high tide under normal circumstances): Article 555 defines the electrical datum plane for tidal land areas as a horizontal plane 2 feet above the highest high tide under normal circumstances. Equipment that must stay above this plane is located by reference to it. Mean sea level is far lower than the highest high tide and would put equipment where tides can reach it. A pier deck reference moves with the structure and is not how the plane is defined.

question: Seasonal campground placement is planned for a recreational unit built on a single chassis, 400 square feet or less in set-up mode, and certified by its manufacturer as a park trailer. The dealer cites Article 550 in the wiring documents. Which article governs the electrical installation of this unit?

options.A: Article 550, which covers mobile and manufactured homes
options.B: Article 551, which covers recreational vehicles and recreational vehicle parks
options.C: Article 552, which covers park trailers installed on a single chassis
options.D: Article 545, which covers manufactured buildings built in a factory

distractor_mistakes.A: applies the mobile home article to a park trailer
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the recreational vehicle article instead of the park trailer article
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses a trailer unit with a factory-built building

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 552, which covers park trailers installed on a single chassis): Park trailers have their own article, Article 552, which applies to wiring in units built on a single chassis within the stated size limit. The dealer's choice of Article 550 is aimed at mobile and manufactured homes, which are larger and permanently sited. Article 551 covers vehicles and parks designed for travel and camping, not certified park trailers. Article 545 covers factory-built buildings and is not a trailer article.

question: At a hospital patient bed location, a contractor feeds receptacles with EMT that contains only phase and neutral conductors, arguing the steel raceway already forms a qualified grounding path. What must the inspector require for branch circuits serving the patient care space under 517.13?

options.A: An insulated copper equipment grounding conductor one size larger than Table 250.122, replacing the raceway path
options.B: An insulated copper equipment grounding conductor in addition to the qualifying metal raceway path
options.C: A bonding jumper from each receptacle box to the nearest building steel or water pipe
options.D: An insulated copper equipment grounding conductor alone, with the metal raceway not counted as a path

distractor_mistakes.A: Upsizes the conductor and drops the raceway path
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses building steel as the redundant grounding path
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats the wire conductor as replacing the raceway

explanation: The correct answer is B (An insulated copper equipment grounding conductor in addition to the qualifying metal raceway path): Section 517.13 requires two grounding paths for branch circuits serving patient care spaces: a qualifying metal raceway or cable armor, and an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor. The EMT alone supplies only one. The conductor is sized from Table 250.122 with no extra upsizing, and it adds to the raceway path rather than replacing it. Bonding to building steel or a water pipe is not the required redundant path back to the panelboard.

question: Because the charger nameplate shows 32 amperes continuous, an inspector fails a residential EVSE circuit wired with 10 AWG copper. All terminations are rated for 75 degrees C. Using 125 percent for the continuous load and the 75 degree column of Table 310.16, what is the minimum copper conductor size?

options.A: 8 AWG, because 125 percent of 32 is 40 amperes and 10 AWG carries only 35
options.B: 10 AWG, because 32 amperes is under the 35 ampere 75 degree rating
options.C: 6 AWG, because 125 percent is applied twice and the 60 degree column is read
options.D: 12 AWG, because 80 percent of 32 is 25.6, within its 30 ampere 90 degree rating

distractor_mistakes.B: skips the 125 percent continuous load factor
distractor_mistakes.C: applies the continuous factor twice and reads the wrong column
distractor_mistakes.D: derates the load instead of increasing it and reads the 90 degree column

explanation: The correct answer is A (8 AWG, because 125 percent of 32 is 40 amperes and 10 AWG carries only 35): An EVSE is a continuous load, so the conductor must carry 125 percent of 32 amperes, which is 40 amperes. In the 75 degree column of Table 310.16, 10 AWG carries 35 amperes, which is too small, and 8 AWG carries 50 amperes, which is enough. Using 32 amperes directly lets 10 AWG pass and is exactly the inspector's failed installation. Applying the factor twice or reading another column leads to a different size than the correct one.

question: At a traveling carnival, the inspector walks the midway checking the disconnecting means for each ride. A Ferris wheel is powered from a distribution box 80 feet from its operator's station. Where must the disconnecting means for that ride be located under Article 525?

options.A: Within sight of the ride's main distribution box, readily accessible and marked with the ride name
options.B: Within sight of the operator station, readily accessible, and lockable
options.C: Inside the ride control cabinet, readily accessible to the operator and lockable by the owner
options.D: At the fair's central generator, lockable, with a sign naming each ride it feeds

distractor_mistakes.A: Locates the disconnect at the source out of the operator's view
distractor_mistakes.C: Hides the disconnect inside a cabinet away from the operator
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses one central generator switch for every ride

explanation: The correct answer is B (Within sight of the operator station, readily accessible, and lockable): Article 525 requires a readily accessible disconnecting means for each ride, located within sight of the operator station and lockable. This lets the operator open the circuit quickly in an emergency without leaving the controls. A disconnect at the distribution box 80 feet away is out of the operator's view. A switch inside a ride cabinet or one central generator switch cannot serve as the individual disconnect for each ride.

question: In an operating suite, routine cleaning leaves standing fluid on the floor of a patient care space while patients are present. The engineer must provide special protection against electric shock for fixed equipment and receptacles there. Which protection method does Article 517 accept for this wet procedure location?

options.A: Arc-fault circuit-interrupter protection on every branch circuit serving the location
options.B: A redundant insulated grounding conductor alone, with no added shock protection
options.C: GFCI protection or an isolated power system serving the location
options.D: Equipment ground-fault protection set at 100 milliamperes on the feeder only

distractor_mistakes.A: uses AFCI protection, which addresses arcing and not shock
distractor_mistakes.B: relies on grounding redundancy without special shock protection
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a feeder level equipment trip instead of personnel protection

explanation: The correct answer is C (GFCI protection or an isolated power system serving the location): Article 517 requires special protection against shock in wet procedure locations, met by GFCI protection or by an isolated power system that limits first-fault current. The risk is current through a wet patient or staff member, so the device must act at personnel trip levels. AFCI protection is aimed at arcing faults, not shock. A feeder-level trip of 100 milliamperes is far above a personnel threshold.

question: To feed its repair shed, a boatyard installs a 75 kVA three-phase 480-volt transformer, and the electrician needs the full-load line current to begin sizing conductors. Use 1.732 for the square root of three. What is the full-load current at 480 volts?

options.A: 90.2 amperes, from 75,000 divided by 1.732 times 480
options.B: 156.3 amperes, dividing 75,000 by 480 without the 1.732 factor
options.C: 270.6 amperes, multiplying by 1.732 instead of dividing
options.D: 52.1 amperes, dividing by 1.732 a second time

distractor_mistakes.B: leaves out the square root of three
distractor_mistakes.C: multiplies by 1.732 instead of dividing
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the 1.732 divisor twice

explanation: The correct answer is A (90.2 amperes, from 75,000 divided by 1.732 times 480): For a three-phase transformer, line current equals kVA x 1000 divided by 1.732 times line voltage. Here 75,000 divided by (1.732 x 480 = 831.4) equals 90.2 amperes. Leaving out the 1.732 factor gives 156.3 amperes, which is the single-phase style answer. Multiplying by 1.732 or dividing by it twice produces 270.6 and 52.1 amperes, both from a reversed or repeated step.

question: With two utility feeds already in place, a hospital facilities manager asks an electrician why Article 517 requires an essential electrical system, believing it only supplies convenience loads during storms. What is the general purpose of the essential electrical system in a hospital?

options.A: To restore power to every load in the hospital within 10 seconds after normal supply failure
options.B: To power life safety lighting and alarms only, with patient care equipment left on battery backup
options.C: To maintain power to operating rooms and intensive care units through isolated power systems only
options.D: To keep power flowing to designated areas and functions when the normal supply is interrupted

distractor_mistakes.A: Treats every load as covered by the 10 second limit
distractor_mistakes.B: Limits the system to life safety and drops critical loads
distractor_mistakes.C: Limits the system to isolated power in critical areas

explanation: The correct answer is D (To keep power flowing to designated areas and functions when the normal supply is interrupted): The essential electrical system exists to keep power flowing to designated areas and functions of a health care facility when the normal supply is interrupted. It is built in branches so life safety, critical and equipment loads receive priority rather than every load. The 10 second restoration limit applies to the life safety and critical branches only, not to all loads. Two utility feeds do not replace it because both can fail together, and it is not limited to life safety lighting or to operating rooms.

question: In a parking garage, the owner installs a 7.2 kW EVSE on a 240-volt single-phase circuit. The charger is a continuous load with 7.2 kW at full output on the nameplate. What is the minimum standard overcurrent protective device rating, using 125 percent of the continuous current?

options.A: 30 amperes, using the continuous current without the 125 percent factor
options.B: 40 amperes, from 30 amperes times 125 percent giving 37.5 amperes
options.C: 37.5 amperes, using the unrounded 125 percent result
options.D: 50 amperes, applying 125 percent twice and then rounding up

distractor_mistakes.A: omits the continuous load multiplier
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a value that is not a standard OCPD size
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the continuous factor twice

explanation: The correct answer is B (40 amperes, from 30 amperes times 125 percent giving 37.5 amperes): The charger draws 7,200 divided by 240, which is 30 amperes. A continuous load requires an OCPD rated at least 125 percent of that, which is 37.5 amperes. Section 240.6 does not list 37.5, so the next standard size, 40 amperes, is used. A 30 ampere device ignores the continuous factor, and 50 amperes comes from applying the factor twice.

question: During a utility outage test at a hospital, the facility engineer times how long the life safety branch takes to be restored on the generator. The inspector says that branch has a short maximum interval, unlike the equipment system. How soon must life safety branch power be available after normal power is lost?

options.A: Within 60 seconds once the generator reaches rated frequency and voltage
options.B: Within 30 seconds after the transfer switch senses a stable alternate source
options.C: Within 10 seconds of the loss of normal power at the main transfer switch
options.D: Within 2 minutes through delayed automatic connection of its loads

distractor_mistakes.A: uses a one minute interval that is far too long
distractor_mistakes.B: uses a 30 second interval that does not match the life safety rule
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the delayed connection timing of the equipment system

explanation: The correct answer is C (Within 10 seconds of the loss of normal power at the main transfer switch): The life safety and critical branches of a hospital essential electrical system must be restored within 10 seconds after normal power is lost. Egress lighting, exit signs, and alarm systems cannot be dark for longer than that. The equipment system is different: its loads connect by delayed automatic or manual means, so a longer interval fits there and not here. The 30 and 60 second values are not the stated limit for this branch.

question: Built in Type II noncombustible construction, a 200-seat restaurant dining room falls under the assembly occupancy rules of Article 518. The contractor wants a concealed wiring method above the finished ceiling. Which wiring method is permitted for this occupancy without any special encasement?

options.A: Type MC cable installed above the ceiling and properly supported
options.B: Type NM cable concealed above the ceiling and supported by staples
options.C: Rigid PVC conduit concealed above the ceiling without concrete encasement
options.D: Type UF cable concealed above the ceiling in the dining room

distractor_mistakes.B: uses a nonmetallic cable that is not allowed in this construction type
distractor_mistakes.C: assumes nonmetallic raceway needs no encasement
distractor_mistakes.D: uses an underground feeder cable inside a building

explanation: The correct answer is A (Type MC cable installed above the ceiling and properly supported): In assembly occupancies of fire-rated Type I and Type II construction, Section 518.4 limits wiring to metal methods such as metal raceways, metal-clad cable, and armored cable. Type MC cable fits that list. Nonmetallic cable such as Type NM is allowed only in the nonrated construction types. Nonmetallic conduit in rated construction needs to be encased in concrete of at least 2 inches, so bare PVC concealed above the ceiling does not meet the rule.

question: Each time the machinery runs, a flour mill's milling room has grain dust suspended in the air in ignitible quantities, which is its normal operation. The electrician must classify the room before choosing luminaires and motors. Under Article 500, which classification fits this area?

options.A: Class II, Division 1, because combustible dust is present in normal operation
options.B: Class II, Division 2, because dust appears only after an equipment failure
options.C: Class I, Division 1, because grain gives off flammable vapors when it is milled
options.D: Class III, Division 1, because grain particles are easily ignitible fibers

distractor_mistakes.B: treats continuous dust as an abnormal condition
distractor_mistakes.C: confuses a dust hazard with a vapor hazard
distractor_mistakes.D: mistakes grain dust for fibers and flyings

explanation: The correct answer is A (Class II, Division 1, because combustible dust is present in normal operation): Class II locations are hazardous because of combustible dust, and Division 1 applies when the dust is in the air in ignitible quantities under normal operating conditions. A running mill meets that condition. Division 2 would fit a room where dust appears only through abnormal events. Class I covers flammable gases and vapors, and Class III covers fibers and flyings, so neither describes grain dust.

question: Gasoline is stored at a tank farm, and the engineer is selecting explosion-proof junction boxes near the fuel transfer pump. The boxes must be marked for the material group of the vapors. Under Article 500, gasoline vapor falls in which Class I group?

options.A: Group B, which covers hydrogen and similar gases
options.B: Group D, which covers gasoline, propane, and natural gas vapors
options.C: Group C, which covers ethylene and similar gases
options.D: Group A, which covers acetylene and acetylene-bearing gas mixtures only

distractor_mistakes.A: picks the hydrogen group for a petroleum vapor
distractor_mistakes.C: picks the ethylene group for gasoline
distractor_mistakes.D: picks the acetylene group because it is first alphabetically

explanation: The correct answer is B (Group D, which covers gasoline, propane, and natural gas vapors): Class I Group D includes gasoline, propane, natural gas, and similar petroleum vapors, so boxes near the transfer pump must be marked for Group D. Group A is acetylene, Group B is hydrogen, and Group C is ethylene and similar gases. Equipment marked for Group B is acceptable in Group D areas, but the question asks which group the vapor belongs to, and that is Group D.

question: Running 200 feet one way, a three-phase 208-volt feeder carries 30 amperes on 8 AWG copper to a boat lift motor. Use K of 12.9, 1.732 for the square root of three, and 16,510 circular mils for 8 AWG. What is the voltage drop on the run?

options.A: 4.69 volts, leaving out the 1.732 factor for three phases
options.B: 9.38 volts, using the single-phase factor of two
options.C: 12.9 volts, using the 10,380 circular mils of 10 AWG
options.D: 8.12 volts, using 1.732 times K times current times length over circular mils

distractor_mistakes.A: omits the three-phase multiplier
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the single-phase factor on a three-phase run
distractor_mistakes.C: reads the circular mils of 10 AWG instead of 8 AWG

explanation: The correct answer is D (8.12 volts, using 1.732 times K times current times length over circular mils): For a three-phase run, voltage drop equals 1.732 x K x current x one-way length divided by circular mils. That is 1.732 x 12.9 x 30 x 200 = 134,057, divided by 16,510, which gives 8.12 volts or about 3.9 percent of 208 volts. Dropping the 1.732 gives 4.69 volts. Using two gives 9.38 volts, and using the circular mils of 10 AWG gives 12.9 volts, so each of those traces to a wrong method.

question: Designers are laying out branch circuits for a general care patient bed location in a hospital ward. The engineer wants to take both circuits from the normal panelboard to simplify the schedule. How must the minimum branch circuits serving each patient bed location be supplied under 517.18?

options.A: At least two circuits, one from the essential system and one from the normal system
options.B: At least two circuits, both from the normal system, on separate ward panelboards
options.C: At least two circuits, one from the essential system and one from the equipment system
options.D: At least two circuits, both from the essential system on separate transfer switches

distractor_mistakes.B: Draws both circuits from normal power only
distractor_mistakes.C: Replaces the normal circuit with an equipment system circuit
distractor_mistakes.D: Draws both circuits from the essential system

explanation: The correct answer is A (At least two circuits, one from the essential system and one from the normal system): Section 517.18 requires each general care patient bed location to have at least two branch circuits, one from the essential system and one from the normal system. This keeps some receptacles live during a normal power outage while the other circuit supports ordinary use. Two normal circuits remove that protection, and two essential circuits drop the normal source. The equipment system uses delayed connection and does not serve bedside receptacles.

question: Emergency egress lighting must stay lit when normal power fails in a concert hall designed for 800 persons, as its building code requires. The electrician needs to know which Chapter 7 article governs the emergency power circuits for that illumination. Which article applies?

options.A: Article 701, which covers legally required standby systems
options.B: Article 700, which covers emergency systems for life safety
options.C: Article 702, which covers optional standby systems chosen by the owner
options.D: Article 708, which covers critical operations power systems

distractor_mistakes.A: picks the standby article meant for nonlife-safety loads
distractor_mistakes.C: picks the optional standby article chosen by the owner
distractor_mistakes.D: picks the article for critical operations power systems
