options.A: Article 625, covering charging systems for road-going electric vehicles and their supply equipment installed on premises
options.B: Article 480, covering storage battery installations and the charging equipment that supplies stationary battery banks
options.C: Article 670, covering industrial machinery and the electrical equipment supplied as part of that machinery
options.D: Article 624, covering power transfer systems for electric self-propelled vehicles such as forklifts and ground equipment

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the road-vehicle EVSE article because the vehicles are electric, ignoring the Article 100 definition.
distractor_mistakes.B: Treats the vehicle battery as a stationary storage battery.
distractor_mistakes.C: Classifies the forklifts as industrial machinery.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Article 624, covering power transfer systems for electric self-propelled vehicles such as forklifts and ground equipment): The 2026 edition adds Article 624 for vehicles that Article 100 does not define as electric vehicles, such as forklifts, airport ground equipment and golf carts. Article 625 remains for the road-going electric vehicles defined in Article 100, so it is the tempting wrong choice here. Article 480 covers stationary storage batteries, and Article 670 covers machinery supply, neither of which governs a charging connection.

question: Plans for a new marina show a feeder to the main pier and several branch circuits feeding boat slip pedestals. The engineer asks what ground-fault protection the 2026 NEC requires for the docking facility distribution, beyond the 30 mA personnel protection at receptacles. What must be provided?

options.A: Ground-fault protection for equipment tripping at no more than 100 mA, on feeders and branch circuits
options.B: A 30 mA GFCI device installed on each feeder as well as every branch circuit
options.C: Ground-fault protection for equipment tripping at 100 mA on the feeder only, leaving branch circuits bare
options.D: A ground-fault protection device with a trip setting of 300 mA, as used for service equipment

distractor_mistakes.B: Applies receptacle personnel protection to feeders.
distractor_mistakes.C: Protects the feeder but forgets the branch circuits.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the service-level 300 mA setting instead of the docking facility value.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Ground-fault protection for equipment tripping at no more than 100 mA, on feeders and branch circuits): Section 555.35 in the 2026 NEC requires ground-fault protection for equipment, tripping at no more than 100 mA, on both feeders and branch circuits of docking facilities. Personnel protection at the 125 volt receptacles is a separate 30 mA requirement and does not replace it. Applying 30 mA to feeders would cause nuisance trips, while a feeder-only or 300 mA scheme leaves the branch circuits outside the rule.

question: During final inspection of a warehouse, the inspector finds a 400 ampere, 208 volt distribution panel fed from the service with no arc flash marking. The installer says only equipment rated 1,000 amperes or more needs one. Under the 2026 NEC, what is the correct finding?

options.A: Marking required, since the 1,000 ampere threshold is gone, showing the assessment completion date
options.B: Marking not required, since the 1,000 ampere threshold still applies to feeder equipment
options.C: Marking required only at 1,200 amperes or more, and it may be handwritten
options.D: Marking required, showing the date the label was applied, not the assessment date

distractor_mistakes.B: Applies the 2023 size threshold.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses an older threshold and allows handwriting.
distractor_mistakes.D: Confuses label application date with the assessment completion date.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Marking required, since the 1,000 ampere threshold is gone, showing the assessment completion date): Section 110.16 in the 2026 NEC removes the 1,000 ampere threshold, so service and feeder-supplied equipment in other than dwelling units needs the marking regardless of rating. The label lists nominal voltage, arc flash boundary, incident energy or PPE level, and the date the assessment was completed. The 2023 edition used the label application date, which is why that option looks right but is outdated.

question: Inside a spray finishing booth, solvent vapor is released at the nozzle every time a part is coated, so ignitable concentrations are present during ordinary operation. The inspector must classify the interior for equipment selection. Which classification applies to the booth interior under the hazardous location rules?

options.A: Class II, Division 1, because dried overspray residue forms a combustible layer on surfaces and equipment
options.B: Class I, Division 2, because vapors are handled only in closed containers or systems
options.C: Class I, Division 2, because dangerous vapor appears only when the booth exhaust system fails
options.D: Class I, Division 1, because ignitable vapor concentrations exist under normal operating conditions

distractor_mistakes.A: confuses combustible coating residue with combustible dust
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the closed container condition of Division 2
distractor_mistakes.C: treats vapor release as abnormal when it is routine

explanation: The correct answer is D (Class I, Division 1, because ignitable vapor concentrations exist under normal operating conditions): Division 1 applies where ignitable concentrations of flammable vapors exist under normal operating conditions. A booth that releases solvent vapor at every coating cycle fits that definition, so the interior is Class I, Division 1. Division 2 covers vapors confined in closed containers or released only through failure of ventilation or equipment, and neither describes routine spraying. Class II is for combustible dust, and dried overspray residue does not make the booth a dust location.

question: Estimating the service load for a 2,400 square foot dwelling by the standard method under the 2026 NEC, where the load rules now sit in Article 120, an estimator must choose a unit load. Which general lighting and receptacle unit load applies to the feeder and service calculation?

options.A: 3 volt-amperes per square foot, the former Article 220 value used for service calculations
options.B: 2 volt-amperes per square foot, from the dwelling minimum unit load part of Article 120
options.C: 3 volt-amperes per square foot, because the branch-circuit count value also applies to services
options.D: 2 volt-amperes per square foot, but only when the optional dwelling method is chosen

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the 2023 unit load and old article.
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the circuit-counting value to the service.
distractor_mistakes.D: Limits the new unit load to the optional method.

explanation: The correct answer is B (2 volt-amperes per square foot, from the dwelling minimum unit load part of Article 120): Part III of Article 120 sets a minimum unit load of 2 volt-amperes per square foot for dwelling feeders and services, reflecting mostly LED lighting. The 3 volt-ampere figure is kept only to determine the minimum number of branch circuits. The 2023 Article 220 used 3 volt-amperes for services, so that choice reflects the old edition.

question: Threaded rigid metal conduit enters an explosionproof starter enclosure in a pump room classified Class I, Division 1. The starter contains contacts that make and break the circuit under load. The electrician must place the sealing fitting in the conduit. Where must it be installed?

options.A: At least 18 inches from the enclosure, measured along the conduit centerline
options.B: At the point where the conduit leaves the Division 1 area, with no distance limit
options.C: In the conduit run no more than 18 inches from the enclosure, along the conduit
options.D: In the conduit run no more than 18 inches from the first coupling past the hub

distractor_mistakes.A: reverses the 18 inch maximum into a minimum
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the boundary seal rule instead of the enclosure seal rule
distractor_mistakes.D: measures the 18 inches from a coupling instead of the enclosure

explanation: The correct answer is C (In the conduit run no more than 18 inches from the enclosure, along the conduit): Section 501.15 requires a seal in each conduit entering an enclosure that houses arcing or high temperature devices in a Division 1 location, placed not more than 18 inches from the enclosure. A boundary seal where the conduit leaves the classified area is a separate requirement and does not replace the enclosure seal. A minimum of 18 inches would leave an unsealed length where flame could travel, and measuring from a coupling moves the reference away from the enclosure.

question: Crushed coal moves through the conveyor gallery of a coal-fired power plant, and the inspector reviews the hazardous classification group for the area. Combustible dust from coal, coke and carbon black is present. Which Class II group applies to this dust under the hazardous location rules?

options.A: Group E, covering combustible metal dusts such as aluminum and magnesium
options.B: Group G, covering combustible grain and flour dusts such as wheat and corn
options.C: Group D, covering flammable vapors such as gasoline and propane in Class I
options.D: Group F, covering carbonaceous dusts such as coal, coke and carbon black

distractor_mistakes.A: Picks the metal dust group.
distractor_mistakes.B: Picks the agricultural dust group.
distractor_mistakes.C: Mixes up Class I gas groups with Class II dust groups.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Group F, covering carbonaceous dusts such as coal, coke and carbon black): Class II dusts are split into Group E for metal dusts, Group F for carbonaceous dusts such as coal, coke and carbon black, and Group G for grain and other non-metallic non-carbonaceous dusts. Coal dust is Group F. Group D belongs to Class I vapors, so it is not a dust group at all.

question: Walking through a mechanical penthouse, an inspector finds the disconnect for a traction elevator controller with a handle that cannot accept a padlock. Maintenance staff plan to work on the hoist motor tomorrow. What is the correct finding under the elevator article?

options.A: It fails, since the disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position
options.B: It passes, since the controller has overload protection and a fused motor branch circuit
options.C: It passes, since a lockout tag on the handle is accepted in place of lock provisions
options.D: It fails, since the disconnect must be located inside the hoistway within reach of the car

distractor_mistakes.B: Treats overload protection as a substitute for lockable isolation.
distractor_mistakes.C: Accepts a tag in place of a lock.
distractor_mistakes.D: Wrongly puts the disconnect in the hoistway.

explanation: The correct answer is A (It fails, since the disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position): Section 620.51 requires the elevator disconnecting means to be lockable in the open position so maintenance workers can control the hazard. Overload protection and fuses protect the circuit but do not give a worker a means to isolate it. The disconnect is placed in or near the machine room, and a tag alone does not satisfy the lockable provision.

question: Corded saws on a four-story building under construction are plugged into 125 volt, 20 ampere receptacle outlets on a temporary panel, and the framing crew works on wet plywood decks. The superintendent asks what protection those outlets need under the temporary wiring article. What is required?

options.A: Only an assured equipment grounding conductor program, with no GFCI at the panel
options.B: Ground-fault protection of equipment rated at 30 milliamperes on each receptacle circuit
options.C: Ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel on the outlets
options.D: GFCI protection only if the finished building will be a dwelling unit

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the assured grounding program as a replacement for GFCI
distractor_mistakes.B: confuses equipment protection with personnel protection
distractor_mistakes.D: ties the temporary requirement to future occupancy

explanation: The correct answer is C (Ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel on the outlets): Section 590.6 requires ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel on 125 volt, 15, 20 and 30 ampere receptacle outlets used on construction sites. The assured grounding program is an alternative only for outlets the GFCI rule does not cover. Ground-fault protection of equipment trips at 30 milliamperes and protects equipment, not people, so it fails the personnel requirement. Future occupancy does not change what a temporary installation needs.

question: Designing a general care room in a hospital, an engineer must decide which receptacles near a bed need to meet the requirements for the patient care vicinity. How far does the patient care vicinity extend around the bed, horizontally and above the floor?

options.A: 3 feet beyond the bed perimeter horizontally and 7 feet 6 inches above the floor
options.B: 6 feet beyond the bed perimeter horizontally and 6 feet 6 inches above the floor
options.C: 10 feet beyond the bed perimeter horizontally and 8 feet above the floor
options.D: 6 feet beyond the bed perimeter horizontally and 7 feet 6 inches above the floor

distractor_mistakes.A: halves the required horizontal distance from the bed
distractor_mistakes.B: uses a lower vertical height than the rule
distractor_mistakes.C: overstates both the horizontal and vertical dimensions

explanation: The correct answer is D (6 feet beyond the bed perimeter horizontally and 7 feet 6 inches above the floor): The patient care vicinity in Article 517 is the space with surfaces likely to be contacted by the patient or an attendant, extending 6 feet horizontally beyond the bed and 7 feet 6 inches above the floor. Shorter horizontal distances leave receptacles outside the vicinity that should be inside it. Larger values overstate the defined space.

question: Module nameplates on a one-family dwelling's rooftop array list an open-circuit voltage of 38 volts. At the site's lowest expected temperature, the manufacturer's coefficient raises each module's voltage by 12 percent. Keeping one series string within the 600 volt dwelling limit, what is the maximum number of modules?

options.A: 14 modules, from 600 volts divided by 42.56 volts, which is 38 volts raised 12 percent
options.B: 15 modules, from 600 volts divided by the uncorrected 38 volts per module
options.C: 17 modules, from dividing 38 by 1.12 first and then dividing 600 by the result
options.D: 23 modules, from 1,000 volts divided by the corrected 42.56 volts per module

distractor_mistakes.B: Skips the cold-temperature correction.
distractor_mistakes.C: Divides by the correction factor instead of multiplying.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the 1,000 volt limit that does not apply to one-family dwellings.

explanation: The correct answer is A (14 modules, from 600 volts divided by 42.56 volts, which is 38 volts raised 12 percent): The corrected voltage per module is 38 times 1.12, or 42.56 volts. Dividing the 600 volt dwelling limit by 42.56 gives 14.1, so 14 modules is the most that can be placed in series. Using the uncorrected 38 volts gives 15 modules, which would exceed 600 volts on a cold morning. The 1,000 volt limit does not apply to one- and two-family dwellings.

question: A school solar canopy has three parallel PV source circuits, each with a short-circuit current of 9 amperes and a nominal 400 volts, joined at one combiner. The installer sizes the overcurrent device on the combined output circuit. Using 125 percent factors and standard sizes, what rating is the minimum?

options.A: 35 amperes, from 33.75 amperes with the second 125 percent factor omitted
options.B: 45 amperes, from 125 percent of 33.75 amperes, rounded up to a standard size
options.C: 30 amperes, from the 27 ampere total short-circuit current rounded up directly
options.D: 60 amperes, from 125 percent applied three times to the 27 ampere total

distractor_mistakes.A: Applies only one 125 percent factor.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses the raw total Isc with no factors.
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies the 125 percent factor three times.

explanation: The correct answer is B (45 amperes, from 125 percent of 33.75 amperes, rounded up to a standard size): Total short-circuit current is 3 times 9, or 27 amperes. Maximum circuit current is 27 times 1.25, or 33.75 amperes, and the overcurrent device is at least 125 percent of that, or 42.19 amperes. The next standard size above 42.19 is 45 amperes. Stopping after one factor gives 35 amperes, which is undersized.

question: Cows in a dairy barn react to small voltages at the metal stanchions and watering equipment, and the milking area has a concrete floor. The electrician proposes installing an equipotential plane under the 2026 NEC agricultural rules. What is its purpose?

options.A: To serve as the grounding electrode for the whole barn, replacing driven ground rods
options.B: To replace the equipment grounding conductor on the branch circuits serving the barn
options.C: To minimize voltage differences between metal structures and the earth surface contacted by the animals
options.D: To isolate stray voltage by separating the barn grounded conductor from the equipment grounding conductor

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the plane as a replacement grounding electrode
distractor_mistakes.B: treats the plane as a substitute for the equipment grounding conductor
distractor_mistakes.D: confuses an equipotential plane with neutral isolation

explanation: The correct answer is C (To minimize voltage differences between metal structures and the earth surface contacted by the animals): An equipotential plane in livestock areas is a bonded network of conductive elements that keeps metal parts and the surface the animals stand on at nearly the same potential. This lowers the voltage an animal can feel between structures and the ground. It is connected to the grounding system but does not replace the grounding electrode or the equipment grounding conductors. Isolating the neutral is a separate stray voltage measure and does not create a common potential surface.

question: A hospital's Article 700 emergency system must pick up exit lighting and life-safety loads after a normal power failure. The electrician sets the automatic transfer equipment timing and checks the code limit. What is the maximum time allowed for the system to restore power?

options.A: 5 seconds from the loss of normal power
options.B: 10 seconds from the loss of normal power
options.C: 30 seconds from the loss of normal power
options.D: 60 seconds from the loss of normal power

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses an invented shorter limit.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses a longer limit that applies to nothing in Article 700.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the legally required standby limit from Article 701.

explanation: The correct answer is B (10 seconds from the loss of normal power): Emergency systems under Article 700 must make power available within 10 seconds of the interruption of normal supply. The 60 second figure belongs to legally required standby systems in Article 701, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer. Neither 5 nor 30 seconds appears as the emergency system limit.

question: An inspector fails a residential solar installation. The 200 ampere busbar panel is fed by a 200 ampere main breaker, and the installer placed a 60 ampere backfed PV breaker. Under the 120 percent busbar rule, by how many amperes does the PV breaker exceed what is allowed?

options.A: 20 amperes over, since 240 amperes minus the 200 ampere main permits only 40 amperes
options.B: 0 amperes over, since the 60 ampere breaker is far below the 200 ampere busbar rating
options.C: 60 amperes over, using 100 percent of the busbar rating rather than 120 percent
options.D: 10 amperes over, using 125 percent of the busbar rating instead of 120 percent

distractor_mistakes.B: Compares the breaker only to the busbar rating.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses 100 percent of the busbar rating.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses 125 percent instead of 120 percent.

explanation: The correct answer is A (20 amperes over, since 240 amperes minus the 200 ampere main permits only 40 amperes): The sum of all overcurrent devices feeding the busbar may not exceed 120 percent of its rating, or 240 amperes. Subtracting the 200 ampere main leaves 40 amperes available for the PV breaker. A 60 ampere breaker therefore exceeds the limit by 20 amperes. Comparing against the busbar rating alone would wrongly pass it.

question: Three identical 240 volt EVSE units, each with a 32 ampere continuous rating, are installed on one feeder in a parking garage. No energy management system is used. Based on 125 percent of the continuous load, what is the minimum standard overcurrent device for the feeder?

options.A: 100 amperes, from the 96 ampere sum rounded up to a standard size
options.B: 150 amperes, from applying 125 percent to each unit and then again to the sum
options.C: 110 amperes, from 125 percent of one unit plus 100 percent of the other two
options.D: 125 amperes, from 125 percent of 96 amperes, which is 120 amperes

distractor_mistakes.A: Omits the continuous load factor.
distractor_mistakes.B: Applies the 125 percent factor twice.
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the factor to the largest unit only.

explanation: The correct answer is D (125 amperes, from 125 percent of 96 amperes, which is 120 amperes): The three units total 96 amperes. EVSE is a continuous load, so the feeder overcurrent device must be at least 125 percent of that, or 120 amperes, and the next standard size is 125 amperes. Leaving out the factor gives 100 amperes, which is undersized. Applying the factor twice oversizes the device and its conductors.

question: Smoke control fans in a hospital must keep running by law if normal power fails, because their loss could hamper rescue and firefighting, though they are not life-safety emergency loads. The engineer needs the right standby article. Which article covers a legally required standby system of this kind?

options.A: Article 700, covering emergency systems that supply exit lighting and other life-safety loads
options.B: Article 702, covering optional standby systems that an owner installs by choice for convenience
options.C: Article 708, covering critical operations power systems for designated critical operations facilities
options.D: Article 701, covering legally required standby systems that a governmental body requires by law

distractor_mistakes.A: Chooses the emergency system article.
distractor_mistakes.B: Chooses the voluntary standby article.
distractor_mistakes.C: Chooses the critical operations article.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Article 701, covering legally required standby systems that a governmental body requires by law): Article 701 covers legally required standby systems, whose loads are those a governmental body requires to be backed up because their loss could create hazards or hamper rescue and firefighting. Article 700 covers life-safety emergency loads such as exit lighting. Article 702 is for loads the owner chooses to back up, and Article 708 applies to designated critical operations.

question: Easily ignitable lint and flyings collect around the machines in the carding rooms of a cotton textile mill, but they are not normally suspended in the air in amounts that make ignitable mixtures. The inspector assigns a hazardous location class. Which class applies?

options.A: Class I, flammable gases or vapors present in quantities sufficient to produce ignitable mixtures
options.B: Class II, combustible dusts present in quantities sufficient to produce ignitable mixtures
options.C: Class III, easily ignitable fibers and flyings that are not normally airborne in ignitable quantities
options.D: Class IV, combustible fibers present in ignitable quantities near rotating machinery

distractor_mistakes.A: Picks the gas and vapor class.
distractor_mistakes.B: Picks the dust class.
distractor_mistakes.D: Invents a fourth class.

explanation: The correct answer is C (Class III, easily ignitable fibers and flyings that are not normally airborne in ignitable quantities): Class III locations contain easily ignitable fibers or flyings, such as cotton lint and textile fibers, that are not likely to be in suspension in ignitable amounts. Class I covers gases and vapors, and Class II covers combustible dusts. There is no Class IV in the hazardous location classification system.

question: Blending solvents in one room, a plant has classified it Class I, Division 1, and the electrician must choose a wiring method for a new lighting circuit. Several conduit and cable types are on the truck. Which of them is permitted in this location?

options.A: Electrical metallic tubing with compression fittings and listed seals
options.B: Standard Type MC cable with ordinary cable connectors and no hazardous location listing
options.C: Type NM cable with sealed connectors installed in the wall cavity
options.D: Threaded rigid metal conduit with fittings listed for the Division 1 location

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses EMT, which is not a Division 1 method.
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses general-purpose MC cable in a hazardous location.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses a nonmetallic building wiring method.

explanation: The correct answer is D (Threaded rigid metal conduit with fittings listed for the Division 1 location): Class I, Division 1 wiring is limited to methods such as threaded rigid metal conduit, threaded steel intermediate metal conduit, and mineral-insulated cable with listed fittings. EMT and nonmetallic cable are not on the list, and general-purpose MC cable lacks the required construction. Rigid conduit with threaded, listed fittings is the standard answer.

question: Under the 2026 Article 100 definition, an electrician must mount a disconnect where it will be readily accessible. The disconnect sits in a cage secured by a padlock whose key the building manager holds, with no obstacles inside. Which condition still counts as readily accessible?

options.A: Reached by opening a door with a key, needing no ladder, tool or obstacle removal
options.B: Reached after a person lifts a portable ladder into place before climbing to the handle
options.C: Reached after removing several stored cartons stacked directly in front of the enclosure
options.D: Reached by loosening a screw fastened cover with a screwdriver to expose the handle

distractor_mistakes.B: accepts a portable ladder as readily accessible
distractor_mistakes.C: accepts removing obstacles as readily accessible
distractor_mistakes.D: accepts using a tool other than a key

explanation: The correct answer is A (Reached by opening a door with a key, needing no ladder, tool or obstacle removal): The 2026 definition of readily accessible requires that the device be reachable quickly without additional actions such as using tools other than a key, climbing over or under barriers, removing obstacles, or using portable ladders. A key is the one permitted item, so a locked cage that opens with a key still qualifies. Lifting a ladder into place, clearing cartons and removing a cover with a screwdriver each add an action that the definition names as disqualifying.

question: Swimmers at a hotel's energized outdoor pool report a tingling feeling when they touch the metal ladder while standing in the water. The GFCI devices on the pool circuits test normally. What is the most likely installation fault in the pool wiring?

options.A: The feeder neutral and grounding bars are separated in the pool equipment subpanel
options.B: The pool pump motor lacks thermal overload protection on its dedicated branch circuit feeding the pump
options.C: The pump motor frame is bonded to the grid with 10 AWG stranded copper conductor
options.D: The ladder is not connected to the equipotential bonding grid with a solid copper conductor

distractor_mistakes.A: treats the required subpanel separation as a fault
distractor_mistakes.B: blames motor protection for touch voltage
distractor_mistakes.C: focuses on the pump bond instead of the ladder bond

explanation: The correct answer is D (The ladder is not connected to the equipotential bonding grid with a solid copper conductor): Perceptible voltage between a metal ladder and the pool water points to a missing equipotential bond. Section 680.26 requires fixed metal parts such as ladders to be connected to the bonding grid with solid copper conductors not smaller than 8 AWG. Separate neutral and grounding bars in a subpanel are correct practice and do not produce voltage at a ladder. Overload protection protects the motor only, and the pump frame bond does not connect the ladder to the grid.

question: Holiday decorative lighting on trees along a main street is being installed by a town. The public works supervisor asks the inspector how long the temporary wiring may stay in place before removal. What is the permitted period under the temporary wiring article?

options.A: 30 days, counted from the date the lighting is first energized
options.B: 90 days, counted from the date the lighting is first installed
options.C: 180 days, counted from the date the wiring permit is issued
options.D: 1 year, as long as the circuits are protected by GFCI devices

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses a shorter invented period.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses double the allowed period.
distractor_mistakes.D: Allows a full year with protection.

explanation: The correct answer is B (90 days, counted from the date the lighting is first installed): Section 590.3 permits temporary wiring for holiday decorative lighting for no more than 90 days. GFCI protection is required but does not extend that time. Longer periods would need permanent wiring methods, so the 180 day and 1 year options do not apply.

question: Installing wiring in a hospital operating wing, an electrician finds that Article 300 permits a certain installation but Article 517 requires an additional grounding conductor. The scope chapter settles the conflict. Which rule governs under the general scope rules of the code?

options.A: Article 300 governs because Chapter 3 wiring methods override the special occupancy chapters
options.B: Whichever rule is less restrictive governs, so the installation may follow Article 300
options.C: Article 517 applies on top of, or instead of, general rules in Chapters 1 to 4
options.D: The inspector may choose either rule, since both articles are mandatory code text

distractor_mistakes.A: reverses the order of general and special chapters
distractor_mistakes.B: assumes the less restrictive rule governs
distractor_mistakes.D: assumes the inspector picks between conflicting rules

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 517 applies on top of, or instead of, general rules in Chapters 1 to 4): Section 90.3 states that Chapters 5, 6 and 7 supplement or modify the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4. A special occupancy article such as Article 517 therefore adds requirements or replaces general ones, and the extra grounding conductor is mandatory. Chapter 3 does not override Chapter 5, and the code does not let the less restrictive rule win. An inspector interprets the code under Section 90.4 but cannot pick between rules to dodge a stricter one.

question: Several LED signs are being added to a 20 ampere, 120 volt sign branch circuit at a strip mall tenant space. Each sign is rated 480 volt-amperes, and the signs are treated as continuous loads. How many signs can this circuit supply?

options.A: 5 signs, from 2,400 volt-amperes at 100 percent of the circuit rating
options.B: 4 signs, from 80 percent of 2,400 volt-amperes, which is 1,920 volt-amperes
options.C: 3 signs, from applying the 80 percent limit and a 125 percent factor together
options.D: 6 signs, from 120 percent of the 2,400 volt-amperes circuit capacity

distractor_mistakes.A: Ignores the 80 percent continuous loading limit.
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies both the 80 percent limit and the 125 percent factor.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses 120 percent of the capacity.

explanation: The correct answer is B (4 signs, from 80 percent of 2,400 volt-amperes, which is 1,920 volt-amperes): The circuit capacity is 20 times 120, or 2,400 volt-amperes. Sign circuits are loaded to no more than 80 percent, which is 1,920 volt-amperes. Dividing 1,920 by 480 gives exactly 4 signs. Using the full 2,400 gives 5 signs, which overloads the circuit for continuous operation.

question: Reading a drawing at a petrochemical plant, a technician sees an area where ignitable concentrations of flammable gas are present continuously or for long periods. The drawing is part of a design review for new instrumentation. Under the Zone classification system of the code, which zone describes this area?

options.A: Zone 1, where ignitable concentrations are likely during normal operation
options.B: Zone 2, where ignitable concentrations are not likely in normal operation
options.C: Zone 0, where ignitable concentrations are present continuously or for long periods
options.D: Zone 20, where combustible dust clouds are present continuously

distractor_mistakes.A: Picks the likely-in-normal-operation zone.
distractor_mistakes.B: Picks the abnormal-only zone.
distractor_mistakes.D: Picks the dust zone.

explanation: The correct answer is C (Zone 0, where ignitable concentrations are present continuously or for long periods): Zone 0 is defined as a location where ignitable concentrations of flammable gases or vapors are present continuously or for long periods. Zone 1 describes likely presence in normal operation, and Zone 2 describes presence only under abnormal conditions. Zone 20 is the dust equivalent, so it does not fit a gas atmosphere.

question: Nameplate data on an EVSE unit at a dental office gives 40 amperes continuous at 240 volts. The electrician is choosing the overcurrent device for the branch circuit that feeds it. What is the minimum standard rating that can be selected?

options.A: 50 amperes, from 125 percent of the 40 ampere continuous load
options.B: 40 amperes, from 100 percent of the nameplate current
options.C: 60 amperes, from 150 percent of the nameplate current
options.D: 70 amperes, from 125 percent applied twice and rounded to the next size

distractor_mistakes.B: Omits the continuous load factor.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses 150 percent instead of 125 percent.
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies the 125 percent factor twice.

explanation: The correct answer is A (50 amperes, from 125 percent of the 40 ampere continuous load): EVSE is a continuous load, so the branch circuit overcurrent device is at least 125 percent of 40 amperes, which is exactly 50 amperes and a standard size. A 40 ampere device would trip under continuous use. Applying the factor twice yields 62.5 amperes and a 70 ampere device, which is oversized.

question: Balanced at 150 kVA on a three-phase, 480 volt, 60 hertz supply, a care facility's emergency system load is tested by a generator run each month. The electrician needs the full-load current of the load to select transfer equipment. What is it?

options.A: 312 amperes, from 150,000 divided by 480 with no three-phase factor
options.B: 104 amperes, from 150,000 divided by 480 and then divided by 3
options.C: 225 amperes, from applying 125 percent to the calculated full-load current
options.D: 180 amperes, from 150,000 divided by the product of 480 and 1.732

distractor_mistakes.A: Omits the three-phase factor.
distractor_mistakes.B: Divides by 3 instead of using 1.732.
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds a continuous factor to a calculated current.

explanation: The correct answer is D (180 amperes, from 150,000 divided by the product of 480 and 1.732): Three-phase current equals volt-amperes divided by the product of line voltage and 1.732. That is 150,000 divided by 831.4, or about 180 amperes. Omitting the three-phase factor gives 312 amperes, and dividing 312.5 by 3 gives 104 amperes, both clearly different from the correct value.

question: Permanently connected EVSE stands in the parking lot of a shopping center, which is not a dwelling. The site owner is planning the layout of the lot now. Under the 2026 NEC emergency shutoff rule for such equipment, how far from the equipment must the disconnect be located?

options.A: Within sight, not less than 20 feet and not more than 100 feet away
options.B: Within sight, not less than 5 feet and not more than 20 feet away
options.C: Within sight, not less than 50 feet and not more than 200 feet away
options.D: Within sight, and adjacent to the equipment so the operator can reach it quickly

distractor_mistakes.B: uses a much shorter distance range than the rule
distractor_mistakes.C: uses a much longer distance range than the rule
distractor_mistakes.D: requires adjacency instead of a distance range

explanation: The correct answer is A (Within sight, not less than 20 feet and not more than 100 feet away): The 2026 emergency shutoff provision for permanently connected EVSE outside one- and two-family dwellings requires a readily accessible disconnect within sight, at least 20 feet and not more than 100 feet from the equipment. It must be marked, have manual reset, and open all phase conductors together. The distance prevents it from being inside the hazard zone.

question: Designing a PV array, an engineer finds a source circuit nameplate short-circuit current of 11 amperes at a nominal 500 volts. Using the 125 percent factors, what is the minimum conductor ampacity before any temperature or conduit fill adjustments are applied?

options.A: 13.8 amperes, from 125 percent applied once to the short-circuit current
options.B: 17.2 amperes, from 125 percent applied twice to the 11 ampere rating given
options.C: 11.0 amperes, from the nameplate short-circuit current without any factor
options.D: 21.5 amperes, from 125 percent applied three times to the 11 ampere rating

distractor_mistakes.A: applies only one 125 percent factor to the current
distractor_mistakes.C: uses the nameplate short-circuit current directly with no factor
distractor_mistakes.D: applies the 125 percent factor three times

explanation: The correct answer is B (17.2 amperes, from 125 percent applied twice to the 11 ampere rating given): Maximum circuit current is 11 times 1.25, or 13.75 amperes. The conductor must carry 125 percent of that, which is 17.19 amperes, or 17.2 amperes. One factor alone gives 13.8 amperes, which is insufficient, and three factors overstate the requirement.

question: Outside a one-family dwelling, a contractor mounts the emergency disconnect and labels it in black letters on a white plate. The inspector reviews that marking under the 2026 NEC. The house has a meter and main outside on the garage wall. What marking does the code require for this disconnect?

options.A: SERVICE DISCONNECT in black letters on a white background, letters at least 1/4 inch high
options.B: EMERGENCY SHUTOFF in white letters on a red background, letters at least 1/2 inch high
options.C: EMERGENCY DISCONNECT in white letters on a red background, letters at least 1/2 inch high
options.D: EMERGENCY DISCONNECT in white letters on a red background, letters at least 1/4 inch high

distractor_mistakes.A: uses the service disconnect marking for other than dwellings
distractor_mistakes.B: uses the wrong wording for the dwelling marking
distractor_mistakes.D: uses a letter height of 1/4 inch instead of 1/2 inch

explanation: The correct answer is C (EMERGENCY DISCONNECT in white letters on a red background, letters at least 1/2 inch high): For one- and two-family dwellings, the enclosure marking must read EMERGENCY DISCONNECT with white text on a red background and letters at least 1/2 inch high, on the outside front. The 1/4 inch height looks right but falls short of the required size. SERVICE DISCONNECT in black on white is the wording for other than dwelling units, and EMERGENCY SHUTOFF is not the required wording.

question: Nameplate wording on a junction box at a pipeline pumping station reads Class I, Group B, Division 1. The purchaser asks which kind of atmosphere the enclosure is suitable for. The nameplate is on the enclosure cover in plain view. What does Group B represent in the classification system?

options.A: Atmospheres containing hydrogen, which belongs to Group B
options.B: Atmospheres containing acetylene, which belongs to Group B
options.C: Atmospheres containing ethylene, which belongs to Group B
options.D: Atmospheres containing gasoline and propane, which belong to Group B

distractor_mistakes.B: Mixes up Group A and Group B.
distractor_mistakes.C: Mixes up Group C and Group B.
distractor_mistakes.D: Mixes up Group D and Group B.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Atmospheres containing hydrogen, which belongs to Group B): Class I groups are A for acetylene, B for hydrogen, C for ethylene and D for gasoline and propane. Equipment marked Group B is suitable for hydrogen atmospheres. Acetylene is Group A, ethylene is Group C, and the common fuels belong to Group D.

question: On a three-phase, 208 volt, 60 hertz system, an emergency panel carries a balanced 120 ampere load, and the owner plans a standby generator. What kVA is required for the load alone, with no allowance for future growth added to it?

options.A: 25.0 kVA, from 120 amperes times 208 volts without the three-phase factor
options.B: 43.2 kVA, from 120 amperes times 208 volts times 1.732
options.C: 28.8 kVA, from 120 amperes times 240 volts as a single-phase load
options.D: 74.9 kVA, from 120 amperes times 208 volts times 3

distractor_mistakes.A: Omits the three-phase factor.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses single-phase 240 volts.
distractor_mistakes.D: Multiplies by 3 instead of 1.732.

explanation: The correct answer is B (43.2 kVA, from 120 amperes times 208 volts times 1.732): Three-phase kVA equals line current times line voltage times 1.732, divided by 1,000. With 120 amperes at 208 volts, that is 43.2 kVA. Omitting the 1.732 factor gives 25.0 kVA, and multiplying by 3 gives 74.9 kVA, which is far too large.

question: Weddings and concerts are held in a church hall designed for 250 people, with a raised stage for a small band. The electrician asks which article governs wiring for the gathering space itself. The building has a fixed stage and a sound system as well. Which article applies to the hall?

options.A: Article 518, assembly occupancies designed for the gathering of 100 or more persons
options.B: Article 520, theaters and similar locations, since a stage is present
options.C: Article 525, carnivals and fairs, since events are temporary gatherings
options.D: Article 540, motion picture projection rooms, since sound equipment is used

distractor_mistakes.B: Picks the theater article.
distractor_mistakes.C: Picks the temporary event article.
distractor_mistakes.D: Picks the projection room article.

explanation: The correct answer is A (Article 518, assembly occupancies designed for the gathering of 100 or more persons): Article 518 covers buildings or portions designed or intended for the gathering of 100 or more persons for purposes such as worship, entertainment or recreation. A 250 person hall fits. Article 520 applies to theaters and performance areas in addition, but the hall itself is the assembly occupancy.

question: Sizing the overcurrent device for a PV source circuit with a short-circuit current of 8 amperes, a designer applies the 125 percent factors and chooses the next standard size. The array uses typical crystalline silicon modules and no combiner. What rating is selected for the device?

options.A: 10 amperes, from 125 percent applied once to the 8 ampere short-circuit current
options.B: 20 amperes, from 125 percent applied three times and rounded up
options.C: 15 amperes, from 8 amperes times 1.25 times 1.25, rounded up to the next size
options.D: 8 amperes, using the nameplate short-circuit current with no multiplier applied

distractor_mistakes.A: applies only one 125 percent factor to the current
distractor_mistakes.B: applies the 125 percent factor three times
distractor_mistakes.D: uses the nameplate short-circuit current directly

explanation: The correct answer is C (15 amperes, from 8 amperes times 1.25 times 1.25, rounded up to the next size): Maximum circuit current is 8 times 1.25, or 10 amperes. The overcurrent device is at least 125 percent of that, or 12.5 amperes, and the next standard size is 15 amperes. A single factor gives 10 amperes, which would trip under full sun on a continuous basis.

question: For a pool lighting system supplied through an isolating transformer, the inspector asks what voltage the code defines as the low-voltage contact limit in Article 680. The pool is a permanently installed outdoor residential unit. What is that limit, and what does it represent for a swimmer?

options.A: 12 volts rms, the maximum considered safe for contact by the swimmer
options.B: 15 volts rms, the maximum considered safe for contact by the swimmer
options.C: 30 volts rms, the maximum considered safe for contact by the swimmer
options.D: 50 volts rms, the maximum considered safe for contact by the swimmer

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the common lamp voltage.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses double the limit.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the general shock threshold.

explanation: The correct answer is B (15 volts rms, the maximum considered safe for contact by the swimmer): Article 680 defines the low-voltage contact limit as 15 volts rms for sinusoidal alternating current. Lighting at or below that limit, supplied through a listed isolating transformer, is treated differently from higher-voltage lighting. Twelve volts is a common lamp rating but not the code limit.

question: Emergency lighting of 600 watts must run for the minimum duration the emergency systems article requires, and the battery system can use only 80 percent of its rated capacity. The loads are all connected to an Article 700 emergency branch circuit. What battery capacity in watt-hours must the system have?

options.A: 900 watt-hours, from 600 watts times 1.5 hours with no capacity allowance
options.B: 720 watt-hours, from multiplying 900 watt-hours by 80 percent
options.C: 540 watt-hours, from 600 watts times 0.9 hours
options.D: 1,125 watt-hours, from 900 watt-hours divided by 0.80 usable capacity

distractor_mistakes.A: ignores the usable capacity of the battery
distractor_mistakes.B: multiplies by 0.80 instead of dividing by it
distractor_mistakes.C: reads 90 minutes as 0.9 hours

explanation: The correct answer is D (1,125 watt-hours, from 900 watt-hours divided by 0.80 usable capacity): The emergency lighting duration is 90 minutes, or 1.5 hours, so the energy required is 600 times 1.5, or 900 watt-hours. Only 80 percent of the rating is usable, so the capacity is 900 divided by 0.80, which is 1,125 watt-hours. Multiplying by 0.80 reduces the capacity when it should increase it.

question: Two identical 300 watt, 12 volt underwater luminaires share one listed isolating transformer in a pool. The electrician needs the load current on the transformer secondary to check the conductors. Both luminaires are wired in parallel on the secondary side. What is that current?

options.A: 25 amperes, from 300 watts divided by 12 volts for a single luminaire
options.B: 5 amperes, from 600 watts divided by the 120 volt primary supply
options.C: 62.5 amperes, from 125 percent applied to the 50 ampere secondary current
options.D: 50 amperes, from the combined 600 watts divided by the 12 volt secondary

distractor_mistakes.A: Counts only one luminaire.
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses the primary voltage.
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds a continuous factor to a load current.

explanation: The correct answer is D (50 amperes, from the combined 600 watts divided by the 12 volt secondary): Two luminaires draw 600 watts together. At 12 volts, secondary current is 600 divided by 12, or 50 amperes. Using one luminaire gives 25 amperes, and using the 120 volt primary gives 5 amperes, which is the primary current rather than the secondary load.

question: After a rapid shutdown is initiated on a PV system, the inspector measures voltage on controlled conductors outside the array boundary. The array is mounted on a commercial roof with module-level devices. Under the rapid shutdown rule, what must those conductors be reduced to, and in what time?

options.A: 30 volts or less, within 10 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown
options.B: 30 volts or less, within 30 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown
options.C: 80 volts or less, within 30 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown
options.D: 50 volts or less, within 60 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the emergency system transfer time.
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses the array-interior voltage limit.
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses a different voltage and time.

explanation: The correct answer is B (30 volts or less, within 30 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown): Controlled conductors outside the array boundary must be reduced to 30 volts or less within 30 seconds of rapid shutdown initiation. The 80 volt limit applies to conductors inside the array boundary under the rule. The 10 second time is an emergency system transfer value, not a PV requirement.

question: Inspecting a homeowner's rooftop PV system that also charges a wall-mounted lithium battery bank, the inspector notes the battery enclosure has no rapid shutdown initiation switch of its own, although the roof array has one. Does the missing switch on the battery enclosure make the installation noncompliant?

options.A: Yes, every energy source tied to the inverter needs its own rapid shutdown initiation switch.
options.B: No, rapid shutdown covers PV conductors, and the battery follows its own Article 706 disconnect rules.
options.C: Yes, because any dc source above 30 volts nominal falls under the PV rapid shutdown rule.
options.D: No, because the array's rapid shutdown switch also serves as the battery's required disconnecting means.

distractor_mistakes.A: Treats rapid shutdown as applying to every energy source on the inverter
distractor_mistakes.C: Extends a PV rule to any dc source above 30 volts
distractor_mistakes.D: Assumes one PV switch satisfies the separate storage disconnect rule

explanation: The correct answer is B (No, rapid shutdown covers PV conductors, and the battery follows its own Article 706 disconnect rules.): Rapid shutdown in Article 690 is aimed at PV system conductors that stay energized on or in a building. A battery is an energy storage system, so Article 706 governs it and requires its own disconnecting means. The inspector cannot cite the battery for lacking a PV rapid shutdown switch. The tempting answer that the PV switch doubles as the battery disconnect fails because each source has its own disconnect requirement.

question: During final inspection, a 7.68 kW single-phase 240 volt inverter's output circuit was found protected by a 40 ampere breaker and wired with 10 AWG THWN-2 copper, and the inspector failed it. All terminals are rated 75 degrees C. What is the minimum copper conductor size that corrects the installation?

options.A: 10 AWG, using the 90 degree column value of 40 amperes against the 40 ampere breaker.
options.B: 10 AWG, since 32 amperes fits the 35 ampere 75 degree column value.
options.C: 6 AWG, applying 125 percent twice and reading the 60 degree column for 50 amperes.
options.D: 8 AWG, since 125 percent of 32 amperes is 40, matching the 75 degree column.

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the 90 degree column even though terminals are rated 75 degrees
distractor_mistakes.B: Skips the 125 percent factor and compares 32 amperes to 35 amperes
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies 125 percent twice and uses the 60 degree column

explanation: The correct answer is D (8 AWG, since 125 percent of 32 amperes is 40, matching the 75 degree column.): Inverter output current is 7,680 watts divided by 240 volts, or 32 amperes. The output circuit is sized at 125 percent of that current, which is 40 amperes, so the conductor must carry at least 40 amperes at the 75 degree terminal rating. In Table 310.16 the 75 degree column gives 35 amperes for 10 AWG and 50 amperes for 8 AWG. The 90 degree value of 40 amperes for 10 AWG cannot be used because the terminals limit the conductor to the 75 degree column.

question: Bidirectional inverters that feed a battery bank and also operate in parallel with the utility raise two permit questions: the energy storage disconnecting means and the utility interconnection point. Which two articles of the 2026 NEC govern these two items in the contractor's design?

options.A: Article 690 for the storage system and Article 710 for the stand-alone interconnection point.
options.B: Article 692 for the storage system and Article 705 for the interconnection point.
options.C: Article 706 for the storage system and Article 694 for the interconnection point.
options.D: Article 706 for the storage system and Article 705 for the interconnected power source.

distractor_mistakes.A: Assigns the PV article to storage and the stand-alone article to interconnection
distractor_mistakes.B: Assigns the fuel cell article to a battery system
distractor_mistakes.C: Assigns the wind article to the utility interconnection

explanation: The correct answer is D (Article 706 for the storage system and Article 705 for the interconnected power source.): Article 706 covers energy storage systems, including their disconnecting means. Article 705 covers interconnected electric power production sources that operate in parallel with a primary source such as the utility. Article 690 is for photovoltaic systems, 692 is for fuel cells, 694 is for wind systems, and 710 is for stand-alone systems. A bidirectional inverter with a battery and a utility tie therefore points to Articles 706 and 705.

question: Upstream of the main service disconnect, an electrician ties a listed inverter output into the service conductors using listed connectors inside a service enclosure. The inspector must classify this connection under Article 705 for the permit file. What is this connection type called?

options.A: A load side connection, made at the busbar of a panelboard fed by the service.
options.B: A feeder tap connection, made with a ten foot tap conductor length limit.
options.C: A supply side connection, made ahead of the service disconnecting means.
options.D: A dedicated branch connection, made through a breaker serving only that inverter.

distractor_mistakes.A: Calls an upstream connection a load side connection
distractor_mistakes.B: Confuses interconnection with a feeder tap rule
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats a dedicated breaker as the supply side method

explanation: The correct answer is C (A supply side connection, made ahead of the service disconnecting means.): Article 705 recognizes supply side connections, made on the service conductors ahead of the service disconnecting means, and load side connections made downstream. The connection described attaches ahead of the main disconnect, so it is a supply side connection. A load side connection would use a breaker or busbar in a panelboard, which is where the busbar rating limit applies. A feeder tap is a separate Article 240 concept.

question: At noon, a crew finishes installing a roof array and opens the dc disconnect for a final check. A meter on the array side conductors between modules and disconnect still reads 400 volts, yet a helper calls the circuit dead because the disconnect is open. What is the correct safety conclusion?

options.A: Treat them as de-energized, since opening the disconnect isolates the entire PV source circuit.
options.B: Treat the array side conductors as energized, since lit modules produce voltage.
options.C: Treat them as de-energized after the 30 second rapid shutdown decay time has elapsed.
options.D: Treat them as energized only if the inverter is still connected to the utility.

distractor_mistakes.A: Believes the open disconnect de-energizes the array side
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the rapid shutdown decay time to conductors inside the array
distractor_mistakes.D: Ties module voltage to the utility connection

explanation: The correct answer is B (Treat the array side conductors as energized, since lit modules produce voltage.): A PV module generates voltage whenever it is lit, and opening a disconnect downstream does not stop the modules from energizing the conductors on the array side. The meter reading proves the conductors are live. The rapid shutdown decay limits apply to controlled conductors outside the array boundary, not to conductors inside the array. Utility connection has no effect on module output.

question: Far from the service equipment, at the roof hatch of a commercial building, sits the disconnecting means of a PV system, while the utility service is in the electrical room. The inspector asks what the code requires at the service disconnecting means so first responders can find the PV disconnect. What is required?

options.A: A permanent plaque or directory showing the location of the PV system disconnecting means.
options.B: A label stating the maximum ac output current of the PV inverter only.
options.C: A label stating the maximum ac output current and nameplate rating of the PV inverter.
options.D: A warning label stating the array can be turned off by rapid shutdown only.

distractor_mistakes.B: Posts an inverter current label instead of a location plaque
distractor_mistakes.C: Places a diagram at the roof instead of a plaque at the service
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses a rapid shutdown warning instead of a location directory

explanation: The correct answer is A (A permanent plaque or directory showing the location of the PV system disconnecting means.): When the PV disconnect is not at the same location as the service disconnect, a plaque or directory at the service equipment must show where the PV disconnect is, so responders can locate every source. Current ratings and diagrams do not meet that requirement. A rapid shutdown label has its own purpose and does not tell anyone where the PV disconnect is mounted.

question: Where a PV system's dc conductors must follow a rule in Article 690 that differs from a general wiring rule in Chapter 3, the inspector asks which one governs. Under the NEC's chapter structure, how do the rules in Article 690 relate to the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4?

options.A: Chapter 3 governs the installation, since wiring method rules override any special equipment article.
options.B: The more restrictive rule governs, whichever chapter it appears in.
options.C: Article 690 supplements or modifies the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4 for PV systems.
options.D: Chapter 9 tables govern, since they apply to every installation.

distractor_mistakes.A: Believes general wiring rules override special equipment articles
distractor_mistakes.B: Applies a most-restrictive tiebreaker the code does not state
distractor_mistakes.D: Treats Chapter 9 tables as the controlling authority

explanation: The correct answer is C (Article 690 supplements or modifies the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4 for PV systems.): Chapters 5, 6 and 7 supplement or modify the general rules in Chapters 1 through 4, and Article 690 sits in Chapter 6. Where Article 690 gives a specific PV rule, it modifies the general rule. Chapter 3 does not override a special equipment article. Chapter 9 tables apply only where another rule refers to them, so they do not decide which article prevails.

question: Continuous output current of 80 amperes flows from a battery energy storage system to the inverter through 75 degrees C terminals. The designer sizes the conductor at 125 percent of the continuous current using Table 310.16 copper values, and no other circuits share the raceway. What is the minimum conductor size?

options.A: 4 AWG, because 85 amperes in the 75 degree column covers 80 amperes without a factor.
options.B: 1 AWG, applying 125 percent twice to reach 125 amperes in the 75 degree column.
options.C: 3 AWG, since 125 percent of 80 amperes is 100, matching the 75 degree column.
options.D: 2 AWG, reading the 60 degree column because 95 amperes is closest to 100 amperes.

distractor_mistakes.A: Skips the 125 percent continuous factor
distractor_mistakes.B: Applies the 125 percent factor twice
distractor_mistakes.D: Reads the 60 degree column and picks the closest value

explanation: The correct answer is C (3 AWG, since 125 percent of 80 amperes is 100, matching the 75 degree column.): A continuous load requires conductor ampacity of at least 125 percent of the current, so 80 amperes times 1.25 equals 100 amperes. In the 75 degree column of Table 310.16, 4 AWG carries 85 amperes, 3 AWG carries 100 amperes and 2 AWG carries 115 amperes. The smallest size meeting 100 amperes is 3 AWG. Using 4 AWG ignores the continuous factor.

question: Once a rapid shutdown switch has been activated on a roof array, an installer measures the controlled conductors located more than one foot outside the array boundary. Under Article 690 as written for the 2026 NEC, what voltage limit applies and within what time?

options.A: 80 volts or less within 10 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown.
options.B: 30 volts or less within 60 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown.
options.C: 80 volts or less within 30 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown.
options.D: 30 volts or less within 30 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown.

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the shorter 10 second time with the inside-boundary voltage
distractor_mistakes.B: Stretches the time limit to 60 seconds
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses the inside-boundary 80 volt limit for outside conductors

explanation: The correct answer is D (30 volts or less within 30 seconds of initiating rapid shutdown.): For controlled conductors outside the array boundary, the limit is 30 volts within 30 seconds. The 80 volt within 30 second limit applies to conductors inside the array boundary, which is the tempting wrong choice here. The other choices mix up the voltage or the time. The measurement location, more than one foot outside the boundary, decides which limit applies.

question: Exposed live parts on the equipment side of the working space and a grounded concrete wall directly opposite describe a utility room housing a 480Y/277 volt battery inverter. The installer must provide working space depth under Table 110.26(A)(1). What is the minimum depth for this condition?

options.A: 3 feet, which is the Condition 1 distance for 151 to 600 volts.
options.B: 4 feet, which is the Condition 3 distance for 151 to 600 volts.
options.C: 3 feet 6 inches, which is the Condition 2 distance for 151 to 600 volts.
options.D: 30 inches, which is the minimum working space width in front of equipment.

distractor_mistakes.A: Uses the Condition 1 depth for a grounded opposite wall
distractor_mistakes.B: Uses the Condition 3 depth meant for live parts on both sides
distractor_mistakes.D: Confuses the 30 inch width minimum with the depth

explanation: The correct answer is C (3 feet 6 inches, which is the Condition 2 distance for 151 to 600 volts.): Live parts on one side of the working space and grounded parts, such as concrete, on the other is Condition 2. For 151 to 600 volts to ground, Condition 2 requires 3 feet 6 inches of depth. Condition 1 gives 3 feet and Condition 3, with live parts on both sides, gives 4 feet. The 30 inch figure is a width requirement, not a depth.

question: Owner of a house with a 200 ampere busbar fed by a 200 ampere main breaker wants a 60 ampere PV backfeed installed. Without replacing the main breaker or the panelboard, which installation approach complies with the NEC and avoids exceeding the busbar rating allowance for the combined source breakers?

options.A: Install the 60 ampere backfed breaker at the end of the busbar opposite the main.
options.B: Make a supply side connection ahead of the service disconnecting means, which avoids the busbar limit.
options.C: Connect through a 60 ampere panelboard breaker, since inverter breakers are exempt from the busbar rule.
options.D: Tap the inverter circuit onto the load side of the main using a ten foot tap.

distractor_mistakes.A: Places the breaker at the opposite end without checking the total
distractor_mistakes.C: Believes inverter breakers are exempt from the busbar calculation
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies a feeder tap rule to an interconnection

explanation: The correct answer is B (Make a supply side connection ahead of the service disconnecting means, which avoids the busbar limit.): The panelboard allows 120 percent of 200, or 240 amperes, so the main plus the PV breaker may total 240 amperes. The main and a 60 ampere breaker total 260 amperes, which exceeds that limit even at the opposite end. A supply side connection is made ahead of the service disconnect, so the busbar rating calculation does not apply. Inverter breakers are not exempt from the busbar rule.

question: Fed by a 200 ampere main breaker at one end, a panelboard has a 225 ampere busbar. A PV inverter will backfeed through a breaker installed at the opposite end of the busbar. Applying the 120 percent busbar rule, what is the largest PV breaker that complies with that rule?

options.A: 45 amperes, subtracting the 225 ampere busbar rating from 120 percent of it.
options.B: 70 amperes, subtracting the 200 ampere main from 120 percent of 225 amperes.
options.C: 25 amperes, subtracting the main breaker from the busbar rating without the 120 percent factor.
options.D: 40 amperes, subtracting the main breaker from 120 percent of the 200 ampere main.

distractor_mistakes.A: Subtracts the busbar rating instead of the main breaker
distractor_mistakes.C: Leaves out the 120 percent factor
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies 120 percent to the main breaker instead of the busbar

explanation: The correct answer is B (70 amperes, subtracting the 200 ampere main from 120 percent of 225 amperes.): The allowable total is 120 percent of the busbar rating: 225 times 1.2 equals 270 amperes. Subtracting the 200 ampere main leaves 70 amperes for the PV breaker, which is a standard size. Subtracting the bus rating instead of the main gives 45 amperes, and omitting the 120 percent factor gives only 25 amperes. Using the main rating as the base gives 40 amperes.

question: Remote cabin owners often ask how an off-grid system is classified. This cabin has a PV array, a battery bank and an inverter with no utility connection, and the electrician needs the article covering the premises wiring supplied by this isolated power source. Which article applies?

options.A: Article 705, which covers interconnected electric power production sources.
options.B: Article 692, which covers fuel cell systems and their output circuits.
options.C: Article 694, which covers small and large wind electric systems.
options.D: Article 710, which covers stand-alone systems that supply premises wiring.

distractor_mistakes.A: Applies the interconnected source article to an isolated system
distractor_mistakes.B: Picks the fuel cell article
distractor_mistakes.C: Picks the wind article

explanation: The correct answer is D (Article 710, which covers stand-alone systems that supply premises wiring.): A system that never connects to a utility and serves loads on its own is a stand-alone system, covered by Article 710. Article 705 applies when a source operates in parallel with another source such as the utility. Articles 692 and 694 address fuel cells and wind systems, which this cabin does not use. The PV array and battery still follow Articles 690 and 706 for their own parts.

question: Running through a conduit into a dwelling, a rooftop PV source circuit operates at a maximum system voltage of 400 volts dc. The inspector asks which protection requirement applies to this circuit under Article 690 before signing off the rough-in. What is required for the circuit?

options.A: Listed dc arc-fault circuit protection, because the circuit operates at 80 volts dc or more.
options.B: Ground-fault circuit interrupter protection rated for 5 milliamperes, because the circuit runs on a dwelling roof.
options.C: Listed dc arc-fault protection only if the circuit enters the building through a raceway.
options.D: Arc-fault protection only above 150 volts dc, the voltage breakpoint used for ground-fault rules.

distractor_mistakes.B: Swaps ground-fault personnel protection for arc-fault protection
distractor_mistakes.C: Ties arc-fault protection to the raceway entry
distractor_mistakes.D: Uses the wrong voltage breakpoint of 150 volts

explanation: The correct answer is A (Listed dc arc-fault circuit protection, because the circuit operates at 80 volts dc or more.): Article 690 requires dc arc-fault circuit protection for PV circuits operating at 80 volts dc or more between any two conductors. A 400 volt circuit is well above that threshold. How the circuit enters the building does not change the requirement. A 5 milliampere GFCI is a personnel protection device used on receptacle circuits, not a PV arc-fault answer.

question: Keeping a dwelling PV system under 600 volts is the designer's goal. Each module has an open-circuit voltage of 41.0 volts at 25 degrees C, and the coldest expected temperature gives a correction factor of 1.14. All modules are in one series string. How many modules may be placed in the string?

options.A: 14 modules, dividing 600 volts by 41.0 volts per module without the temperature correction.
options.B: 13 modules, rounding 12.84 up to the next whole module.
options.C: 10 modules, applying 125 percent to the corrected module voltage before dividing.
options.D: 12 modules, since 12 times 46.74 volts is 561 volts and 13 would exceed 600 volts.

distractor_mistakes.A: Ignores the cold temperature correction factor
distractor_mistakes.B: Rounds the quotient up instead of down
distractor_mistakes.C: Adds a 125 percent factor to the corrected voltage

explanation: The correct answer is D (12 modules, since 12 times 46.74 volts is 561 volts and 13 would exceed 600 volts.): The corrected voltage per module is 41.0 times 1.14, or 46.74 volts. Dividing 600 by 46.74 gives 12.84, so only 12 whole modules fit. Thirteen modules would total 607.6 volts, over the limit. Skipping the correction gives 14, and adding a 125 percent factor gives 10 modules, both wrong methods.

question: Selecting the mounting location for the PV system disconnecting means on a single family dwelling, a solar contractor reviews Article 690, which gives a specific accessibility requirement so personnel can operate the disconnect without special equipment. What requirement governs the location of this disconnect?

options.A: Within 6 feet of the array on the roof, where the conductors first leave it.
options.B: A readily accessible location, reached without climbing over obstacles or using ladders.
options.C: Only inside the building at the point where the conductors enter.
options.D: Within sight of the utility meter and no more than 10 feet from it.

distractor_mistakes.A: Places the disconnect on the roof at the array
distractor_mistakes.C: Requires an indoor location the code does not require
distractor_mistakes.D: Ties the disconnect to the meter location

explanation: The correct answer is B (A readily accessible location, reached without climbing over obstacles or using ladders.): The PV disconnecting means must be installed at a readily accessible location. By definition that means it can be reached quickly without climbing over or removing obstacles or using a portable ladder. The code does not fix it at 6 feet from the array, require it indoors, or tie it to the meter. A roof mounted disconnect that needs a ladder fails the rule.

question: Fed by a 200 ampere main breaker at the top of a panelboard, a 200 ampere busbar will receive a 40 ampere PV backfeed breaker, which fits within 120 percent of the busbar rating. The installer must choose a position. Where must the breaker be installed so the calculation applies?

options.A: At the end of the busbar opposite from the main breaker's feed point.
options.B: Directly adjacent to the main breaker, where bus current is lowest.
options.C: In the middle of the busbar, since either end gives the same result.
options.D: At any position, because the 120 percent figure already protects the busbar.

distractor_mistakes.B: Places the backfeed beside the main breaker
distractor_mistakes.C: Treats middle and end positions as equal
distractor_mistakes.D: Believes the percentage alone makes position irrelevant

explanation: The correct answer is A (At the end of the busbar opposite from the main breaker's feed point.): The 120 percent allowance depends on the busbar being fed from opposite ends, so the PV breaker is placed at the end farthest from the main breaker. Next to the main, bus loading can exceed the busbar rating. The middle position does not satisfy the location condition, and the percentage by itself does not remove the location rule.

question: Sizing a service for an added PV system, an electrician searches Article 220 of the 2026 NEC for the standard load calculation rules and cannot find them. Where do the branch-circuit, feeder and service load calculation rules now appear in this edition of the code?

options.A: In Article 230, which absorbed the load calculation rules after Article 220 was deleted.
options.B: In Article 120, which received the relocated load calculation content from former Article 220.
options.C: In Article 210, which now contains the feeder and service demand factor tables.
options.D: In Article 235, which was renamed for branch-circuit, feeder and service calculations.

distractor_mistakes.A: Assumes the services article absorbed the calculations
distractor_mistakes.C: Assumes the branch circuit article holds the demand tables
distractor_mistakes.D: Picks a deleted article as the renamed one

explanation: The correct answer is B (In Article 120, which received the relocated load calculation content from former Article 220.): In the 2026 edition, Article 220 became Article 120, titled for branch-circuit, feeder and service load calculations. Article 235 was deleted, with its over 1,000 volt content split into new articles, so it is not the answer. Articles 210 and 230 cover branch circuits and services but did not take over the calculation rules.

question: Short-circuit current of 12 amperes flows in a PV source circuit that runs to the inverter on 75 degrees C terminals. The designer sizes the conductor using the 125 percent factor for maximum current and again for continuous duty. What minimum conductor ampacity is required before adjustment?

options.A: 15 amperes, applying 125 percent to the short-circuit current only one time.
options.B: 18.75 amperes, applying 125 percent to the short-circuit current and again to that result.
options.C: 12 amperes, using the short-circuit current with no factors applied.
options.D: 24 amperes, doubling the short-circuit current of the string.

distractor_mistakes.A: Applies the 125 percent factor only once
distractor_mistakes.C: Uses the short-circuit current with no factors
distractor_mistakes.D: Doubles the current instead of using the two factors

explanation: The correct answer is B (18.75 amperes, applying 125 percent to the short-circuit current and again to that result.): Maximum PV circuit current is the short-circuit current times 125 percent, which is 15 amperes. Conductors and overcurrent devices are sized at another 125 percent of that, giving 12 times 1.25 times 1.25, or 18.75 amperes. Applying the factor only once gives 15 amperes, and using the raw 12 amperes ignores both factors. Doubling the current has no basis in the code.

question: Voltage drop of 4.2 percent at full output is shown by the designer's calculation for a PV home-run circuit 190 feet long. The inspector points to the 3 percent recommendation in an informational note and demands a larger conductor. Can the inspector require the larger conductor on that basis?

options.A: Yes, because informational notes carry the same enforcement force as mandatory rules.
options.B: No, because informational notes are explanatory material and not enforceable requirements.
options.C: Yes, because exceeding 3 percent at any length makes the conductor undersized under mandatory text.
options.D: No, because voltage drop limits are enforced only for feeders and not for dc circuits.

distractor_mistakes.A: treats informational notes as enforceable requirements
distractor_mistakes.C: treats the recommendation as a mandatory sizing limit
distractor_mistakes.D: limits voltage drop guidance to feeders

explanation: The correct answer is B (No, because informational notes are explanatory material and not enforceable requirements.): Informational notes are explanatory and are not enforceable as code requirements. The 3 percent figure is a recommendation for performance, not a mandatory limit, so the inspector cannot demand a larger conductor on that basis. Voltage drop is not a mandatory sizing limit in any circuit length, so claiming undersizing under mandatory text misreads where the figure appears. The feeder-only claim also misstates the note, which addresses branch circuits as well.

question: Large-scale PV electric supply stations are covered by their own article, and an engineer reviewing a solar farm design asks which article that is and what minimum generating capacity brings a project under it. Which choice correctly names the article and the capacity threshold?

options.A: Article 691, which applies at 5,000 kilowatts or more of generating capacity.
options.B: Article 691, which applies at 1,000 kilowatts or more of total generating capacity.
options.C: Article 690, which applies once an array exceeds 500 kilowatts of capacity.
options.D: Article 705, which applies once a source exceeds 2,500 kilowatts of capacity.

distractor_mistakes.B: Names the right article with a 1,000 kilowatt threshold
distractor_mistakes.C: Applies the general PV article with an invented cutoff
distractor_mistakes.D: Applies the interconnection article with an invented capacity

explanation: The correct answer is A (Article 691, which applies at 5,000 kilowatts or more of generating capacity.): Article 691 covers large-scale PV electric supply stations with a generating capacity of no less than 5,000 kilowatts. Article 690 covers PV systems in general and has no 500 kilowatt cutoff. Article 705 covers interconnection of power sources and has no capacity trigger like the one stated. The 1,000 kilowatt choice names the right article with the wrong threshold.

question: On the nameplate of an inverter, the maximum continuous ac output current is listed as 48 amperes at 240 volts. Under Article 690, the output circuit overcurrent device is sized at no less than 125 percent of that current. What is the smallest standard breaker rating that complies?

options.A: 50 amperes, rounding the 48 ampere nameplate current up to the next size.
options.B: 80 amperes, applying 125 percent twice to reach 75 amperes, then moving up a size
options.C: 40 amperes, using 80 percent of the nameplate current before sizing up
options.D: 60 amperes, since 125 percent of 48 amperes is exactly 60, a standard rating
